profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-05T09:49:48.005+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Later scholars [of] Tiāntái.
Zhōu (Guō Wēi) considered himself a descendant of Zhōu Guó Shū.
During the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods,
records state that the descendants of Guó Shū who established a state were known as Guó Gōng,
later called Guō Gōng.
Guó and Guō are close in pronunciation.
Yú’s grand master Gōng Zhīqí said: Guó Zhòng and Guó Shū
were King Jì’s younger sons.
The Guō surname originated from Zhōu;
thus, the state was named Zhōu,
and the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn consequently refers to it as the Later Zhōu.
In the 1st year of Guǎngshùn (Xīnhài, 951)
spring,
the 1st month,
on the dìngmǎo day,
the Hàn empress dowager issued an edict
granting the regent the imperial seals
and to immediately ascend the imperial throne.
The regent entered the palace through Gāomén.
Gāomén
is the name of a village outside Daliáng City.
The imperial decree stated:
"I am a descendant of the Zhōu house,
a scion of Guó Shū.
The state name should appropriately be Zhōu."
The era name was changed,
and a general amnesty was proclaimed.
Yáng Bīn, Shǐ Hóngzhào, Wáng Zhāng, and others were all posthumously granted official titles,
and officials were ordered to arrange their burials.
The deaths of Yáng Bīn and others are mentioned in the previous year of the preceding volume.
為 (wéi)
is pronounced yúwěi (yúwěi) fan.
斂 (liǎn)
is pronounced lìshàn (lìshàn) fan.
All officials in charge of collecting goods at granaries, storehouses, and treasuries
were forbidden from taking "dǒuyú" or "chēnghào."
Dǒuyú means
taking extra beyond the standard measure.
It refers to taking a surplus.
Chēnghào means
taking extra beyond the calculated amount in catties, jun, or shi,
as an allowance for spoilage or loss.
Now all of these are abolished,
correcting the abuses of Wáng Zhāng's harsh levies.
稱 (chēng)
is pronounced chǐzhèng (chǐzhèng) fan.
All were completely abolished.
Those who committed theft and adultery
were to be judged according to the penalties in place before the 1st year of Tiānfú of the Jìn dynasty.
Except for treason, criminals
were not to have their relatives punished
or their family property confiscated.
This corrected the abuses of Shǐ Hóngzhào's cruel punishments.
The staff and palace women of the Hàn Gāozǔ mausoleum,
as well as the mausoleum guards, were to remain as before, performing monthly offerings and sacrifices.
Originally,
during the decline of the Táng dynasty,
there were many bandits,
and the regular laws were not used.
Instead, severe laws were enacted:
those who stole goods worth three bolts of silk were put to death.
During the Tiānfú period of the Jìn dynasty,
this was increased to five bolts.
For adultery with a married woman,
regardless of whether it was by force or consent,
both the man and woman were put to death.
By "force" (qiáng)
is meant when a man used power and might against a woman,
and the woman was compelled to commit adultery with him.
By "consent" (hé)
is meant when a man and woman mutually desired each other,
and lust arose leading to adultery.
For theft, anything above one cash resulted in death.
Moreover, for crimes other than treason,
often entire clans were executed and their property confiscated.
Therefore, upon the emperor's ascension,
he first reformed these abuses.
Originally,
Yáng Bīn believed that many meritorious officials and imperial relatives serving as regional commanders were not skilled in administration.
閑 (xián) means
skilled.
These individuals, relying on their imperial appointments,
often acted autocratically,
and the Military Governors could not control them.
By this time, all such appointments were abolished.
The emperor ordered Shǐ Hóngzhào’s personal scribe Lǐ Chóngjǔ of Shàngdǎng to seek out Hóngzhào’s relatives.
Chóngjǔ said:
"Hóngzhào's younger brother, Hóngfú, is still alive."
Initially,
Hóngzhào had made Chóngjǔ responsible for the inventory of his family's wealth.
Thus, he acquired all of Hóngzhào's property,
which he handed over to Hóngfú.
The emperor admired him
and assigned him to serve under the imperial prince Róng.
2 On the wùchén day,
Wáng Yànchāo, formerly Defense Commissioner of Fùzhōu, was appointed acting Military Governor of Wǔníng.
At that time, Liú Yūn, with Gǒng Yánměi and others, was defending Xúzhōu.
3 Hàn Empress Dowager Lǐ moved to the Western Palace.
According to Xuē Shǐ, the Hàn Tàipíng Palace was probably the Western Palace.
On the jǐsì day,
she was granted the venerable title of Zhāoshèng Huáng Tàihòu.
4 Liú Xūn, the Kaifeng Magistrate and concurrently Grand Imperial Secretary, passed away.
5 On the guǐyǒu day,
Wáng Jùn was promoted to Co-administrator of Affairs with the Grand Imperial Secretary.
6 Liú Hào, the Palace Grandee of the Guard, was put in charge of the mourning rites for Hàn Emperor Yǐn.
Since Liú Xūn had passed away,
there were no other relatives.
7 Initially,
Liú Chóng, Military Governor of Hédōng and concurrently Grand Imperial Secretary, heard that Emperor Yǐn had been murdered.
He intended to raise an army and march south.
However, upon hearing that the Duke of Xiāngyīn was being welcomed to ascend the throne,
he stopped,
saying:
"My son will be emperor,
what more could I ask for!"
Lǐ Xiāng, the Junior Magistrate of Tàiyuán, secretly persuaded Chóng, saying:
"Observing Gūo Gōng's intentions,
he ultimately wishes to take the throne for himself.
It would be better for you to quickly lead your troops over the Tàiháng Mountains,
occupy Mèngjīn,
and await the ascension of the Minister of Xúzhōu.
The Duke of Xiāngyīn's original post was in Xúzhōu,
hence he was referred to as such.
Then Gūo Gōng will not dare to act;
otherwise,
you will be sold out by him."
Chóng angrily said:
"You rotten scholar,
you wish to alienate my father and son!"
He ordered his attendants to drag him out and behead him.
Xiāng cried out:
"I possessed talent for governing but planned affairs for a fool.
I am content to die!
I have an aged wife at home,
I wish to die with her."
Chóng killed his wife as well,
and reported it to the court,
showing that he had no disloyal intentions.
When Yūn was deposed,
Chóng then sent an envoy to request Yūn's return to Jìnyáng.
The imperial edict replied:
"The Duke of Xiāngyīn was recently in Sòngzhōu,
and is now being brought back to the capital.
He will certainly be well provided for,
so you need not worry.
If you can work together to assist,
you will be granted a princely title
and perpetually govern Hédōng."
Gǒng Tíngměi and Yáng Wēn, hearing that the Duke of Xiāngyīn had lost his position,
took Lady Dǒng, Yūn's wife,
and held Xúzhōu, awaiting reinforcements from Hédōng.
Liú Yūn had ordered Gǒng Tíngměi and others to defend Xúzhōu.
This matter was first mentioned in the previous year of the preceding volume.
Tíngměi and Wēn wished to surrender but feared death.
The emperor again sent a letter to Yūn, saying:
"I consider that these individuals have been devoted to their lord,
which is sufficient to reward their loyalty and righteousness.
Why should they be blamed for errors?
When the new Military Governor enters the city,
the new Military Governor refers to Wáng Yànchāo.
You may again show them clemency."
In the late Táng dynasty, a commander-in-chief's personal letter of instruction to his officers
was generally called "wěiqū."
8 When the Khitan attacked Nèiqiū,
this matter is mentioned in the previous year of the preceding volume.
There was also a lunar eclipse,
and many strange phenomena occurred in the army.
The Khitan lord was afraid
and dared not advance further.
He led his troops back.
When the Hu people wage war,
they use the moon as an omen.
A lunar eclipse,
and many strange phenomena,
therefore they were afraid and dared not advance.
妖 (yāo)
is pronounced yīyáo (yīyáo) fan.
還 (huán)
is pronounced cóngxuān (cóngxuān) fan,
and also as written.
Coinciding with the fall of Hàn,
Liú Cí, Military Governor of Ānguó, sent his envoy to Daliáng.
The emperor dispatched Zhū Xiàn, General of the Left Chief Cattle Guard, to return the visit,
and to explain the reasons for the change of dynasty,
presenting him with gold vessels and a jade belt.
9 The emperor considered Yèdū vital for pacifying Héběi
and controlling the Khitan,
and wished to entrust it to a trusted confidant.
On the yǐhài day,
Wáng Yīn, Military Governor of Níngjiāng and Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Army, was appointed Defense Commissioner of Yèdū,
Military Governor of Tiānxíong, and Co-administrator of Affairs with the Grand Imperial Secretary.
He retained his command as before,
still leading the Palace Army.
On the 10th day, *bǐngzǐ*,
the Emperor led the hundred officials to the Western Palace
to mourn for Hàn Yǐndì and don mourning attire.
All ceremonies were conducted as for a Son of Heaven.
Last year,
Hàn Yǐndì’s coffin was moved to the Western Palace;
this event is detailed in the previous volume.
*Shuài*
is read as *shuài*.
*Wèi*
is pronounced *yúwěi*.
On the 11th day, Mùróng Yànchāo sent an envoy to present tribute.
The Emperor, fearing he might be suspicious and afraid,
issued an edict to reassure him,
saying:
"Now that the matter with *xiōng* has come to this,
I do not wish for many words.
I hope my brother will support me
so that together we may bring peace to the countless common people."
Hàn Zǔ was Mùróng Yànchāo’s elder brother.
"Jīn xiōng"
is written "lìng xiōng"
in Xuē Shǐ;
this should be followed.
On the 12th day, *wùyín*,
the Duke of Xiāngyīn was killed in Sòngzhōu.
On this day,
Liú Chóng ascended the imperial throne in Jìnyáng.
Liú Chóng was Hàn Zǔ’s younger maternal brother.
He held twelve prefectures: Bìng, Fén, Xīn, Dài, Lán, Xiàn, Lóng, Wèi, Qìn, Liáo, Lín, and Shí.
Sòng Bái said: Xiànzhōu
was formerly the Lóufán Supervisorate for Pastures.
In the first year of Lóngjì of Táng Zhāozōng (889 CE),
Lǐ Kèyòng memorialized for the establishment of Xiànzhōu.
When Sòng Tàizōng pacified Tàiyuán,
Zhé Yùqīng led troops from Fǔzhōu to attack Liú Jìyuán.
He first captured Kèlán Jūn,
then Lóngzhōu,
then Lánzhōu.
Thus, Lóngzhōu was probably established between the Jìn and Hàn dynasties,
and its territory was between Kèlán and Lán Gǔ.
*Qìn*
is pronounced *qiānzhèn*.
The Observation Commissioner’s Judicial Officer, Zhào Huá of Xíngyáng, was made Minister of Revenue
and concurrently Grand Chancellor (*Píngzhāng Shì*).
His second son, Chéngjūn, was appointed Commander of the Palace Army and Prefect of Tàiyuán.
The Deputy Military Governor Lǐ Cúnwánghuái was made Defense Commissioner of Dàizhōu.
The general Wǔān Zhāng Yuánhuī was made Commander of the Infantry and Cavalry.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Wǔān County belongs to Míngzhōu,
95 *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
The ruler of Běi Hàn said to Lǐ Cúnwánghuái and Zhāng Yuánhuī:
The *Tōngjiàn* refers to the Hàn of Língnán as Nán Hàn and
the Hàn of Hédōng as Běi Hàn.
"I lament that Gāozǔ’s enterprise fell to the ground in an instant.
Today, the imperial title
is something I assume out of necessity;
what kind of Son of Heaven am I,
and what kind of Military Governors are you!?"
Because of this, no ancestral temple was built,
and sacrifices were like those of a common family.
Prime ministers’ monthly salary was only one hundred *mín*,
and Military Governors’ only thirty *mín*.
According to the *Táng Shì*, the salaries of officials
from the Huìchāng era onwards
were no longer increased or decreased:
the Three Grand Preceptors received two million,
the Three Dukes one million six hundred thousand,
the Grand Councillor one million five hundred thousand,

the Director of the Central Secretariat, the two Imperial Secretariats’ Vice Ministers, the two Ministers of the Right and Left, and the three Grand Preceptors of the Eastern Palace one million four hundred thousand.
The Ministers, the Grand Censor, and the three Junior Mentors of the Eastern Palace received one million.
Military Governors received three hundred thousand.
By the fifth year of Kāipíng of Liáng (911 CE),
a Grand Councillor’s salary was two hundred *qiān*.
In the fourth year of Tóngguāng of Hòu Táng (926 CE),
the monthly allowance for a Deputy Military Governor was set at forty *qiān*;
thus, a Military Governor’s salary would have been even higher.
Now, the Běi Hàn ruler reduced all these amounts.
*Fèng*
is pronounced *fúyòng*.
Consequently, there were few incorruptible officials in his country.
The Palace Usher Lǐ Guāngměi of Hénán had once been a Palace Duty Officer.
The Three Departments had Palace Duty Officers;
whenever officials visited the Grand Chancellor,
a Palace Duty Officer was assigned to escort them.
This position was equivalent to the usher for guests from external garrisons.
The court system of Běi Hàn
was all devised by Lǐ Guāngměi.
When the ruler of Běi Hàn heard of the death of the Duke of Xiāngyīn,
he wept and said:
"I did not heed the words of a loyal minister,
and it has come to this!"
He established a shrine for Lǐ Xiāng
and sacrificed to him annually.
On the 14th day, *jǐmǎo*,
Grand Preceptor Féng Dào was made Director of the Central Secretariat.
Dòu Zhēnggù was promoted to Grand Councillor,
and Sū Yǔguī to Minister of Works.
On the 15th day, Wáng Yànchāo memorialized to send an envoy with an imperial edict to Xúzhōu.
Gǒng Tíngměi and others hesitated and refused to open the city gates.
An edict ordered troops to attack them.
On the 16th day, the Emperor said to Wáng Jùn:
"I rose from humble beginnings,
experienced many hardships,
and encountered a time of chaos and war, becoming an emperor overnight.
How dare I indulge myself with lavish provisions
to burden the common people!"
He ordered Wáng Jùn to list out the various rare and delicious foods contributed from all directions.
On the *gēngchén* day,
an edict was issued to abolish them all.
According to the *Xuē Shǐ Běnjì*: The edict stated:
"All old tributes of flavorful foods and dishes from the prefectures and counties across the realm
should be abolished or reduced.
As for the fine wines, seafood, ginger, and melons from the two Zhè regions;
the wood [*wúyōu*] seeds tea, milk sugar, white granulated sugar, and olives from Húnán;
the Gāogōng rice and water pears from Zhènzhōu;
the chestnuts from Yìdìng;
the white *dù* pears, rice flour, mung bean flour, and *yùxiè shēnzi* [*miàn*] from Hédōng;
the imperial red glutinous rice and new barley [*miàn*] from Yǒngxīng;
the *sū* chestnuts from Xīngpíng;
the musk, antelope horn, bear gall, otter liver, vermilion persimmons, and bear fat from Huázhōu;
the tree red dates, *wǔwèizi*, and light molasses from Hézhōng;
the stone golden [*áo*] cakes from Tóngzhōu;
the grapes and yellow *xiāo* pears from Jìn and Jiàng;
the *fèngqī* pears from Shǎnfǔ;
the purple ginger, new bamboo shoots, and oranges from Xiāngzhōu;
the broken glutinous rice and pickled foods from Ānzhōu;
the water pears from Qīngzhōu;
various fruits from Héyáng;
the imperial plums from Xǔzhōu;
the new bamboo shoots and goose pears from Zhèngzhōu;
the cold food almonds from Huáizhōu;
the *ránghé* from Shēnzhōu;
the *bìxiè* from Bózhōu;
and the white fish from the Huái River from the prefectures and counties along the Huái:
henceforth, there is no need to present them as tribute."
"What is offered is only for my person,
but what is lost affects the common people."
It also said:
"Accumulating in the offices,
these are very useless items."
Another edict stated:
"I grew up in the military
and am not learned,
and do not know the way to govern the realm.
If civil and military officials have methods that benefit the state and the people,
each should submit a sealed memorial to make it known.
All should state the matter directly,
without using elaborate rhetoric."
The Emperor bestowed Sū Féngjí’s residence upon Wáng Jùn.
Wáng Jùn said:
"This is why Féngjí exterminated Lǐ Sōng’s family!"
This event is detailed in Volume 288, the first year of Qiányòu of Hàn.
If Wáng Jùn had always acted with this mindset
when he held power,
he would not have suffered the calamity in Shāngzhōu.
*Chǔ*
is pronounced *chānglǚ*.
Originally,
the Khitan ruler returned north; this is detailed in Volume 287, the twelfth year of Tiānfú of Hàn Gāozǔ.
The Khitan ruler appointed Yùniǎn as the Southwestern Route Pacification Commissioner.
When the Běi Hàn ruler was enthroned,
the Khitan ruler had Yùniǎn send a letter to Liú Chéngjūn.
The Běi Hàn ruler had Chéngjūn write a reply,
stating:
"As our dynasty collapsed and fell,
I inherited the imperial throne.
I wish to follow the precedent of the Jìn court
and seek aid from the Northern Court."
The Khitan ruler was greatly pleased.
The Běi Hàn ruler dispatched troops to garrison Yīndì, Huángzé, and Tuánbǎi.
Those garrisoned at Yīndì
intended to spy on Jìn and Xí.
Those garrisoned at Huángzé
intended to spy on Xíng and Zhào.
Those garrisoned at Tuánbǎi
intended to spy on Zhèn and Dìng.
On the *dīnghài* day,
Chéngjūn was appointed Pacification Commissioner,
and with Deputy Pacification Commissioner Bái Cónghuī and Superintendent Lǐ Cúnwánghuái, led ten thousand infantry and cavalry to raid Jìnzhōu.
Bái Cónghuī
was a Tuyuhun.
On the 18th day, Guō Chóngwēi changed his name to Chóng,
and Cáo Wēi changed his name to Yīng.
Both were to avoid the Emperor’s personal name.
*Gēng*
is pronounced *gōnghéng*.
In the second month of the 19th year [of Guǎngshù],
on the day Dīngyǒu,
Ruò, Imperial Prince Tiānxióng Yánèi Dūzhīhuīshǐ, was appointed Zhènníng Jiédùshǐ.
Court officials were selected to serve as his subordinates.
Shìyùshǐ Wáng Mǐn was made Jiédù Pànguān,
Yòubǔquē Cuī Sòng was made Guānchá Pànguān,
and Jiàoshūláng Wáng Pǔ was made Zhǎngshūjì.
This laid the groundwork for Wáng Pǔ's future prominence under Shìzōng.
[Cuī Sòng was] the son of [Cuī] Xié;
Cuī Xié served as a prime minister under Hòutáng Míngzōng.
[Cuī Sòng] was a native of Dōngpíng.
On the 20th, day Wùxū,
Northern Hàn troops attacked Jìnzhōu in five columns.
The Jiédùshǐ Wáng Yàn closed the city gates and did not sally forth.
Liú Chéngjūn, thinking him cowardly,
scaled the walls like ants.
Yàn's ambushers burst out and counterattacked,
and over a thousand Northern Hàn soldiers were killed or wounded.
Chéngjūn sent the Fùbīngmǎshǐ Ān Yuánbǎo to burn the west wall of Jìnzhōu,
but Yuánbǎo came and surrendered.
Chéngjūn then moved his army to attack Xízhōu.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: Jìnzhōu is 250 lǐ northwest of Xízhōu.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Xízhōu Cìshǐ Xǔ Qiān sent Bùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ Sūn Jìyè to meet and attack the Northern Hàn forces at Chángshòu Cūn.
In the second year of Táng Wǔdé,
Chángshòu Xiàn was established by dividing Shílóu within Xízhōu;
in the first year of Zhēnguàn, it was abolished and merged back into Shílóu.
[They] killed [many of the enemy].
Shortly thereafter,
Northern Hàn troops attacked the city of Xízhōu,
but could not overcome it after several days,
and with many dead and wounded,
they withdrew.
Qiān
was from Yùnzhōu.
On the 21st, day Jiǎchén,
Chǔ Wáng Xī'è sent his Zhǎngshūjì Liú Guāngfǔ to present tribute to Táng.
Kǎoyì states: Húxiāng Gùshì
has "Guāngfǔ"
written as
"Guānghàn."
We follow Shíguó Jìnián here.
On the 22nd, the Emperor took out dozens of precious jade objects from the Hàn palace
and smashed them in the courtyard,
saying:
"What use are these things for an emperor!
I heard that Hàn Yǐndì spent his days amusing himself with his favorites in the inner palace,
with precious trinkets never leaving his side.
This matter is not far off;
it should serve as a warning."
He then admonished his attendants,
saying that from now on, no precious and eye-pleasing objects
were to enter the palace.
On the 23rd, day Dīngwèi,
the Qìdān ruler sent his minister Wūyī Gǔzhī to come with Zhū Xiàn
to congratulate [the Emperor] on his enthronement.
On the 24th, day Wùshēn,
an edict ordered former officials to reside in outer prefectures as they pleased.
In the winter of the second year of Qiányòu under Hàn Yǐndì,
Yáng Bīn submitted a memorial proposing that former officials be divided to reside in the two capitals;
the matter is found in Volume 288.
On the 25th, before Chén Sīràng reached Húnán,
Mǎ Xī'è had already taken Chángshā;
Sīràng remained stationed at Yǐngzhōu,
and an edict recalled him.
In the eleventh month of last year,
the Hàn court deliberated dispatching troops to rescue Tánzhōu,
but internal strife arose and it was not carried out.
During the change of surnames between Liú and Guō,
there would certainly not have been leisure to send generals south to conquer.
It is unknown by which court Chén Sīràng was dispatched;
this needs investigation.
According to Xuē Shǐ,
after Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he sent Chén Sīràng to lead a division to Ān and Yǐng,
intending to advance.
After Chángshā fell,
he recalled the army.
So he was dispatched by the Emperor.
On the 26th, day Dīngsì,
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Tián Mǐn was sent as an envoy to Qìdān.
The Northern Hàn ruler sent Tōngshì Shèrén Lǐ Biàn as an envoy to Qìdān.
"[AS-FDB3] [AS-FBEC]yán" [Biàn],
is a common character for
"biàn,"
formed from
"[AS-FDB3]"
and
"yán."
Sòng Jǐngwén's notes state: During the Northern Qí period,
commoners often created false characters.
Initially,
"qiǎoyán"
was used for
"biàn."
By the Suí dynasty, there was Liǔ Biàn,
and his name character again replaced
"qiǎo"
with "[AS-FDB3]."
On the 27th, an edict added Zhōngshūlìng to Tàiníng Jiédùshǐ Mùróng Yànchāo,
and Hànlín Xuéshì Yú Chóngliàng was sent to Yǎnzhōu to convey the imperial will.
Chóngliàng
is the same as Chóngyuǎn.
Yú Chóngliàng
had previously changed his name to avoid the Hàn progenitor's tabooed name.
In the third month,
on the first day, Rénxū,
an edict replied to him saying:
"Previously, due to the former court's lack of virtue
and the young ruler's reliance on slanderers,
in a moment of crisis,
you were summoned to the capital.
You immediately rushed to answer the call,
arriving in the capital overnight,
saving the nation's peril without regard for yourself,
and hearing the sovereign's summons, you did not wait for your carriage.
Then, when the Hàn mandate was lost by heaven,
and the troops scattered in the plains of Liáng,
surrendered generals and defeated armies
arrived one after another,
you immediately turned your horse's head
and went straight back to Guīyīn.
Yǎnzhōu is south of Guīshān.
Mùróng Yànchāo went to Dàliáng and returned to Yǎnzhōu;
these matters are all found in the previous volume's previous year.
You had both a beginning and an end.
This is what is meant by 'loyalty is seen in times of danger and chaos,'
and 'a strong grass is known in a fierce wind.'
If all ministers could be like this,
then which ruler would not wish to employ them!
You mentioned that when I was a 'hidden dragon' in Hèshuò
and when I pacified the rebellion in Jùnjiao,
because no clear instructions were given,
you could not send anyone to my temporary palace.
However, the way of serving a lord

If you were ambivalent towards the Hàn court,

To be apprehensive about this

You just need to wholeheartedly exert yourself,

Let your loyalty to me
be as it was to your former lord;
not only will the common people find peace,
but the state will also rely on you.
Just remain a steadfast leader;

My sincere feelings
are fully expressed here."
Because Mùróng Yànchāo was uneasy,

On the 28th, Táng appointed Chǔ Wáng Xī'è as Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn, Wǔ'ān-Wǔpíng-Jìngjiāng-Níngyuǎn Jiédùshǐ concurrently Zhōngshūlìng, and Chǔ Wáng.

After Chǔ Wáng Xī'è achieved his ambition,

If one pats his back,

By custom,

As the government buildings had been burned down and destroyed, Xī'è

The forced labor was extremely strenuous,
and there were no rewards or provisions.
All the soldiers resented this,

"Convicts are spared death so that they can perform labor.
We followed the Great King, facing ten thousand deaths to capture Húnán,
what crime have we committed to be treated as convicts for labor?

Kuí and Xíngféng heard this

"The people's resentment is deep.

On the *rénshēn* day, in the morning,

Bóxīng,

In the fourth year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty, Lǐlíng County was established by partitioning Chángshā County.
Both belonged to Tánzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: Lǐlíng County is one hundred and sixty lǐ east of Tánzhōu.
Fàn Chéngdà's Travelogue says: From Píngxiāng County of Yuánzhōu to Lǐlíng County of Tánzhōu is only a two-day journey.
On the day Guǐsì,
Mǎ Xīchóng, the King of Chǔ, sent an envoy to reward the army.
On the day Rén'yín,
he sent Tuòbá Héng, a scholar from the Heavenly Policy Academy, to present a letter to Biān Hào to request surrender.
Tuòbá Héng sighed and said:
"I have lived too long,
to now deliver a letter of surrender for a mere child!"
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Mǎ Xīchóng led his younger brothers and nephews to welcome Biān Hào.
They bowed to him as soon as they saw his dust cloud.
Biān Hào dismounted and proclaimed an imperial edict to comfort them.
On the day Jiǎchén,
Mǎ Xīchóng and others followed Biān Hào into the city.
Biān Hào took up lodging in the gate tower of Liúyáng Gate.
All the generals and officials of Húnán came to congratulate him.
Biān Hào generously rewarded them all.
At that time, Húnán was suffering from famine.
Biān Hào greatly distributed grain from the Mǎ clan's granaries to relieve them.
The people of Chǔ were greatly pleased.
Mǎ Yīn occupied Tán and Láng,
passing the rule to his sons Mǎ Xīshēng, Mǎ Xīfàn, Mǎ Xīguǎng, Mǎ Xī'è, and Mǎ Xīchóng.
It was at this point that their state perished.
The return of Chǔ to the Wú was like what the defeated general Miáo Lín,
Xǔ Déxūn, had said:
"Wait until the young colts fight over the feeding trough, and then Hú and Xiāng can be taken."
Now it truly happened as he said.
57 The Qìdān dispatched Xiāo Yǔjué, the Military Commissioner of Zhāngguó, to lead fifty thousand Xī and Qìdān troops to join the Northern Hàn army in an invasion.
The Northern Hàn ruler personally led twenty thousand troops from Yīndì Pass to invade Jìnzhōu.
On the day Dīngwèi,
they encamped north of the city,
setting up camps on three sides.
They attacked day and night,
and their skirmishers reached Jiàngzhōu.
At that time, Wáng Yàn had already left his post,
and Wáng Yànchāo had not yet arrived.
The巡檢使 (xúnjiǎnshǐ) Wáng Wàngǎn was temporarily in charge of Jìnzhōu.
He, along with Shǐ Yànchāo, the Commander of the Dragon Swift Cavalry, and Hé Huī, the Commander of the Tiger Swift Infantry, resisted them.
The Chronicle of Xuē Shǐ says: In the first year of Guǎngshùn,
the names of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry were changed.
The cavalry, formerly called Hùshèng,
was changed to Lóngjié;
the infantry, formerly called Fèngguó,
was changed to Hǔjié.
He was a person from Yúnzhōu.
58 On the day Guǐchǒu,
Liú Rénshàn, the Military Commissioner of Wǔchāng of Táng, led two hundred warships to take Yuèzhōu.
He pacified and embraced those who surrendered,
making people forget their plight.
Liú Rénshàn was a good general,
thus he was able to bravely defend Shòuzhōu for Táng.
He was the son of Jīn.
Liú Jīn was a general under Yáng Shì.
The Táng officials collectively congratulated the pacification of Húnán.
Gāo Yuǎn, the Gentleman of the Palace for Editorial Revisions, said:
"We took advantage of the chaos in Chǔ,
and taking it was very easy.
Observing the talents of our generals,
I only fear that holding it will be difficult!"
Gāo Yuǎn
was a person from Yōuzhōu.
Lǐ Jiànxūn, the Sītú who had retired due to illness, said:
"Perhaps the disaster will begin here!"
The disaster and defeat of Táng
indeed came to pass later, as predicted by the two officials.
Since the Táng ruler ascended the throne,
he had never personally performed sacrifices at the suburban and ancestral temples.
The ritual officials petitioned for this.
The Táng ruler said:
"I will wait until the world is unified,
and then I will offer thanks."
When Chǔ was taken in one swift action,
he believed that all other states could be subdued by issuing orders.
Wèi Cén, while attending a banquet, said:
"When I was young, I traveled to Yuánchéng
and enjoyed its customs.
I request to be the Military Commissioner of Wèibó
after Your Majesty pacifies the Central Plains."
The Táng ruler granted his request,
and Wèi Cén quickly bowed to express his gratitude.
The ruler's arrogance and the minister's sycophancy were thus.
Mǎ Xī'è hoped that the Táng people would install him as the commander of Tán,
but the people of Tán hated Mǎ Xī'è
and jointly requested Biān Hào to be the commander.
The Táng ruler then appointed Biān Hào as the Military Commissioner of Wǔ'ān.
This foreshadows Biān Hào being driven out by the Lángzhou army.
Wáng Jùn had an old friend named Shēn Shīhòu.
He once served as a general in Yǎnzhōu's military headquarters.
Having lost his position and suffering from hunger and cold,
he saw Wáng Jùn's carriage and prostrated himself in homage on the road.
At this time, Zhébù Jiāshī, the acting military commissioner of Liángzhōu, submitted a memorial to the imperial court requesting an appointment.
Zhébù
was a Qiāng clan,
and thus used it as their surname.
They sought out those among the Imperial Guards who were willing to go.
"Imperial Guards"
refers to the ten Imperial Guards of the Eastern Palace.
No one responded to the recruitment.
Wáng Jùn recommended Shēn Shīhòu to the emperor.
On the *dīngsì* day,
Shēn Shīhòu was made Military Commissioner of Héxī.
Táng Biān Hào urged Mǎ Xīchóng to lead his clan to the imperial court.
The Mǎ clan gathered, weeping together,
wanting to heavily bribe Biān Hào
and memorialize to beg to remain in Chángshā.
Biān Hào slightly smiled and said:
"The state and your family have been enemies for
almost sixty years,
yet we have never dared to harbor intentions of coveting your state.
Now your brothers are quarreling,
distressed and surrendering themselves.
If this happens two or three more times,
I fear there will be unforeseen troubles."
Mǎ Xīchóng had no response.
In the eleventh month,
on the *xīnyǒu* day,
he and his clan, along with over a thousand officers and aides, wailed as they boarded the boats.
All those who saw them off cried,
their lamentations echoing through the rivers and valleys.
The emperor, considering that the armies of Běi Hàn and Qìdān were still in Jìnzhōu,
on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
appointed Wáng Jùn as the acting commander-in-chief of the expeditionary forces,
leading troops to relieve them.
An imperial edict ordered all armies to be under Wáng Jùn's command,
allowing him to act at his discretion
and choose his own generals and officials.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Wáng Jùn set off.
The emperor personally went to the west of the city to bid him farewell.
It was the west of Dàliáng city.
Mǎ Xīyǐn, Deputy Military Commissioner of Jìngjiāng of Chǔ and Administrator of Guìzhōu,
was the youngest son of King Wǔmù Yīn.
When Chǔ Kings Mǎ Xīguǎng and Mǎ Xī'è, brothers, contended for the throne,
the Southern Hàn ruler sent the palace attendant Wú Huái'ēn as the Northwestern Pacification Commissioner,
leading troops to garrison at the border,
secretly plotting to advance and seize territory when an opportunity arose.
Mǎ Xīguǎng sent Commander Péng Yànhuī to lead troops to garrison at Lóngdòng to guard against him.
To the south of Guìzhōu's streams there was Báilóng Cave,
located on a hillside in flat terrain.
Mǎ Xīyǐn disliked Péng Yànhuī and secretly sent someone to inform Xǔ Qióng, the Prefect of Méngzhōu.
Xǔ Qióng, fearing the imminent pressure from Southern Hàn,
immediately abandoned Méngzhōu
and led his troops towards Guìzhōu.
Méngzhōu and Guìzhōu were over four hundred *lǐ* apart.
is pronounced *qū*.
Péng Yànhuī was defeated
and fled to Héngshān.
Xǔ Qióng remained and garrisoned Guìzhōu.
Wú Huái'ēn occupied Méngzhōu
and advanced his troops, plundering the area.
The Guì commandery was greatly disturbed.
Mǎ Xīyǐn and Xǔ Qióng did not know what to do,
merely drinking wine and weeping together.
The Southern Hàn ruler sent a letter to Mǎ Xīyǐn,
saying:
"King Wǔmù completely possessed Chǔ,
prosperous, strong, and peaceful for over fifty years.
It is precisely because the thirty-fifth maternal uncle and the thirtieth maternal uncle, brothers, drew swords against each other,
preying on each other.
The 'thirty-fifth maternal uncle'
refers to Mǎ Xīguǎng.
The 'thirtieth maternal uncle'
refers to Mǎ Xī'è.
The Hàn ruler Gǎnmíng married a daughter of Chǔ King Yīn,
hence he called Mǎ Xīguǎng and others 'maternal uncles.'
They turn their faces north to the enemy.
This means the entire state submitted to Táng.
I secretly estimate that Guìlín will subsequently be taken by them.
Our court has been an allied state for generations,
further strengthened by marriage.
Witnessing this peril,
how can we bear not to come to your rescue!
We have already dispatched a large army, advancing by land and water.
We shall ensure that Duke Maternal Uncle forever holds the symbols of authority
and always governs the region."
Mǎ Xīyǐn received the letter and discussed surrender with his officials.
The aide Pān Xuánguī believed it was not permissible.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
Wú Huái'ēn led his troops and suddenly arrived at the city walls.
Mǎ Xīyǐn and Xǔ Qióng, leading their forces,
cut open the gates at night and fled to Quánzhōu.

During the reign of Jìn Gāozǔ,
the Mǎ clan changed Xiāngyuán County of Yǒngzhōu to Qīngxiāng County,
and established Quánzhōu.
This was originally the territory of Táo Yáng County of Hàn,
and there was the Táo River north of Qīngxiāng County.
is pronounced *shuài*.
Wú Huái'ēn then used his troops to conquer and settle Yí, Lián, Wú, Yán, Fù, Zhāo, Liǔ, Gōng, and Xiàng prefectures.
In the second year of Táng Qiánfēng,
they attracted the raw *Láo* people
and established Yánzhōu in the former Guìlín Commandery of Qín.
Fùzhōu was probably established in Fùchuān County of Hèzhōu.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
Táng Biān Hào sent the vanguard commander Lǐ Chéngjiǎn to lead troops to Héngshān
and urge Mǎ Xī'è to come to the imperial court.
On the *gēngchén* day,
Mǎ Xī'è, with over ten thousand officers, soldiers, and aides, descended eastward from Tánzhōu.
Wáng Jùn stayed in Shǎnxī for ten days.
The emperor, concerned that Běi Hàn's urgent attack on Jìnzhōu
might lead to its fall,
discussed personally leading troops via the Zézhōu road to join Wáng Jùn and relieve it.
The emperor wanted to go west from Zézhōu,
and Wáng Jùn would cross the river from Shǎnxī northward,
take Jiàngzhōu, and meet at Jìnzhōu.
is pronounced *shǎn*.
is pronounced *jiàng*.
In the twelfth month,
on the *wùzǐ* day (the first day of the month),
an imperial edict was issued to embark on a western expedition in three days.
When the messenger arrived in Shǎnxī,
Wáng Jùn spoke to the emperor through the messenger, saying:
"Jìnzhōu's city walls are strong,
not easily breached.
Liú Chóng's military edge is sharp right now,
so it is not advisable to contend by force.
The reason for halting the troops
is to wait for his morale to wane,
not because your servant is timid.
Your Majesty has just ascended the throne,
and should not move rashly.
If the imperial carriage leaves Sìshuǐ,
Mùróng Yànchāo will lead troops into Biàn,
and the great enterprise will be lost!"
When the emperor heard this,
he personally tugged his ear with his hand and said:
"I almost ruined my affairs!"
Wáng Jùn's words
pointed out something the emperor had overlooked in his precautions,
and it struck him deeply,
so he instinctively tugged his ear.
is pronounced *jī*.
is pronounced *bài*.
On the *gēngyín* day,
an imperial decree abolished the personal expedition.
Originally,
Mùróng Yànchāo, Military Commissioner of Tàiníng and concurrent Chancellor, heard that Xúzhōu was pacified,
meaning Gǒng Tíngměi and others had died.
So he gathered fugitives,
accumulated firewood and provisions,
and secretly corresponded with Běi Hàn.
An official seized his letter and reported it.
He also sent someone posing as a merchant to seek aid from Táng.
The emperor sent the Executive Secretary Zhèng Hǎoqiān to comfort and appease him,
and made a vow with him.
Mùróng Yànchāo became even more uneasy
and repeatedly sent his chief aide Zhèng Lín to the imperial court,
falsely expressing sincerity,
but actually spying on military affairs.
He also presented a letter from Gāo Xíngzhōu, Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng.
The words in it slandered the imperial court and suggested an alliance with Mùróng Yànchāo.
The emperor smiled and said:
"This is Mùróng Yànchāo's trick!"
He showed the letter to Gāo Xíngzhōu.
Gāo Xíngzhōu submitted a memorial thanking the emperor for his grace.
In the early Hàn dynasty,
Mùróng Yànchāo and Gāo Xíngzhōu jointly attacked Wèi,
which created a rift between them.
Moreover, Yǎn and Yùn were neighboring prefectures.
If Mùróng Yànchāo raised an army,
he feared Gāo Xíngzhōu would attack him from behind.
Therefore, he forged the letter,
hoping to sow discord.
The emperor, however, showed the letter to Gāo Xíngzhōu to win his trust.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
he sent the Court Usher Zhāng Níng to lead troops to garrison Yùnzhōu for inspection and defense.
The *Zhígān Fēnjì* states: Court Ushers and Deputy Ushers
were in charge of serving the imperial carriage,
attending court assemblies, imperial tours, grand banquets, and announcing princes, chancellors, various officials, and foreign guests for audiences and farewells,
and censuring those who lost propriety.
Since the Five Dynasties,
these positions were often given to military officers,
who were dispatched on missions or commanded armies.
65 On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Wáng Jùn arrived at Jiàngzhōu;
on the *yǐsì* day,
he led his troops to Jìnzhōu.
South of Jìnzhōu was Méngkēng,
which was extremely strategic and dangerous.
Jùn worried that the Northern Hàn forces would occupy it.
On that day,
upon hearing that his vanguard had already crossed Méngkēng,
he joyfully said:
"My mission is accomplished!"
66 Mùróng Yànchāo submitted a memorial requesting to enter court.
The Emperor knew it was a trick
and immediately assented.
Afterward, he again claimed that there were many bandits in his territory
and that he dared not leave his post.
67 The Northern Hàn ruler attacked Jìnzhōu,
but could not overcome it for a long time.
He had attacked Jìnzhōu on the *gēngzǐ* day of the tenth month of that year,
and by this time, more than fifty days had passed.
The people gathered to defend mountain strongholds,
leaving nothing to plunder in the countryside,
and the army was short of food.
The Qìdān desired to return home.
Hearing that Wáng Jùn had reached Méngkēng,
they burned their camps and fled during the night.
Jùn entered Jìnzhōu.
His generals requested to pursue them immediately,
but Jùn hesitated and could not decide.
The next day,

he then dispatched the Commissioner for Expeditions of the Cavalry, Qiú Hóngchāo, the Commissioner for Deploying Formations, Yào Yuánfú, and the Commissioners for Deploying Formations of the Left Flank, Chén Sīràng and Kāng Yánzhǎo, to lead cavalry in pursuit.
They caught up with them at Huòyì.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Huòyì
is 135 *lǐ* north of Jìnzhōu.
A great many Northern Hàn soldiers fell into ravines and died.
The road at Huòyì was narrow.
Yánzhǎo was timid and did not pursue urgently,
thus the Northern Hàn soldiers were able to cross.
Yào Yuánfú said:
"Liú Chóng dispatched all his forces,
bringing along Khitan cavalry,
aiming to swallow Jìn and Jiàng.
Now their spirit is flagging, their strength exhausted,
and they are fleeing in disarray.
If we do not seize this opportunity to cut them down,
they will surely become a future menace."
The generals did not wish to advance,
and Wáng Jùn again sent an envoy to stop them,
so they returned.
By the time the Qìdān reached Jìnyáng,
three or four tenths of their soldiers and horses had been lost.
Xiāo Yǔjué, ashamed of his lack of achievement,
had one great chieftain nailed in the marketplace
and executed him more than ten days later.
The Northern Hàn ruler then abandoned his ambition for conquest.
The Northern Hàn land was barren and its people poor.
Internally, they supplied the military and the state,
externally, they served the Qìdān.
Taxes were numerous and labor service heavy,
so the people could barely survive.
Many fled into Zhōu territory.
68 The Táng ruler appointed Sòng Qíqiū, Jiedushi of Zhènnán and concurrently Grand Chancellor, as Grand Tutor.
He appointed Mǎ Xī'è as Inspector of Jiāngnánxīdào,
stationed
in Hóngzhōu,
and additionally bestowed upon him the title Prince of Chǔ.
He appointed Mǎ Xīchóng as Jiedushi of Yǒngtài,
stationed
in Shūzhōu.
The Táng likely established the Yǒngtài Army at Shūzhōu.
Those of high rank were appointed as governors, generals, court ministers,
while those of lower rank were appointed to official positions accordingly.
The Táng ruler commended Liáo Yǎn and Péng Shīhào for their loyalty.
He appointed Yǎn as Left Commander of the Palace Guard and Governor of Láizhōu.
Láizhōu belonged to Zhōu territory;
Liáo Yǎn's appointment was merely nominal.
They were richly rewarded.
All the governors of Húnán entered court in Táng,
but Wáng Yūn, Governor of Yǒngzhōu, was the last to arrive.
The Táng ruler poisoned him to death.
69 The Southern Hàn ruler dispatched Pān Chóngchè, Vice Director of the Palace Domestic Service.
The Táng Palace Domestic Service had a Director
and a Junior Director,
but never a Vice Director;
this was an innovation of Southern Hàn.
Biān Hào of Táng sent troops to rescue them;
Chóngchè defeated the Táng forces at Yìzhāng
and consequently took Chēnzhōu.
Biān Hào requested the appointment of governors for Quán and Dào prefectures to guard against Southern Hàn.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
the Táng ruler appointed Liáo Yǎn as Governor of Dàozhōu
and Zhāng Luán, Commander of the Black Cloud, as acting Governor of Quánzhōu.
Quán and Dào prefectures bordered the Southern Hàn prefectures of Hè, Zhāo, and Guì.

the Táng ruler appointed Wáng Yánzhèng, Prince of Póyáng and Jiedushi of Ānhuà, as Jiedushi of Shānnánxīdào.
Xīngyuán,
Shānnánxīdào,
belonged to Shǔ;
the Táng ruler merely appointed Wáng Yánzhèng to a nominal position.
Previously,
Xián Shīlǎng, the garrison commander of Méngchéng, led his troops to surrender to Táng.

He followed Biān Hào in pacifying Húnán.
Táng collected all the gold, silk, precious items, grain from granaries, and even the beautiful boats, pavilions, flowers, and fruits from Húnán,
and moved them all to Jīnlíng.
They dispatched Yáng Jìxūn, Bureau Director of the Department of Public Works, and others, to collect rents and taxes from Húnán to support the garrisoned troops.

5 Cáo Yīng and others arrived at Yǎnzhōu
and established a long siege.
Mùróng Yànchāo repeatedly sallied out to fight,
but Yào Yuánfú defeated him every time,
so Mùróng Yànchāo dared not leave the city again.
After more than ten days,
the long siege was complete,
and they proceeded to attack.
Originally,
when Mùróng Yànchāo was about to rebel,
his *pànguān*, Cuī Zhōudù, remonstrated, saying:
"Lǔ
was a state of poetry and books.
Since Bóqín, it could not dominate the feudal lords,
yet by upholding propriety and righteousness,
it could endure for a long time.
Your Excellency has no personal grudge against the state,
why do you doubt yourself?
Moreover, the Emperor has diligently exhorted and enlightened you.
If you would but remove your defenses and return to loyalty,
you would enjoy the peace of Tài Shān while sitting still.
Do you not see what Lord Dù Zhōnglìng, Ān Xiāngyáng, and Lǐ Hézhōng ultimately accomplished?!"
(Dù Zhōnglìng
refers to Dù Zhòngwēi;
Ān Xiāngyáng
refers to Ān Cóngjìn;
Lǐ Hézhōng
refers to Lǐ Shǒuzhēn.
All rebelled and were defeated and died,
and their affairs are all recorded in previous annals.)
When the imperial army besieged the city,
Mùróng Yànchāo expropriated the wealth of the common people to support his army.
Many who hid their wealth were put to death.
Yán Hónglǔ, former Military Advisor of Shǎnzhōu,
was the son of Yán Bǎo.
(Yán Bǎo abandoned Liáng and submitted to Táng,
and served as a military commissioner.)
He offered his entire family fortune,
yet Mùróng Yànchāo still believed he was hiding something.
He ordered Cuī Zhōudù to search his house.
Cuī Zhōudù said to Yán Hónglǔ:
"Your life or death
depends on the abundance or scarcity of your wealth.
You should not hold anything back."
Yán Hónglǔ wept and bowed to his wives and concubines, saying:
"Bring out everything you have to save my life!"
They all said:
"It's all gone!"
Cuī Zhōudù reported this to Mùróng Yànchāo,
but Mùróng Yànchāo did not believe him.
He arrested Yán Hónglǔ and his wife and imprisoned them.
A wet nurse dug up a gold armlet from the mud
and offered it,
hoping to redeem her master.
Mùróng Yànchāo said:
"What
they're hiding must still be much more."
He flogged Yán Hónglǔ and his wife,
until their flesh was爛, and they died.
He accused Cuī Zhōudù of protecting them,
and had him beheaded in the marketplace.
6 Northern Hàn dispatched troops to raid Fǔzhōu.
Zhé Déyǐ, the Defense Commissioner, defeated them,
killing over two thousand men.
In the second month,
on the *gēngzǐ* day,
Zhé Déyǐ reported that he had attacked and captured Kělán Garrison of Northern Hàn,
and garrisoned it with troops.
(The *Jìu Táng Shū Dìlǐ Zhì* says: Lán Valley County of Lánzhōu
was formerly Kělán Garrison.
It was in the northern border of Yífāng County of Lánzhōu.
In the second year of Cháng'ān (702),
Yífāng was divided,
and Lán Valley County was established at the old Kělán Garrison.
In the second year of Shénlóng (706),
the county was abolished,
and a garrison was established.
In the twelfth year of Kāiyuán (724), the county was re-established.
This is probably when the Later Táng re-established the garrison.)
The *Jǐuyù Zhì* says: Kělán Garrison administered Lán Valley County,
and was ninety *lǐ* south of Lánzhōu.
岢 (Kě),
pronounced *kū wǒ*.
7 On the *jiǎchén* day,
the Emperor released Yān Jìngquán and others and sent them back to Táng.
He said to the Lord of Táng:
"Rebellious ministers
are universally detested.
I did not expect Your Lordship of Táng to assist them.
Is this not unwise?"
The Lord of Táng was greatly ashamed
and respectfully sent back all the Chinese people
he had previously captured.
Those who offered advice in Táng still presented strategies to conquer the Central Plains.
Hán Xīzài, a Scholar of the Central Secretariat, said:
"Although the Guō clan's possession of the state is recent,
their governance is already solid.
If our troops move lightly,
there will surely be harm and no benefit."
Since Emperor Lièzǔ of Táng,
(The Lord of Táng, Lǐ Shēng,
was given the temple name Lièzǔ.)
Táng desired to unite with Qìdān to control the Central Plains,
exchanging gifts
and swearing brotherhood.
However, the Qìdān, coveting their goods,
only exchanged empty words,
and in reality were not used by Táng.
The Lord of Táng was fond of literature,
so Hán Xīzài, Fēng Yánjǐ, Fēng Yánlǔ, Jiāng Wénwèi, Pān Yòu, Xú Xuàn, and their ilk all attained high offices.
(Pān Yòu
was from Yōuzhōu.)
At that time, Táng's literary elegance flourished more than in other states.
However, they had never established civil service examinations,
and officials were often appointed based on their memorials and advice.
It was only at this point
that the Emperor first ordered Jiāng Wénwèi, a Hanlin Academician, to supervise the imperial examinations.
Three *jìnshì*, including Wáng Kèzhēn of Lúlíng, passed the examination.
(Lúlíng
was a Hàn county,
and in Táng was administered by Jízhōu.)
蔚 (Wèi),
pronounced *yū wù*.
The Lord of Táng asked, "How does your selection of scholars compare to the previous dynasty?"
Jiāng Wénwèi replied:
"In the previous dynasty, public nominations and private solicitations were half and half.
Your servant is dedicated solely to impartiality!"
The Lord of Táng was pleased.
Zhāng Wěi, a Scholar of the Central Secretariat,
who had passed the examination in the previous dynasty,
heard this and held a grudge.
At that time, none of the high officials had entered through the civil service examinations,
so they joined together to obstruct and discredit the system,
eventually abolishing the imperial examinations.
(When Southern Táng abolished the imperial examinations,
the Central Plains had never abolished them.)
8 In the third month,
on the *wùchén* day,
Zhèng Rénhoùi of Jìnyáng, who was the Inner Guest House Envoy and Prefect of Ēnzhōu Training Militia, was appointed Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs.
(Note that there was no Ēnzhōu in the Central Plains at this time.
This was the Ēnzhōu of Southern Hàn,
and Zhèng Rénhoùi merely held the title of Prefect of the Training Militia remotely.)
In the eighth year of Qìnglì of Sòng (1048),
after Wáng Zé was suppressed,
Bèizhōu was renamed Ēnzhōu.
Only then was the Ēnzhōu in Língnán called Southern Ēnzhōu to distinguish it.
9 On the *jiǎxū* day,
Wēishèng Military Command was renamed Wǔshèng Military Command.
(Dèngzhōu was formerly Wēishèng Military Command; it was now renamed to avoid the imperial name.)
The Lord of Táng appointed Féng Yánjǐ, Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince and Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì, as Left Púshè;
Xú Jǐngyùn, former Jìedùshǐ of Zhènhǎi, as Zhōngshū Shìláng;
and Sūn Shèng, Right Púshè, all with the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
When the edict was announced,
Cháng Mèngxī, Minister of Revenue, spoke loudly among the crowd:
"The white edict is excellent,
but it cannot compare to Jiāng Wénwèi's memorial!"
Jiāng Wénwèi's memorial can be found in Volume 287, under Tiānfú 12th year of Hàn.
He said to people,
"Will golden cups and jade bowls
be used to store dog excrement?"
Yánjǐ said to the Lord of Táng:
"Your Majesty personally handles all the miscellaneous affairs,
hence the prime ministers cannot fully utilize their talents.
This is why the path to good governance has not been perfected!"
The Lord of Táng then entrusted all political affairs to him,
merely approving what was submitted.
However, Yánjǐ was not diligent in his duties;
all documents were left to the clerks,
and military matters were delegated to border generals.
After a while,
affairs became even more mismanaged,
so the Lord of Táng resumed overseeing them himself.
Xiāo Yǎn, Grand Judge, disliked Yánjǐ's character
and repeatedly submitted memorials attacking him.
It happened that Yǎn was implicated in a case of accidentally causing a person's death,
and Zhōng Mó, Lǐ Démíng, and their ilk were determined to have him killed.
Yánjǐ said,
"Yǎn accidentally killed a woman,
and you gentlemen believe he deserves death.
Yǎn is one of the Nine Ministers;
can he be mistakenly killed?"
He alone memorialized,
"Yǎn has always had a reputation for integrity.
The crime he is accused of has already been covered by an amnesty,
so leniency should be granted."
Yǎn was thus spared;
people also praised him for this.
Jǐngyùn was soon dismissed and made Junior Tutor of the Crown Prince.
According to records, since Táng had already established officials for the Crown Prince's Younger Brother (Tàidì),
there should not have been a Junior Tutor of the Crown Prince.
This needs investigation.
fourth month,
on the day Bǐngxū, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
on the day Yǐmǎo,
issued an edict to personally lead an expedition.
He appointed Lǐ Gǔ as acting Left-Behind Administrator of Dōngjīng and concurrently Governor of Kāifēng Prefecture,
Zhèng Rénhuì as acting Grand Palace Patrol
Inspector,
and Guō Chóng, Grand Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry, as the capital's acting Patrol Inspector.
he dispatched his general Lǐ Jiànqī to station troops at Yìyáng to plan for Lǎngzhōu,
and appointed Zhāng Luán, Prefect of Quánzhōu, concurrently as Envoy for Pacification of Guìzhōu to plan for Guìzhōu.
After a long time,
no achievements were made.
The Lord of Táng said to Féng Yánjǐ and Sūn Shèng:
"The people of Chǔ sought respite from us,
meaning the people of Húnán suffered from their lord's tyranny and exorbitant taxes and sought respite from Táng.
This is not how we fulfill the hopes of the suffering people;
The Classic of History says: 'Later, the people will be relieved.'
This means the people of Chǔ hoped for Táng's relief and rest, but Táng again raised troops and imposed labor to exhaust them,
which is not how to fulfill their hopes.
If the Lord of Táng could act on his words
and not be swayed by public opinion,
how could there have been such a defeat on another day!
Withdraw the garrison from Yìyáng,
and bestow the insignia of authority upon Liú Yán,
what do you think?"
Shèng believed it was appropriate.
'Appropriate'
means 'it should be so'.
"I sent a partial general to take Húnán,
shocking those near and far;
suddenly losing two-thirds,
gaining Tán but losing Lǎng and Guì,
thus it is called losing two-thirds.
'Sàng' is pronounced 'sìlàng fān'.
I request that we entrust border generals to assess the situation."
The Lord of Táng then dispatched General of the Imperial Army Hóu Xùn with five thousand soldiers from the Jízhōu road to proceed quickly to Quánzhōu,
to join forces with Zhāng Luán and attack Guìzhōu.
The Southern Hàn ambushed them in the mountain valleys.
When Luán and others first arrived at the city,
they were exhausted.
The ambushing troops rose from all sides,
and troops from the city came out to attack them from both sides.
The Táng army was utterly defeated;
Xùn died,
and Luán gathered a few hundred scattered soldiers and fled back to Quánzhōu.
on the day Gēngshēn,
the Emperor departed from Dàliáng;
on the day Wùchén,
he arrived at Yǎnzhōu.
On the day Jǐsì,
the Emperor sent messengers to persuade Mùróng Yànchāo,
but the people on the city walls spoke disrespectfully.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
he ordered all armies to advance and attack.
Previously,
diviners had deceived Yànchāo, saying:
"The planet Zhènxīng (Saturn) has reached Jiǎo and Kàng constellations,
which are associated with Yǎnzhōu.
Those below it will have good fortune."
Yànchāo then erected a shrine and prayed,
ordering all households to display yellow banners.
The color of the earth is yellow;
Yànchāo ordered the banners to be yellow to conform to its color.
If people's hearts are pleased, the will of Heaven is obtained;
if people's hearts are alienated, what good are charms?
As the imperial army pressed the attack on the city,
he was still burying and hiding treasures.
Consequently, the people had no will to fight,
and generals and soldiers successively surrendered.
On the day Yǐhài,
the imperial army captured the city.
Yànchāo was still praying at the Zhènxīng shrine.
He led his troops to fight fiercely,
but could not prevail.
He then burned the Zhènxīng shrine
and, with his wife, jumped into a well to die.
His son, Jìxūn, fled,
but was pursued, captured,
and killed.
The imperial army plundered extensively,
and nearly ten thousand people died in the city.
Initially,
when Yànchāo planned to rebel,
he recruited bandits and placed them under his command.
Over two thousand came,
all fierce and wild from the mountains and forests,
but ultimately they were not used.
The Emperor intended to execute all the generals and officials of Yǎnzhōu.
Dòu Yí, Hanlin Academician, met Féng Dào and Fàn Zhì,
and together with them pleaded with the Emperor:
"They were all coerced."
So he pardoned them.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Yán Kàn, Academician of the Duānmíng Hall, was appointed acting Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
An amnesty
was granted to Mùróng Yànchāo's partisans within the jurisdiction of Yǎnzhōu;
those who had fled and hidden were given one month to surrender,
and the relatives of those already executed were pardoned.
On the day Guǐwèi,
Tàiníng Commandery was downgraded to a Defense Prefecture.
Because Mùróng Yànchāo had held Yǎnzhōu and defied orders,
the Jíezhèn was downgraded to a Defense Prefecture.
Before his death,
he admonished his family:
"Given the state of affairs,
it is fortunate that I can die a natural death!
Do not build a mound or erect a stele.
Allow people to farm over it,
to avoid it becoming a target for future excavation."
When Jiāngnán fell,
referring to the time Sòng pacified Jīnlíng,
only Jiànxūn's tomb remained unknown.
Lǐ Jiànxūn knew that the country's affairs were dire,
and his remains were preserved in their hiding place. Can this not be called wisdom?
In the 6th month of the 16th year,
on the *Yǐyǒu* day, the new moon occurred.
The Emperor went to Qūfù
to worship at Kǒngzǐ's ancestral temple.
In ancient times, the Shàohào clan migrated from Qióngsāng to Qūfù;
it was the residence of Bóqín, the Marquis of Lǔ,
and the former site of the Shàohào clan.
Yìng Shào said: Qūfù is within the city of Lǔ,
winding for seven or eight *lǐ*.
Liú Zhāo said: In Qūfù there is Quèlǐ,
where Kǒngzǐ lived,
and later generations erected Kǒngzǐ's ancestral temple there.
Since the Táng dynasty,
Yǎnlü zhōu was governed from Xiáqiū,
and Qūfù was a subordinate county.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It is forty *lǐ* east of the prefecture.
In the 5th year of Dàzhōng Xiángfú of the Sòng dynasty,
Qūfù was renamed Xiānyuán County.
When the Emperor was about to bow,
his attendants said:
"Kǒngzǐ was
a minister of a subordinate state,
it is not proper for Your Majesty to bow to him as an emperor."
The Emperor said:
"Kǒngzǐ is the teacher of emperors for a hundred generations,
how dare I not be respectful!"
Thereupon he bowed.
He also bowed at Kǒngzǐ's tomb,
ordered the renovation of Kǒngzǐ's ancestral temple,
and prohibited woodcutting and foraging in Kǒnglín.
Kǒngzǐ's temple is in Quèlǐ, in the southwest corner of Qūfù city.
Kǒngzǐ's tomb is north of Qūfù city, by the Sǐshuǐ river,
one *lǐ* from the city.
The burial ground covers about one *qǐng*,
the mound is ten paces north-south,
thirteen paces east-west,
and one *zhàng* two *chǐ* high.
In front, there is a brick platform,
serving as an altar,
six *chǐ* square,
level with the ground.
Within the burial enclosure, there are hundreds of exotic trees,
all brought by his disciples from various regions,
and planted in the enclosure.
The people of Lǔ did not recognize them.
He appointed officials to Qūfù County and a Chief Clerk.
On the *Bǐngxū* day,
the Emperor departed from Yǎnlü zhōu.
On the 17th, *Yǐwèi* day,
Wú Yuè's Shùndé Tàifūrén, Lady Wú, passed away.
On the 18th, *Dīngyǒu* day,
a great flood entered Chéngdū in Shǔ.
During the Qín dynasty,
Lǐ Bīng, the Administrator of Shǔ, dug two rivers within Chéngdū,
both navigable.
*Jùnxuàn Zhì* states: Lǐ Bīng carved Líduī,
and also opened two canals:
one went from Yǒngkāng, passed Xīnfán, and entered Chéngdū,
called the Outer River;
another canal
went from Yǒngkāng, passed Pí, and entered Chéngdū,
called the Inner River.
Before Gāo Pián built the outer city wall,
both the Inner and Outer Rivers entered from the west of the city.
Since Pián built the wall,
they then created the Mízhǎo Weir from the northwest.
The Outer River circled north of the city and flowed eastward into Héjiāng.
The Inner River followed south of the city and flowed into the river together with the outer water.
As the rivers came from the west,
the terrain there was high,
which is why there were floods.
Over five thousand people drowned,
and four rooms of the Tàimiào were destroyed.
On the *Wùxū* day,
Shǔ declared a general amnesty
and provided relief to families affected by the flood.
On the 19th, *Jǐhài* day,
the Emperor arrived at Dàliáng.
He returned to Dàliáng from Yǎnlü zhōu.
On the 20th, Fény Hūi, the Jìedùshǐ of Shuòfāng and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, Prince of Chénliú, passed away.
His son, Yánèi Dūyúhòu Jìyè, killed his elder brother Jìxūn
and took charge of the military administration himself.
On the 21st, Huǎn, the younger brother of Lǐ Tāo, Taizǐ Bīnke,
was a Qínzhèng Diàn Xuéshì in Qìdān.
He was on good terms with Xiāo Hǎizhēn, the Jìedùshǐ of Yōuzhōu.
Hǎizhēn was
the younger brother of Qìdān Lord Wùyù's wife.
Huǎn persuaded Hǎizhēn to join the central government,
and Hǎizhēn gladly agreed.
Huǎn then had Tián Zhòngbà, a spy from Dìngzhōu, carry a silk memorial to report this,
and also sent a letter to Tāo,
saying:
"The Qìdān Lord is childish and foolish,
solely devoted to banquets and excursions,
without grand ambitions,
unlike his predecessors.
'Predecessors' refers
to Ābǎojī, Déguāng, and others.
We will surely conquer them;
if not,
and we make peace,
we will surely succeed.
Both options benefit from speed.
Judging their situation,
they will ultimately be unable to provide strong assistance to Hédōng in the future."
On the *Rényín* day,
Zhòngbà arrived at Dàliáng.
However, China was preoccupied with many matters,
so the plan could not be carried out.
Not gaining Yàn and Yún in the north, nor Hé, Shàn, Líng, and Xià in the west,
Sòng people considered this a regret for a thousand ages.
Observing Wēn Gōng's record of this matter,
one knows that
when Mǐzhī and the other four forts were abandoned in the early Yuányòu era,
the strength of China was insufficient.
On the 22nd, *Xīnhài* day,
Fény Jìyè was appointed Shuòfāng Liúhòu.
On the 23rd, Wáng Jùn, the Shūmìshǐ,
was of a light and impetuous nature,
skilled in calculations,
fond of power and profit,
and liked people to be subservient to him.
He considered the world his responsibility.
Whenever he spoke of matters,
if the Emperor followed him, he was pleased;
if at times he was not approved,
he would become resentful
and often utter disrespectful words.
The Emperor, considering him an old acquaintance
and having rendered meritorious service in his ascension,
from the Emperor's entry into Biàn from Yèdū to his enthronement, Wáng Jùn's contributions were numerous.
always showed great tolerance.
Jùn was older than the Emperor.
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
he still called him "brother"
or used his courtesy name.
Because of this, Jùn became even more arrogant.
Zhèng Rénhuì, the Fùshǐ, Xiàng Xùn, the Huángchéngshǐ, and Lǐ Chóngjìn, the Ēnzhōu Tuánliànshǐ,
were all trusted generals and staff when the Emperor was a regional governor.
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
they were gradually promoted.
Jùn was jealous of them in his heart,
and repeatedly submitted memorials claiming illness,
requesting to be relieved of his duties,
to test the Emperor's intentions.
The Emperor repeatedly sent his attendants to persuade him,
but Jùn's words and demeanor to the envoys were arrogant and sharp.
He also sent letters to various Jìedùshǐ to seek their endorsement.
Each of the Jìedùshǐ presented his letter.
The Emperor was startled and alarmed for a long time,
then again sent attendants to comfort and encourage him,
ordering him to attend to his duties,
and furthermore said:
"If you
do not come,
I will personally go."
Still, he did not come.
The Emperor knew that Chén Guān, the Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì, was close to Jùn,
so he ordered Guān to convey his message.
Guān said:
"Your Majesty only needs to announce that you will personally visit his residence,
and Jùn will surely not dare not to come."
In autumn,
the 7th month,
on the *Wùzǐ* day,
Jùn came to court.
The Emperor comforted and encouraged him, ordering him to attend to his duties.
Chóngjìn was
from Cāngzhōu,
and his mother was
Fúqìng Chánggōngzhǔ, the Emperor's own sister.
Lǐ Gǔ suffered a fall,
injuring his right arm,
and was on leave for more than a month.
The Emperor, considering Gǔ's duties complex and urgent,
promptly ordered him to come to court.
"On leave" means "on vacation."
The character *qù*
is pronounced "cù."
"Court"
is read as *zhāo*;
the same below.
On the *Guǐsì* day,
an imperial edict exempted him from morning audiences,
but only ordered him to attend to his duties.

The Grand Secretary (尚書) of the Board of Works (工部) of Shǔ, [Guō Yánjūn] 郭延鈞, who also held the concurrent post of Commissioner (判) of Wǔdé Army (武德軍), treated the supervising escort [Wáng Chéngpī] 王承丕 disrespectfully.
[Chéngpī] 承丕 plotted a rebellion.
On the day of Xīnchǒu,
[Sūn Qīn] 孫欽, the Left Commander (都指揮使) of the Fèngshèng Army (奉聖都),
who was from [Āncì] 安次 County,
which belonged to [Yōuzhōu] 幽州.
[Sūn Qīn] 孫欽 was originally from [Yān] 燕 but served in Shǔ.
He went to bid farewell to [Chéngpī] 承丕.
[Chéngpī] 承丕 invited him to go together to see the Prefectural Duke.
The Prefectural Duke,
referred to [Guō Yánjūn] 郭延鈞.
The term "Duke" ([gōng] 公)
is an honorific title for a person.
[Yánjūn] was respected by the entire prefecture,
hence he was called the Prefectural Duke.
[Qīn] agreed.
When [Chéngpī] 承丕 arrived,
he ordered his attendants to strike and kill [Yánjūn] 延鈞,
slaughtered his household,
and declared that he was acting on an imperial edict to take charge of the military government.
He immediately opened the treasury to reward the soldiers,
released the prisoners,
and mobilized the garrisons.
All the generals and officials assembled,
and [Qīn] 欽 said to [Chéngpī] 承丕:
"Now that [Yánjūn] 延鈞 has been executed,
Your Grace should issue an imperial edict to show the masses."
[Chéngpī] 承丕 said:
"I can bring you wealth and honor;
do not ask about an imperial edict."
[Qīn] 欽 then realized that [Chéngpī] 承丕 was rebelling,
and so he deceived him, saying:
"Now the internal and external situations are not yet stable;
I request to lead my troops to patrol for Your Grace."
He immediately jumped on his horse and rode out.
[Chéngpī] 承丕 called out to him repeatedly,
but he did not stop.
When [Qīn] 欽 arrived at his camp,
he explained the situation to his troops,
led them into the prefectural office,
and attacked [Chéngpī] 承丕.
[Chéngpī]'s attendants wanted to resist and fight,
but [Qīn] 欽 shouted at them,
and they all threw down their weapons and fled.
So [Chéngpī] 承丕 was captured
and executed,
along with his close associates.
Their heads were sent to [Chéngdū] 成都.
The Military Commissioner (節度使) of Tiānpíng (天平), who also held the title of Grand Secretary (守中書令) [Gāo Xíngzhōu] 高行周, passed away.
[Xíngzhōu] 行周 was brave and knew righteousness;
his achievements were great but he was not boastful.
When he spurred his horse and faced the enemy,
his shouts stirred up the wind.
In ordinary times, when he banqueted with his guests and officials,
he was frank, amiable, and easygoing.
People respected him for this.
On the day of Guǐmǎo,

later simply the Liùzhái.
