11 On the day of Wùshēn,
Shé Cóngruǎn reported the surrender of twenty-one tribes of savage chickens.
12 Shào Táng, a commoner from Táng, memorialized:
A commoner who has not received an imperial appointment
is called a "cǎozé" (grass and marsh).
The character “上” (shàng)
was pronounced “fān” at the time.
“Recently I traveled to Huáishàng
and heard that the Zhōu ruler is modest and frugal,
and has increased the cultivation of virtuous governance.
Our troops have recently been defeated at Tán and Lǎng,”
referring to Biān Hào’s defeat at Tánzhōu.
“It is advisable to prepare for this.”
Intellectuals and knowledgeable people,
which country does not have them!
It is only a matter of whether they are employed or not.
13 Initially,
after Wáng Kuí obtained Tánzhōu—
the matter is detailed in the tenth month of the previous volume—
Zhū Quánxiù was Wǔ’ān Jìedù Fùshǐ,
Zhāng Wénbiǎo was Wǔpíng Jìedù Fùshǐ,
and Zhōu Xíngféng was Wǔ’ān Xíngjūn Sīmǎ.
Jìngzhēn and Quánxiù each established their own personal guards,
and shared the office with Kuí to handle affairs.
The officials and common people did not know whom to obey.
Whenever there was a banquet,
the generals would get drunk
and quarrel like in a marketplace,
with no distinction between superior and subordinate.
Only Xíngféng and Wénbiǎo treated Kuí with full courtesy,
and Kuí held them dear.
Jìngzhēn was not in harmony with Kuí
and resigned to return to Lǎngzhōu.
He also could not serve Liú Yán,
and plotted rebellion with Quánxiù.
Yán had always been wary of Kuí’s strength,
suspected Kuí of using Jìngzhēn to spy on him,
and was about to punish him.
Kuí heard of this
and was greatly afraid.
Xíngféng said:
“Liú Yán has always not been of the same mind as us.
Hé Jìngzhēn and Zhū Quánxiù are ashamed to be beneath you.
You should plan early.”
Kuí rejoiced, saying:
“Let us together eliminate the wicked faction and jointly govern Tán and Lǎng.”
Zhōu Xíngféng’s seizure of Tán and Lǎng
began from this point.
The character “治” (zhì)
was pronounced “zhí” at the time.
Coincidentally, Nán Hàn attacked Quán, Dào, and Yǒngzhōu.
Xíngféng requested:
“I will go to Lǎngzhōu to persuade Yán
to send Jìngzhēn and Quánxiù to campaign in the south.”
“Campaigning in the south”
means to repel the Nán Hàn troops.
“I will take them by strategy,
like an object in my palm.”
Kuí agreed.
When Xíngféng arrived at Lǎngzhōu,
Yán appointed Jìngzhēn as Nánmiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ
and Quánxiù as Xiānfēngshǐ,
leading over a hundred of their personal guards to meet the Tánzhōu troops to resist Nán Hàn.
When the two arrived at Chángshā,
Kuí went out to the suburbs to welcome them.
They met happily
and feasted for several days,
often tempting them with beautiful courtesans.
Jìngzhēn consequently lingered and did not advance.
Lǐ Zhòngqiān, the Zhǐhuīshǐ of Lǎngzhōu, had commanded three thousand troops stationed in Tánzhōu for a long time.
Jìngzhēn ordered him to set off first,
heading north of the mountains.
Quán, Dào, and Yǒng three prefectures are all north of Dàyǔlǐng.
The character “趣” (qù)
was pronounced “yù” at the time.
He forced Zhòngqiān to return to Lǎngzhōu.
Kuí, taking advantage of Jìngzhēn’s drunkenness,
sent someone to falsely pose as Yán’s messenger,
reproaching Jìngzhēn with:
“The southern invaders are deeply encroaching,
yet you do not hasten to defend but are solely engrossed in debauchery.
The Grand Preceptor orders you to be chained and brought back to the Western Residence.”
“Grand Preceptor”
refers to Liú Yán.
The Lǎng government was west of Tánzhōu,
hence it was called the Western Residence.
Quánxiù fled,
and troops were dispatched to pursue and capture him.
In the second month,
on the Xīnhài Day which was the first day of the month,
Jìngzhēn was beheaded and displayed to the public.
Not long after,
Quánxiù and more than ten of his associates were captured,
and all were beheaded.
14 On the day of Guǐchǒu,
Róng, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhènníng, returned to Chánzhōu.
15 At first,
Qìdān zhǔ Déguāng returned north.
See 286 scrolls, Tiānfú 12th year.
Up to this point,
they again made two treasures out of jade.
These were the Seal of Transmitted State and the Seal of Mandate Received.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: At that time, two treasure seals were made,
using white jade,
six inches square,
with a chīhǔ knob.
FÉNG Dào inscribed the seal script.
One was
inscribed with "Seal of the Emperor Who Receives the Mandate from Heaven",
and
the other was
inscribed with "Seal of the Emperor's Divine Treasure".
SÒNG Bái said: At that time, the Inner Secretariat made two treasures.
An imperial edict ordered the Tàicháng to prepare the regulations and report them.
The officials concerned reported: The Táng Liùdiǎn states: The Fúbǎoláng is in charge of the Son of Heaven's eight seals,
one is called the Divine Treasure (Shénbǎo),
and the second is called the Seal of Mandate Received (Shòumìngbǎo).
The Divine Treasure is six inches square,
four inches six fen high,
one inch seven fen thick,
with a coiled dragon knob,
and its inscription is the same as the Seal of Transmitted State.
The Seal of Transmitted State was
carved by Qín Huáng from Lántián jade,
with LǏ Sī's篆 script.
It was four inches square,
and its face was inscribed with
"Received Mandate from Heaven,
May Longevity and Prosperity Endure."
The knob was a coiled five-dragon design.
These two treasures were passed down through generations,
regarded as divine instruments.
There were also six other seals: one was the Emperor's Traveling Seal (Huángdì Xíngxǐ),
second was the Emperor's Seal (Huángdì Zhīxǐ),
third was the Emperor's Trust Seal (Huángdì Xìnxǐ),
fourth was the Son of Heaven's Traveling Seal (Tiānzǐ Xíngxǐ),
fifth was the Son of Heaven's Seal (Tiānzǐ Zhīxǐ),
and sixth was the Son of Heaven's Trust Seal (Tiānzǐ Xìnxǐ).
These six seals
were named after their inscriptions,
all of white jade,
with chīhǔ knobs.
They were passed down through generations,
and if lost, they were replaced.
The Northern Dynasties cast them in gold.
In the 16th year of Zhēnguàn,
another dark seal was made,
inscribed with
"Great Mandate of Heaven,
May the Virtuous Prosper."
It was of white jade,
with a chīhǔ knob.
During Tóngguāng, a seal was made,
inscribed:
"Seal of the Emperor Who Receives the Mandate."
In the 4th year of Tiānfú, a seal was made,
inscribed with
"Seal of the Emperor's Divine Treasure."
As for the two seals of Tóngguāng and Tiānfú,
they were manufactured by the Inner Secretariat,
but their knob, script, and dimensional specifications are not found.
An imperial edict commanded that two national seals be made.
One should be
inscribed with "Seal of the Emperor Who Receives the Mandate from Heaven",
and
the other with
"Seal of the Emperor's Divine Treasure".
It was decreed that Zhōngshūlìng FÉNG Dào inscribe the seals.
Commentators said: The state taking a jade seal as a divine instrument for transmission has not been heard of since ancient times.
The Yùndòushū says: When Shùn and Yǔ were Sons of Heaven,
a yellow dragon bore a seal.
The Shìběn says: Lǔ Zhāogōng first made a seal.
When Qín conquered the six states,
he called himself emperor.
According to ritual, Lántián jade was used,
and the jade craftsman SŪN Shòu carved it.
It was four inches square,
and LǏ Sī wrote the great seal script for it.
Its form was like a dragon, fish, phoenix, and bird,
a rare and supreme treasure.
When Qín fell,
Zǐyīng surrendered the seal to Hàn.
The Hàn dynasty cherished and passed it down through generations.
When WÁNG Mǎng usurped power,
he demanded the seal from Yuánhòu.
The empress threw it onto the steps,
chipping a corner slightly.
After Mǎng was executed,
it returned to Gēngshǐ.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
it went to Pénzǐ.
And when Xióng'ěr was defeated,
Pénzǐ surrendered the seal to Guāngwǔ.
At the end of Hàn,
the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out, and
the seal was thrown into a well.
SŪN Jiān entered Luò,
saw a five-colored aura in the well,
retrieved it,
and returned it to YUÁN Shù.
When Shù was defeated,
Jīngzhōu cìshǐ XÚ Qiú obtained it,
went to Xǔ,
and presented it to Xiàndì.
Wèi received it from Hàn,
and passed it to Jìn.
When Luòyáng fell,
LIÚ Cōng obtained it.
When LIÚ Yào was captured by SHÍ Lè,
the seal returned to Yè.
During the chaos of the Shí clan,
RǍN Mǐn obtained it.
When Mǐn was defeated,
the Jìn general DÀI Shī entered Yè and obtained it,
sending it to Jiāngdōng,
where it was passed through Sòng, Qí, and Liáng.
When Táichéng was broken,
HÓU Jǐng obtained it.
When Jǐng was defeated,
his general HÓU Zǐjiàn fled with the seal.
Pursued by soldiers,
he threw it into a well at Qīxiá Temple.
The monk Yǒngzhù obtained and concealed it.
In the 2nd year of Chén Yǒngdìng,
Yǒngzhù's disciple Pǔzhì presented the seal to Chén Wéndì.
Suí pacified Chén,
and thus obtained the true Qín Seal of Transmitted State.
During Yángdì's disaster in Jiāngdū,
YǓWÉN Huàjí obtained it.
When Huàjí was defeated,
the seal returned to DÒU Jiàndé.
When Jiàndé was defeated,
his wife, Lady CÁO, presented the seal to Táng.
When Táng abdicated,
YÁNG Shè sent the treasure to Dàliáng.
Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng and obtained it.
At the end of Tóngguāng,
internal strife arose,
and the treasure was scorched by fire.
The characters were distorted and incomplete.
Míngzōng obtained it.
When Qīngtài was defeated,
he kept the treasure with him
and immolated himself, thus the treasure was lost.
As for the Divine Treasure,
it was six inches square,
one inch seven fen thick,
four inches six fen high,
with a coiled dragon subtly raised.
Its inscription was the same as the Qín seal,
but the color of the jade was inferior,
and its form was taller and larger.
It is unknown in which dynasty it was manufactured.
In the 19th year of Dōngjìn Xiàowǔ,
Yōngzhōu cìshǐ XĪ Huī obtained it.
MÙRÓNG Yǒng sent it to Jīnlíng,
where it was passed through Sòng, Qí, and Liáng.
When Táichéng was broken,
HÓU Jǐng obtained it.
When Jǐng was defeated,
Shìzhōng ZHÀO Sīqí carried it north across the river,
and presented it to Qí Wénxuāndì.
YǓWÉN destroyed Qí and obtained it.
When YǓWÉN fell,
it entered Suí.
Suí Wéndì changed its name to Seal of Transmitted State,
and later changed it to Seal of Mandate Received.
After pacifying Chén,
he finally obtained the true Qín Seal of Transmitted State.
Nevertheless, because the Qín seal appeared later,
obtained from the fallen Chén,
the Divine Seal passed down by the Northern Dynasties was considered first,
and the Qín seal second.
When Suí fell,
DÒU Jiàndé's wife presented it along with the Divine Seal to Cháng'ān.
At the end of Táng,
its whereabouts became unknown.
This account has a clear origin and progression,
so it is recorded here.
Gēng (更),
pronounced gōnghéng.
16 WÁNG Kuí sent an envoy to inform LIÚ Yán of HÉ Jìngzhēn's execution.
Yán had no choice.
On the gengshen day,
he executed FÚ Huì and several others.
This was because FÚ Huì and others had provoked the rebellion.
17 The Grand Councilor (Shūmìshǐ) and Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Pínglú, concurrently Grand Commissioner (Tóng Píngzhāngshì), Wáng Jùn,
became increasingly arrogant and irritable in his later years.
He memorialized, requesting that Yán Kàn, Academician of the Duānmíng Hall,
and Chén Guān, Academician-in-waiting of the Bureau of Military Affairs, replace Fàn Zhì and Lǐ Gǔ as chancellors.
The Emperor said:
"The appointment and dismissal of high officials
cannot be done hastily.
Wait until I have given it more thought."
Wáng Jùn argued forcefully,
his words becoming increasingly disrespectful.
It was approaching noon,
and the Emperor had not yet eaten,
but Wáng Jùn continued to press the issue.
The Emperor said:
"It is currently the Hànshí Festival.
After the holidays,
I will act as you have proposed."
Wáng Jùn then withdrew.
According to old regulations,
the Hànshí Festival holiday lasted five days in total, before and after.
(The character "假" [jiǎ],
is pronounced "jū yà" fan.)
On the guǐhài day,
the Emperor urgently summoned the chancellors and the Grand Councilors,
and confined Wáng Jùn to a separate residence.
The Emperor met Fēng Dào and others,
and wept, saying:
"Wáng Jùn has excessively bullied me;
he wants to drive away all the high officials
and clip my wings.
I have only one son,
and he deliberately creates estrangement.
I merely ordered him to the court,
and he already harbors resentment.
How can one hold the pivotal military authority,
concurrently be a chancellor,
and also seek a major military post!
Looking at his ambition,
he is far from satisfied.
To be so unfilial to the sovereign,
who can tolerate this!"
On the jiǎzǐ day,
Wáng Jùn was demoted to Sīmǎ of Shāngzhōu.
The imperial edict roughly stated:
"He regards the empress as mere flesh,
and treats Us as an infant."
This meant that he viewed court officials as meat on a chopping block,
and treated the Emperor as a baby.
Wáng Jùn and Wáng Yīn were both instrumental in the founding of the dynasty.
As Wáng Jùn was disgraced, the Emperor feared Wáng Yīn might become suspicious and afraid.
The Imperial Food Administrator (Shàngshíshǐ)
was a position equivalent to Tang's Shàngshí Fèngyù.
When Wáng Jùn arrived at Shāngzhōu,
he contracted an abdominal illness.
The Emperor still pitied him,
and ordered his wife to visit him.
He died not long after.
18 The Emperor ordered Zhé Cóngruǎn to divide his troops and garrison Yánzhōu.
Zhé Cóngruǎn was then the commander of Jìngnán,
and had returned from suppressing the Yějī tribe.
He frequently made contributions.
The Emperor also ordered the Palace Aide (Gòngfèngguān) Zhāng Huáizhēn to lead two divisions of imperial guards to garrison Fū and Yán.
Shàojī then completely handed over the affairs of the military administration to the Deputy Envoy (Fùshǐ) Zhāng Kuāngtú.
On the jiǎxū day,
Xiàng Xùn, Palace Messenger (Kèshěngshǐ),
was granted provisional authority to govern Yánzhōu.
19 In the third month,
on the jiǎshēn day,
Róng, Military Governor of Zhènníng, was made Magistrate of Kāifēng and Prince of Jìn.
Only after Wáng Jùn was demoted,
was Róng summoned.
On the bǐngxū day,
Zhèng Rénhuì, Deputy Grand Councilor, was made Military Governor of Zhènníng.
20 Initially,
the Shāniú tribe and the Yějī tribe had a feud.
Hearing that the government army was attacking the Yějī,
the Shāniú provided provisions and welcomed them.
The government troops, coveting their wealth and livestock, plundered them;
the Shāniú tribe rebelled
and joined forces with the Yějī,
defeating Zhāng Jiànwǔ, the Prefect of Níngzhōu, at Bāoshān.
The Emperor blamed Guō Yànqīn for disturbing the Hú,
leading to their rebellion.
This incident was mentioned in the tenth month of the previous year.
21 Initially,
Guō Yuánzhāo of Jùnyí, Prefect of Jiězhōu, had a feud with Lǐ Wēnyù, the Salt Monopoly Envoy.
Emperor Yǐn of Hàn had divided Jiě, Ānyì, and Wénxǐ from Hézhōng to form Jiězhōu.
(The character "解" [jiě],
is pronounced "hù mǎi" fan;
"榷" [què],
is pronounced "gǔ yuè" fan.)
During the Jìn dynasty, there were eight Secretaries (Shàngshū Dōulìngshǐ),
with a rank of 200 piculs, who, along with the Left and Right Vice Presidents, oversaw all affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
During the Liáng dynasty, there were five,
known as the Five Secretaries.
In the early years of the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
the title Dōulìngshǐ was changed to Dōushì,
and eight were appointed.
Later, during the Northern Wèi, Chief Clerks (Zhǔshì Lìngshǐ) were established in various departments of the Imperial Secretariat.
During the Suí dynasty, Zhǔshì Lìngshǐ were also established in various ministries.
Emperor Yáng later removed the name Lìngshǐ,
changing them all to Zhǔshì.
Initially, scholars were employed for these positions,
but by the Táng dynasty, only those outside the regular official ranks were used.
By the Five Dynasties, the Bureau of Military Affairs also established Zhǔshì.
At the time of Lǐ Shǒuzhēn's rebellion,
Wēn Yù had a son in Hézhōng.
Yuánzhāo arrested and imprisoned Wēn Yù,
memorializing that he was a rebel,
and implicating Rénpǔ.
The Emperor, then a Grand Councilor,
knew it was a false accusation
and released him without questioning.
By this time,
Rénpǔ was a Grand Councilor's Attendant (Shūmì Chéngzhǐ).
Yuánzhāo, on his way back after being replaced,
was very afraid.
Passing through Luòyáng,
he told Rénpǔ's younger brother, Réndí.
Réndí said:
"My elder brother has never held a grudge against anyone in his life,
much less would he harm public affairs for private reasons!"
Upon his arrival,
on the dīnghài day,
Rénpǔ informed the Emperor,
and Yuánzhāo was made Prefect of Qìngzhōu.
22 On the jǐchǒu day,
Wáng Rénhào of Tàiyuán, Militiaman Commissioner (Tuánliànshǐ) of Dìzhōu, was made Commissioner of the Northern Bureau of the Palace Affairs (Xuānhuī Běiyuànshǐ) concurrently Deputy Grand Councilor.
23 The Lord of Táng again made Fēng Yánjǐ, Left Senior Assistant (Zuǒ Púyè), concurrently Grand Commissioner.
In the tenth month of last year,
Táng lost Tánzhōu,
and Fēng Yánjǐ was dismissed as chancellor.
24 Zhōu Xíngfēng disliked Zhāng Fǎng, Deputy Military Governor of Wǔpíng.
He said to Wáng Kuí:
"Hé Jìngzhēn, a relative of Zhāng Fǎng,
entrusted his affairs to Fǎng before his execution.
You should be wary of him."
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the gēngshēn day,
Wáng Kuí invited Zhāng Fǎng to drink,
and killed him while he was drunk.
25 On the bǐngyín day,
Cháng Sī, Military Governor of Guīdé and concurrently Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng), came to court.
On the wùchén day,
he was transferred to be Military Governor of Pínglú.
As he was about to depart,
he memorialized, saying:
"While I was in Sòngzhōu,
I lent out over 40,000 liǎng of silk to the common people.
I respectfully submit this for Your Majesty,
requesting that it be collected."
"Lent out silk" (jǔ sī) meant
lending goods to the people
and collecting silk when it was harvested.
(The character "上" [shàng],
is pronounced "shí zhǎng" fan.)
In the fifth month,
on the dīnghài day,
an imperial edict was posted in Sòngzhōu,
remitting all that Cháng Sī had lent out.
Cháng Sī
showed no sign of shame.
26 Since the late Táng dynasty,
schools everywhere had fallen into disuse.
Shǔ Wú Zhāoyì used his private wealth of a million to build schoolhouses,
and also requested that the Nine Classics be carved onto printing blocks.
The Lord of Shǔ agreed.
From then on, literature in Shǔ flourished again.
Since Sīmǎ Xiàngrú and Yáng Xióng of the Hàn dynasty,
Shǔ had been known for producing many scholars,
and the prosperity or decline of this culture depended on those in power.
27 In the sixth month,
on the rénzǐ day,
Cāngzhōu reported that Zhāng Cángyīng of Fányáng, who was in charge of military affairs at Lútái for the Qìdān, had surrendered.
28 Initially,
during the reign of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng,
the chancellors Fēng Dào and Lǐ Yú requested that Tián Mǐn, acting director of the Directorate of Education,
proofread the Nine Classics and have them carved onto printing blocks for sale.
The court approved.
On the dīngsì day,
the blocks were completed
and presented.
The carving and printing of the Nine Classics, totaling 277 volumes,
began in the third year of Chángxīng of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng
and were completed by this time,
spanning a total of twenty-eight years.
Despite the era of turmoil,
the Nine Classics were widely disseminated.
Historians say that the reason the path of the sages has not perished
is because of the transmission through writings and documents.
29 Wáng Kuí (王逵) made Zhōu Xíngfēng (周行逢) governor of Tánzhōu (潭州),
and personally led troops to attack Lǎngzhōu (朗州).
He captured it,
killed the commander Zhèng Jiào (鄭珓),
and seized Liú Yán (劉言), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wǔ'ān (武安) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
He imprisoned him in a separate lodge.
Liú Yán (劉言) was the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wǔpíng (武平) and stationed in Lǎngzhōu (朗州),
not Wǔ'ān (武安).
"Ān" (安)
should be
"Píng" (平).
Yán (言) obtained Lǎngzhōu (朗州) in the seventh month of the first year,
and was defeated at this time.
30 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Wáng Yīn (王殷) submitted three memorials requesting to enter the court,
but the emperor doubted his sincerity
and sent an envoy to stop him.
31 The Táng (唐) suffered a great drought;
wells and springs dried up,
the Huái (淮) River was fordable,
and starving people continuously crossed the Huái (淮) to the north.
Háo (濠) and Shòu (壽) dispatched troops to defend against them,
but the people fought with the soldiers and came north.
Observing the people's allegiance,
the Táng (唐) monarch and ministers could be said to be in peril.
"The people on both sides are one,
allow them to purchase rice and cross the Huái (淮)."
The Táng (唐) people then built granaries
and bought much rice to supply the army.
In the eighth month,
on the day of Jǐwèi (己未),
an edict was issued stating that Táng (唐) people carrying rice on persons or animals were allowed,
but those transporting it by boat or cart were not to be given it.
32 Wáng Kuí (王逵) sent an envoy to present a memorial,
falsely accusing
"Liú Yán (劉言) of planning to surrender Lǎngzhōu (朗州) to Táng (唐),
and also wishing to attack Tánzhōu (潭州);
his followers did not agree,
so he was deposed and imprisoned.
Your subject has already arrived in Lǎngzhōu (朗州) to pacify the military headquarters."
He also requested to move the administrative seat back to Tánzhōu (潭州).
Last year,
Liú Yán (劉言) had memorialized to move the administrative seat to Lǎngzhōu (朗州).
On the day of Jiǎxū (甲戌),
the Tongshì Shèrén (通事舍人) Zhái Guāngyì (翟光裔) was sent to Húnán (湖南) to inspect and pacify,
and Wáng Kuí's (王逵) request was granted.
Kuí (逵) returned to Chángshā (長沙),
appointed Zhōu Xíngfēng (周行逢) to manage affairs in Lǎngzhōu (朗zhou),
and then sent Pān Shūxì (潘叔嗣) to kill Liú Yán (劉言) in Lǎngzhōu (朗州).
This laid the groundwork for Pān Shūxì (潘叔嗣) to kill Wáng Kuí (王逵) and Zhōu Xíngfēng (周行逢) to kill Shūxì (叔嗣).
33 In the ninth month,
on the day of Jǐhài (己亥),
Bái Chóngzàn (白重贊), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wǔchéng (武成), reported that the breached river had been dammed.
Since the Táng (唐) dynasty, Huázhōu (滑州)
had been designated Yìchéng Jìedù (義成節度);
in the first year of Tàipíng Xīngguó (太平興國) of the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
due to Tàizōng's (太宗) former name,
it was first changed to Wǔchéng Jūn (武成軍).
At this time,

Táng Míngzōng, due to rumors among the soldiers, excessively distributed rewards,

disregarding the ruler's diligence and frugality,

All were greatly alarmed and begged forgiveness.
Upon their departure,

"Propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame
are the four pillars of a nation;
if the four pillars are not upheld,
the nation will perish."
These are the words of Guǎnzǐ.
These are the great principles for governing people;
integrity and shame
are the great virtues for establishing one's character.
How much more so for a high minister who lacks integrity and shame?
How could the world not be in chaos,
and how could the nation not perish?
I read Fényíng Dào's *Chánglèlǎo Xù*,
and saw that he described it as an honor,
which can only be called shameless.
From this, the state of the world and the nation can be understood.
Among the Five Dynasties, I found three individuals of complete integrity:
Wáng Yànzhāng, Péi Yuē, and Liú Rénshàn.
I also list Zhāng Yuándé, Xià Lǔqí, Yáo Hóng, Wáng Sītóng, Zhāng Jìngdá, Zhái Jìnzōng, Shěn Bīn, Wáng Qīng, Shǐ Yànchāo, Sūn Shèng, Mǎ Yànchāo, Sòng Lìngxún, Lǐ Xiá, Zhāng Yànqīng, and Zhèng Zhāoyè,
a total of fifteen individuals.
Could it be that there were truly no such people among scholars?
Was it that those of high integrity disdained the chaos of the times,
despised their era, and were unwilling to serve?
Or was it that those who ruled the world were not worthy of consideration,
and thus no one could attract them?
I once heard that during the Wǔdài period, there was a man named Wáng Níng,
whose home was between Qīng and Qí.
He served as Sīhù Cānjūn of Guózhōu
and died of illness while in office.
Wáng Níng's family was always poor;
he had one young son.
His wife, Lǐ Shì,
carried her son
and bore her husband's remains home.
They passed through Kāifēng to the east
and stopped at an inn,
but the innkeeper would not let them in.
Lǐ Shì saw that night had fallen
and refused to leave.
The innkeeper then grabbed her arm and forced her out.
Lǐ Shì looked up to heaven and wailed:
"I am a woman
who could not preserve her integrity,
yet this arm was seized by a man!"
She immediately took an axe and cut off her own arm.
Those who witnessed it sighed and wept for her.
The Kāifēng Yǐn heard of the matter
and reported it to the court,
generously compensating Lǐ Shì and flogging the innkeeper.
Ōuyáng Gōng obtained this story from a Wǔdài novel.
朝 (cháo),
pronounced zhí yáo fān;
same below.
Those gentlemen who do not cherish their own bodies but endure shame to cling to life,
upon hearing of Lǐ Shì's spirit,
should surely feel a little ashamed!
Chén Guāng says: Heaven and Earth established their positions,
and the sages modeled themselves on this
to formulate rites and laws,
with husband and wife within [the home]
and ruler and minister without.
A wife's devotion to her husband
remains unchanged throughout her life;
a minister's service to his ruler
is unwavering unto death.
These are the great principles of human relations.
If they are abandoned,
there is no greater chaos!
Fàn Zhì praised Féng Dào for his profound virtue and knowledge of antiquity,
his vast talent and great magnanimity.
He said that even as dynasties shifted and changed,
people had no critical remarks,
and he stood [yì] like a giant mountain,
immovable.
Upon examining Fàn Zhì's character,
it appears he was a follower of Féng Dào.
山[AS-FBEC]乞 (yì),
same as 屹 (yì),
pronounced yú qì fān.
A loyal minister does not serve two rulers.
If a woman is not proper,
even if she possesses beauty
and skill in weaving,
she is not worthy of esteem.
If a minister is not loyal,
even if he possesses great talent and intelligence,
and excels in governance,
he is not worthy of honor.
Why is this?
Because his fundamental integrity is already compromised.
Féng Dào served as prime minister
through five dynasties and eight rulers.
The five dynasties were:
Táng, Jìn, Liáo, Hàn, and Zhōu.
The eight rulers were:
Táng Zhuāngzōng, Míngzōng, and Lù Wáng, each counted as one ruler;
Shí Jìn, Yēlǜ, Liú Hàn, Zhōu Tàizǔ, and Shìzōng, each counted as one ruler.
In the morning they were enemies,
in the evening they were ruler and minister.
He changed his face and altered his words,
never once showing shame or remorse.
With such a lack of fundamental integrity,
even if he had minor virtues,
what praise is he truly worthy of?
Some might argue that ever since the fall of the Táng house,
heroes struggled for power,
and emperors rose and fell.
The longer reigns lasted a dozen years,
the shorter ones three or four years.
Even if there were loyal and wise men,
what could they do?
At such a time,
Féng Dào was not the only one who failed in his duty as a minister;
how can he alone be blamed?
My humble opinion is that a loyal minister cares for the public as his own family,
and risks his life in times of danger.
If the ruler has faults, he strongly remonstrates and argues vigorously.
If the state falls, he exhausts his loyalty unto death.
A wise man appears when the state has the Way,
and hides when the state lacks the Way,
either disappearing into the mountains and forests
or leisurely serving in lower offices.
Now, Féng Dào, in terms of honor, ranked above the Sānshī;
in terms of power and responsibility, he headed all the prime ministers.
When the state existed, he prevaricated and remained silent,
usurping his position and eating without working.
When the state fell, he sought self-preservation and escape,
welcoming and urging the new ruler to ascend.
While rulers rose and fell in succession,
Féng Dào enjoyed wealth and status as before.
This is the epitome of a treacherous minister;
how can he be compared to others?
Some say that Féng Dào was able to preserve himself and avoid harm in a chaotic world,
which is also admirable.
I say that a gentleman sacrifices his life to uphold benevolence,
and does not seek to live by harming benevolence.
This quotes the Master's words in the Lúnyǔ.
If so, then Dào Zhí died of illness, while Zǐ Lù was pickled;
who then was truly admirable?
Dào Zhí commanded nine thousand followers,
roamed freely under heaven,
and died of old age.
Zǐ Lù served in Wèi;
during the trouble involving Kǒng Kuī,
Zǐ Lù died,
and was pickled at the eastern gate of Wèi.
However, this was not merely Féng Dào's fault.
愆 (qiān),
meaning fault.
The contemporary rulers,
referring to the rulers of the five dynasties and eight surnames.
A disreputable woman
is a shame for an average gentleman to take as his wife.
A disloyal man
is a shame for an average ruler to take as his minister.
中士 (zhōngshì) and 中君 (zhōngjūn),
speaking of character,
refer to those whose insight is not superior but can be spoken to about superior matters.
To speak of his loyalty is to say he turned against his ruler to serve an enemy;
to speak of his wisdom is to say he rendered the altars of soil and grain desolate.
Yet later rulers
neither executed nor abandoned him,
but instead reinstated him as prime minister.
How then could he be willing to be truly loyal to them and be of use to them?
Therefore, it is said,
it was not merely Féng Dào's fault,
but also the responsibility of the contemporary rulers.
Wēn Gōng used this to deeply warn future rulers and ministers.
On the 25th, Xīnyǒu day,
Fú Yànqīng reported that Hán Guāngyuàn, the Cìshǐ of Xiànzhōu in Běi Hàn, and Guō Yán, the Cìshǐ of Lánzhōu, had both surrendered their cities.
Although the subordinate prefectures surrendered,
the capital prefecture was not yet captured,
making it ultimately useless.
Once the main army retreated,
the territory would again belong to the enemy.
26Previously,

His rebellious intent was thus confirmed.
When he was defeated,
Chóngxùn first killed his younger siblings
and then sought Fú Shì.
Fú Shì hid under a curtain,
and Chóngxùn, in his haste, could not find her

When the chaotic soldiers entered,
Fú Shì sat calmly in the hall
and shouted at the chaotic soldiers:

you must not be disrespectful!"
Tàizǔ sent an envoy to return her to Fú Yànqīng.
When the Emperor was stationed in Chánzhōu (
In the first year of Guǎngshùn,

On Rénxū day,

The Empress was kind, gentle, and decisive,

1. Spring,
First month,
Bǐng-wǔ day.

Xiàng Xùn, Commissioner of the Southern Bureau of Military Affairs and Jìedùshǐ of Zhèn'ān, was made acting Grand Administrator of Dōngjīng.

belonged to Yǐngzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 117 lǐ east of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Yǐngshàng County,
was Shèn County during the Hàn dynasty.
The Huái River served as a defensive line dividing north and south,
and fortifications were never more cautious than here.
In the second year of Dàyè of the Suí dynasty,
Yǐngshàng County was established south of the present county, at the old city of Zhèng,
named for its location near the upper reaches of the Yǐng River.
Rén-yín day,
the Emperor departed from Dàliáng.
Lǐ Gǔ attacked Shòuzhōu,
but failed to take it for a long time.
Liú Yànzhēn of Táng led troops to relieve it,
reaching Láiyuǎn Zhèn.
Jiǔyù Zhì states: Ānfēng County in Shòuzhōu has Láiyuǎn Zhèn.
Currently, Láiyuǎn Zhèn is Dōng Zhèngyáng,
ten lǐ west of the Féi River.
He also used hundreds of warships to approach Zhèngyáng,
creating a posture to attack the pontoon bridge.
Lǐ Gǔ feared this,
and summoned his generals and advisors to deliberate, saying:
"Our army is not skilled in naval warfare.
If the enemy cuts off the pontoon bridge,
we will be attacked from front and rear,
and none will return!
It is better to retreat and defend the pontoon bridge, awaiting the imperial carriage."
When the Emperor reached Yǔ Zhèn,
Jiǔyù Zhì states: Yōngqiū County in Kāifēng has Yǔchéng Zhèn.
he immediately sent an imperial envoy by post-horse to stop him.
By the time the envoy arrived,
Lǐ Gǔ had already burned the forage and provisions,
and retreated to secure Zhèngyáng.
Dīng-wèi day.
The Emperor arrived at Chénzhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Kāifēng Fǔ south to Chénzhōu is 330 lǐ.
Xīn-hài day.
Lǐ Gǔ memorialized that the enemy ships were advancing in midstream,
beyond the range of crossbows and catapults.
"If the pontoon bridge cannot be held,
the morale of the troops will waver,
and we will have to retreat.
Now the enemy ships are advancing daily,
and the Huái River is rising daily.
Spring waters are just beginning to rise,
which is why Lǐ Gǔ was concerned about the rising Huái River.
Should the supply route be cut off by any chance,
the danger would be immeasurable.
I request that Your Majesty temporarily stay at Chén and Yǐng,
Your servant will assess whether the enemy ships can be resisted,
and the pontoon bridge secured.
I will immediately report my findings.
However, if we sharpen our weapons and feed our horses,
and wait from spring to winter,
it would be sufficient to exhaust the enemy,
and it would not be too late to capture them."
The Emperor read the memorial,
and was displeased.
Liú Yànzhēn had always been arrogant and held noble status.
He lacked talent and strategy,
and was inexperienced in warfare.
In the various garrisons he governed,
he was exclusively greedy and tyrannical.
He amassed enormous wealth,
using it to bribe influential figures.
He believed he could govern the people like Gōng and Huáng,
and use troops like Hán and Péng.
The Táng ruler first employed him.
His subordinate generals, Xián Shīlǎng and others, were all brave but lacked strategy.
Hearing of Lǐ Gǔ's retreat,
they rejoiced,
and led troops directly to Zhèngyáng.
Their banners and baggage trains stretched for hundreds of lǐ.
Liú Rénshàn and Zhāng Quányuē, the Prefect of Chízhōu, tried firmly to stop them.
Rénshàn said:
"Your army has not yet arrived, but the enemy has already fled.
This is due to their fear of your prestige and renown.
What is the need for a swift battle?
Should we suffer a defeat by any chance,
then the great enterprise will be lost!"
Yànzhēn did not listen.
After they had set out,
Rénshàn said:
"If they indeed encounter [the enemy],
they will surely be defeated."
He then added troops to man the city walls as a precaution.
(He) engaged the enemy in battle east of Zhèngyáng,
and utterly defeated them.
Xián Shīlǎng and others were captured alive.
Over ten thousand heads were cut off.
Corpses lay strewn for thirty lǐ.
Over three hundred thousand items of military supplies and equipment were seized.
At this time, Jiāng and Huái had long been peaceful,
and the people were unaccustomed to warfare.
Once Yànzhēn was defeated,
the Táng people were greatly alarmed.
Zhāng Quányuē gathered the remaining troops and fled to Shòuzhōu.
Liú Rénshàn memorialized to appoint Quányuē as Commander-in-chief of the Left Flank of Cavalry and Infantry.
Huángfǔ Huī and Yáo Fèng retreated to defend Qīngliú Guān.
The Liáng dynasty established Nánqiáo Zhōu south of Sānggēn Shān,
80 lǐ southwest of Qīngliú Xiàn in Chúzhōu.
The Suí dynasty first established Qīngliú Xiàn,
which became the seat of Chúzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
Qīngliú Guān is over 20 lǐ southwest of the county seat,
and was established by the Nán Táng.
On the day of Rénzǐ,
the Emperor arrived at Yǒngníngzhèn.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: "Huángzhōu's Máchéngxiàn has a Yǒngníngzhèn."
This is incorrect.
Máchéng is several hundred *lǐ* southwest of Shòuzhōu,
and the Emperor had not yet crossed the Huái River.
How could he have reached the Yǒngníngzhèn of Máchéng?
Upon further examination of the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Yǐngzhōu's Rǔyīnxiàn has a Yǒngníngzhèn,
which is over a hundred *lǐ* east of Zhèngyáng.
This is the correct one.
"It is heard that the siege of Shòuzhōu has been lifted,
and many peasants have returned to their villages.
Now that the great army is heard to be approaching,
they will surely re-enter the city.
Pitying them for gathering together only to starve to death,
it is advisable to first send envoys to comfort and reassure them,
and order each to settle in their livelihoods."
On the day of Jiǎyín,
the Emperor arrived at Zhèngyáng.
He replaced Lǐ Gǔ with Lǐ Chóngjìn as the Dūzhāotǎoshǐ of the Huáinán Dào Xíngyíng,
and appointed Gǔ to manage the affairs of Shòuzhōu Xíngfǔ.
Sòng Mǐnqiú said: "Generally, a Jiédùzhōu is of the third rank,
and an Cìshǐzhōu is of the fifth rank.
In the early days of the dynasty,
Cáo Hàn, as Guānchásǐ, managed Yǐngzhōu,
which was a fourth-rank official overseeing a fifth-rank prefecture.
'Zhī' (知) is used for officials of the same rank,
'Pàn' (判) for officials of a different rank.
Thereafter, only Fǔchén, Xuānhuīshǐ, Tàizǐ Tàibǎo, and Púshè were designated 'Pàn,'
while all others were 'Zhīzhōu.'"
On the day of Bǐngchén,
the Emperor arrived beneath the walls of Shòuzhōu,
camping on the sunny side of the Féishǔi.
The Féishǔi flows from the borders of Ānfēngxiàn into the borders of Shòuchūnxiàn,
passing north of Shòuchūn city and entering the Huái River,
two *lǐ* from the city.
The north bank is the sunny side.
The pontoon bridge from Zhèngyáng was moved to Xiàcàizhèn.
Táng Yǐngzhōu had a Xiàcàixiàn;
at that time, the county was abolished and made into a town,
fifty-five *lǐ* west of Zhèngyáng.
On the day of Dīngsì,
tens of thousands of able-bodied men from Sòng, Bó, Chén, Yǐng, Xú, Sù, Xǔ, and Cài prefectures were conscripted to attack the city,
ceaselessly, day and night.
Over ten thousand Táng soldiers moored their boats on the Huái River,
camping at the foot of Túshān.
Túshān is in Háozhōu,
originally the city of the Túshān clan,
where Yǔ gathered the feudal lords;
it is now ninety-five *lǐ* west of Zhōnglíxiàn.
By the Huái River is the old city of the Hàn dynasty's Dāngtúxiàn,
which, during the wars of the Southern and Northern Dynasties,
became the city of Mǎtóujùn.
The Huái River flows east to the north of the city,
and the Wō River comes from the northwest to join the Huái,
forming the Wōkǒu,
with the south bank directly opposite Mǎtóuchéng.
On the day of Gēngshēn,
the Emperor ordered Tàizǔ Huángdì to attack them.
Tàizǔ Huángdì sent over a hundred cavalrymen to approach their camp and feign retreat.
Ambush troops intercepted them,
heavily defeating the Táng soldiers at Wōkǒu,
beheading their Dūjiān Hé Yánxī and others,
and capturing over fifty warships.
5 An imperial edict appointed Wǔpíng Jiédùshǐ and concurrently Zhōngshūlìng Wáng Kuí as the Dūtǒng of the Nánmiàn Xíngyíng,
ordering him to attack Táng's Èzhōu.
Kuí led his troops past Yuèzhōu.
Yuèzhōu Tuánliànshǐ Pān Shūxì (潘叔嗣) lavishly prepared feasts and provisions,
serving him with great deference.
Kuí's attendants were insatiably demanding.
Those whose desires were not met slandered Shūxì to Kuí,
saying he was plotting rebellion.
Kuí's anger showed in his words and demeanor,
causing Shūxì to be afraid and unsettled.
This sets the stage for Pān Shūxì's killing of Wáng Kuí.
The Táng ruler, hearing that the Húnán army was approaching,
ordered Wǔchāng Jiédùshǐ Hé Jìngzhū to move the populace into the city,
as a strategy for firm defense.
Jìngzhū did not comply,
but instead cleared the ground for a battlefield,
saying:
"When the enemy arrives,
I shall die here with the army and people!"
Hé Jìngzhū, as a general,
was also a good man of Táng.
Due to Wáng Kuí's misfortune at the hands of Pān Shūxì,
his name was further cemented.
6 In the second month,
on the day of Bǐngyín,
the Xiàcài pontoon bridge was completed, and the Emperor personally went to inspect it.
On the day of Wùchén,
the Lú, Shòu, Guāng, and Huáng Xúnjiǎnshǐsī

Sī,

captured Dūjiān Gāo Bì and others,
and seized over forty warships.
The Emperor ordered Tàizǔ Huángdì to march double speed to ambush Qīngliúguān.
Huángfǔ Huī and others arrayed themselves at the foot of the mountain,
fighting with the vanguard,
while Tàizǔ Huángdì led troops out from behind the mountain.
Huī and his men were greatly alarmed,
and fled into Chúzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: "The land of Chúzhōu,
during the Liú Sòng dynasty, was Xīnchāng Jùn.
The Liáng dynasty established Nánqiáozhōu west of Sānggēnshānxī.
The old city of Nánqiáo, eighteen *lǐ* southwest of the current prefectural seat, is it.
The Northern Qí moved Xīnchāng Jùn from Nánqiáo;
the current prefectural city is it.
The Suí dynasty abolished the prefecture,
making its territory Qīngliúxiàn.
The Táng dynasty made it Chúzhōu."
Tàizǔ Huángdì spurred his horse and waved his troops to cross the water,
directly reaching the city walls.
Huī said:
"Each man fights for his own lord.
I wish to be allowed to form ranks and fight."
Huángfǔ Huī received the grace of being nurtured by Táng Zhuāngzōng.
When he suddenly rebelled,
Zhuāngzōng perished because of him.
Abandoning the Central Plains and fleeing to Jiāngnán,
he pledged allegiance to Táng,
and now says "each man fights for his own lord."
This was likely due to the pressure of the advancing army,
in panic and disarray,
making this statement to parley with the enemy.
Tàizǔ, confident in his wisdom and bravery to handle Huángfǔ Huī,
therefore permitted it.
Tàizǔ Huángdì, gripping his horse's neck, charged into the formation,
shouting loudly:
"I only seek Huángfǔ Huī!
No one else is my enemy!"
He struck Huī with his sword,
hitting him in the head,
capturing him alive,
and also capturing Yáo Fèng,
thus conquering Chúzhōu.
Several days later,
Xuānzǔ Huángdì, who was the Mǎjūn Fù Dūzhīhuīshǐ,
Xuānzǔ's taboo name was Hóngyīn.
called out to open the city gates.
Tàizǔ Huángdì said:
"Though father and son are the closest of kin,
the city gate is a matter of state.
I dare not obey your command."
The Emperor sent Hànlín Xuéshì Dòu Yí to inventory the treasury of Chúzhōu.
Tàizǔ Huángdì sent a trusted subordinate to take silk from the treasury.
Yí said:
"When Your Excellency first captured the city,
even if you had emptied the treasury,
there would have been no harm.
Now that it has been inventoried as government property,
without an imperial edict,
it cannot be taken."
Dòu Yí was steadfast.
How could Tàizǔ's sagacity and discernment
be matched by any ordinary general of his time!
Earlier,
Yǒngxīng Jiédùshǐ Liú Cí left a memorial recommending his staff member Zhào Pǔ from Jì as a talented individual who could be useful.
Coincidentally, after Chúzhōu was pacified,
Fàn Zhì recommended Pǔ as the Jūnshì Pànguān of Chúzhōu.
Tàizǔ Huángdì spoke with him
and was pleased.
At that time, over a hundred bandits were captured,
all of whom deserved death.
Pǔ requested that they first be interrogated before judgment,
saving seventeen or eighteen lives.
Tàizǔ Huángdì admired him even more.
Tàizǔ valued Dòu Yí and admired Zhào Pǔ,
both during his hidden and rising periods.
Pǔ thereafter became a chief architect of the founding of the dynasty,
while Yí was eventually envied by Pǔ and did not reach the rank of prime minister.
Tàizǔ Huángdì's prestige and fame grew daily.
Whenever he approached the battle lines,
he would always adorn his horse with elaborate tassels,
and his armor and weapons would be brightly polished.
Someone said:
"Doing this
makes you recognizable to the enemy."
Tàizǔ Huángdì said:
"I indeed wish for them to recognize me!"
The ruler of Táng dispatched Wáng Zhīlǎng (王知朗), an aide-de-camp from Sīzhōu, bearing a letter to Xúzhōu,
stating:
"The Táng Emperor respectfully presents this letter to the Great Zhōu Emperor,
requesting to cease hostilities and restore friendly relations.
We wish to serve Your Majesty as an elder brother,
and annually supply goods and wealth to aid in military expenses."
On the Jiǎxū day,
Xúzhōu reported this;
the Jiǔyù Zhì states: Sīzhōu is seven hundred and fifty *lǐ* northwest of Xúzhōu.
Wáng Zhīlǎng did not dare to go to the front lines but instead went to Xúzhōu,
fearing to encounter the point of the sword and die.
This was because the Táng ruler still dared to insist on equal status,
wishing to establish a brotherhood of nations.
On the Wùyín day,
an order was given to Hóu Zhāng (侯章) and others, formerly military governors of Wǔshèng, to attack the water fortresses of Shòuzhōu,
breaching the northwest corner of their moats,
and diverting the moat water into the Féi River.
Grand Ancestor Emperor dispatched an envoy to present Huángfǔ Huī (皇甫暉) and others.
Huī was severely wounded,
and when he saw the Emperor,
he lay down and said:
"This subject was not disloyal to whom he served,
but merely the bravery and cowardice of the soldiers differ."
"In the past, this subject frequently fought against the Qìdān."
Huángfǔ Huī was originally a Wèi soldier.
Táng Zhuāngzōng sent him to garrison Wǎqiáo to resist the Qìdān,
and he subsequently rebelled.
His claim of frequently fighting the Qìdān
was likely during his time garrisoning Wǎqiáo.
He then extensively praised the bravery of Grand Ancestor Emperor.
The Emperor pardoned him,
and he died a few days later.
The Emperor secretly learned that Yángzhōu was unprepared.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
he ordered Hán Lìngkūn (韓令坤) and others to lead troops to attack it,
admonishing them not to harm the civilians.
As for the ancestral tombs of the Lǐ clan,
he sent people to guard them jointly with members of the Lǐ clan.
The Táng ruler's forces were repeatedly defeated,
and fearing annihilation,

he dispatched Zhōng Mó (鍾謨), a Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of Revenue, and Lǐ Démíng (李德明), a Vice Minister of Works and Academician of the Wénlǐyuan, to present a memorial declaring allegiance
and request peace,
offering imperial robes, medicinal
concoctions, one thousand *liǎng* of gold vessels,
five thousand *liǎng* of silver vessels,
two thousand bolts of silk brocade,
five hundred oxen for the army,
and two thousand *hú* of wine.
On the Rénwǔ day,
they arrived at the foot of Shòuzhōu city.
Mó and Démíng were known for their eloquence.
The Emperor knew they intended to use persuasion,
so he displayed a grand array of armed soldiers when he received them,
and said:
"Your ruler claims to be a descendant of the Táng imperial house."
Southern Táng's ancestor was Lǐ Kè (李恪), the Prince of Wú, son of Emperor Táng Tàizōng.
"This makes you different from other states.
Only a single body of water separates you from Us."
It means the Huái River served as the boundary between Southern Táng and Zhōu.
"Yet you sail across the sea to communicate with the Qìdān,
abandoning the Huá (Chinese) to serve the Yí (barbarians).
Where is your propriety and righteousness?"
Ever since Xú Wēn took control of Wú's government, he repeatedly sailed across the sea to send envoys to the Qìdān,
wishing to collude with them to conquer the Central Plains.
This continued with Táng Lièzǔ and the current ruler.
"We are not the foolish rulers of the Six States;
how can We be swayed by your glib tongues?"
This refers to the Six States all having foolish rulers,
which allowed Su (Su Qin) and Zhang (Zhang Yi) to engage in their persuasive rhetoric.
If they had met a sagacious and wise monarch,
even with their eloquence,
they could not have swayed him.
"Come quickly to see Us,
kowtow and apologize for your faults,
and there will be no trouble.
Otherwise,
We wish to view the city of Jīnlíng,
and borrow its treasuries to reward Our army.
Will your ruler and subjects not regret it then?"
Mó and Démíng trembled and dared not speak.
Wúyuè Wáng Hóngchù (吳越王弘俶) dispatched troops to garrison the border, awaiting Zhōu's command.
Chén Mǎn (陳滿), the Commander of Field Operations in Sūzhōu, spoke to Chancellor Wú Chéng (吳程), saying:
"The Zhōu army is campaigning southwards,
and the entire Táng state is in turmoil and alarm.
Chángzhōu is unprepared
and easy to take."
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Sūzhōu is over one hundred and eighty *lǐ* northwest of Chángzhōu.
Yì,
pronounced like *chǐ*.
Jiāngyīn Xiàn
was originally Jìyáng Xiàn of Jìn's Pílíng Commandery.
On the left bank of the Yangzi, Lánlíng Xiàn was established by division.
During the time of Liáng Jìngdì,
Jiāngyīn Commandery and Jiāngyīn Xiàn were once established.
The Suí abolished them.
The Táng established Jìzhōu.
Southern Táng first established Jiāngyīn Jūn.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is ninety *lǐ* northeast of Chángzhōu.
"The Zhōu edict has already arrived."
Chéng spoke to Hóngchù about this,
requesting to immediately dispatch troops according to his plan.
Chancellor Yuán Dézhāo (元德昭) said:
"Táng is a great state and should not be underestimated yet.
If we enter Táng territory and the Zhōu army does not arrive,
who will combine forces with us?
Will we not be in danger?
I request that we wait for a while."
Chéng strongly argued,
believing that the opportunity should not be lost,
and Hóngchù ultimately followed Chéng's advice.
On the Guǐwèi day,
he dispatched Chéng to supervise Bāo Xiūrang (鮑脩讓), the Prefect of Qúzhōu, and Luó Shèng (羅晟), the Commander of the Middle Guard, to proceed to Chángzhōu.
Chéng said to his officers and soldiers:
"Chancellor Yuán does not wish to send out the army."
The officers and soldiers were enraged,
and rumors circulated that they wanted to attack Dézhāo.
The Wúyuè officers and soldiers, emboldened by their victory at Fúzhōu,
believed that Táng could be exploited.
That arrogant troops are defeated,
how can that be empty words!
He ordered the arrest of those who spread rumors
and sighed,
saying:
"Just as we are about to launch an expedition, the soldiers want to attack the Chancellor.
How extremely inauspicious!"
On the Yǐyǒu day,
Hán Lìngkūn arrived suddenly at Yángzhōu.
At dawn,
he first sent Bái Yányù (白延遇) with several hundred cavalry to gallop into the city,
and the city residents did not notice them.
Lìngkūn followed shortly after.
Jiǎ Chóng (賈崇), the Táng Director of Barracks in the Eastern Capital, burned government offices and civilian homes,
abandoning the city and fleeing south.
Fēng Yánlǔ (馮延魯), the Vice Administrator of the Eastern Capital and Vice Minister of Works, shaved his head and donned monastic robes,
hiding in a Buddhist temple.
Táng designated Yángzhōu as the Eastern Capital,
hence the establishment of a Vice Administrator.
Kūn,
pronounced like *kǔkūn*.
Bèi,
pronounced like *píyì*.
Lìngkūn comforted and pacified the people,
ensuring they all settled down.
On the Gēngyín day,
Wáng Kuí (王逵) reported the capture of the Chángshān fortress in Èzhōu.
Chángshān
is on the southern border of Èzhōu.
Táng had established fortresses to defend against Tánzhōu and Lǎngzhōu.
He presented it.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
Grand Ancestor Emperor reported that Gěng Qiān (耿謙), the Táng Commissioner of Tiāncháng, had surrendered.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo of Táng,
land from Jiāngdū, Lùhé, and Gāoyóu counties was divided
to establish Qiānqiū Xiàn.
In the seventh year,
its name was changed to Tiāncháng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Tiāncháng Xiàn is one hundred and ten *lǐ* west of Yángzhōu.
The Táng ruler dispatched Yǐn Yánfàn (尹延範), the Director of Imperial Gardens, to Tàizhōu.
The Liáng dynasty had a Palace Garden Director,
and also an Inner Garden Grafting Director.
The Táng establishment of a Director of Imperial Gardens was similar.
In the fourth year of Tiānfú of Jìn,
Táng Lièzǔ moved the imperial clan of Rànghuáng from Rùnzhōu to Tàizhōu.
Now, with the Zhōu army pressing,
they were again moved to Rùnzhōu.
Fearing that the Yáng clan would cause trouble,
he executed all sixty of their male members.
Upon his return and report,
the Táng ruler was enraged
and had him cut in half at the waist.
Hán Lìngkūn and others attacked Tài
zhōu

Southern Táng had elevated Hǎilíng Town to Tàizhōu.

From Tàizhōu, they hurried south to Tàixīng Xiàn,
crossed the river to seize Rùnzhōu, and then proceeded to Jīnlíng.
The Táng ruler sent someone with a wax pill message to seek help from the Qìdān.
On the Rénchén day,
Hé Jìyūn (何繼筠), the Commander of Jìng'ān Jūn, captured and presented it.
Last year, the Emperor established Jìng'ān Jūn at Lǐyànkǒu.
Gāo Fáng (高防), a Minister of the Remonstrance Bureau, was temporarily appointed as the Administrator of Tàizhōu.
On the Guǐsì day,
Wúyuè Wáng Hóngchù dispatched Lù Yànzhū (路彥銖), the Commander of the Palace Guard, to attack Xuānzhōu.
Luó Shèng led warships and garrisoned Jiāngyīn.
Yáo Yànhóng (姚彥洪), the Táng Commissioner of Jìnghǎi, led ten thousand soldiers and civilians to flee to Wúyuè.
14 Pān Shūsì (潘叔嗣) addressed his officers and soldiers, saying:
"I have served the Lord Commander (lìng gōng 令公) to the utmost.
Now he believes slanders and is angered by suspicions.
When the army returns,

The multitude was enraged [and]
requested to go.
Shūsì (叔嗣) led them west to raid Lǎngzhōu (朗州).

"Wáng Kuí (王逵) received an imperial edict to attack Wú (吳).
Innumerable bees gathered on Kuí's (逵) umbrella canopy.
Zhōu Xíngfèng (周行逢) was secretly pleased,
and secretly plotted with Pān Shūsì (潘叔嗣), Zhāng Wénbiǎo (張文表), and others, saying: 'I see a strange omen for Lord Wáng (Wáng Gōng 王公) (bees) entering his umbrella.
If he should one day fall into the hands of another,
where would we stand?
If the three of us are united,
and together preserve the old foundation of the Mǎ (馬) family,
and together achieve wealth and honor,
would that not be a true man's deed!'
Shūsì (叔嗣) and Wénbiǎo (文表), hearing Xíngfèng's (行逢) words,
already understood the deep meaning.
So they bowed and accepted these words,
and each dispersed to their camps."
The Guǎngběn (廣本) says:
"Kuí (逵) ordered the Assistant Field Army Commander Máo Lì (毛立) to be the Yúan zhōu (袁州) Camp Commander,
and Pān Shūsì (潘叔嗣) and Zhāng Wénbiǎo (張文表) to be the vanguards.
When the army reached Lǐlíng Xiàn (醴陵縣),
the officials requested to provide oxen and wine to reward the army,
but Lì (立) refused.
Shūsì (叔嗣) and Wénbiǎo (文表), seizing on the anger of the soldiers,
bound Lì (立)
and sent him to Xíngfèng (行逢),
and reported their rebellion to Kuí (逵) with their troops.
Kuí (逵) was greatly frightened,
and fled to Lǎngzhōu (朗州) on a light boat.
Shūsì (叔嗣) pursued him to Lǎngzhōu (朗州)
and killed him."
The Húxiāng Gùshì (湖湘故事) says:
"Kuí (逵) fled back to Lǎngzhōu (朗州) overnight.
Several days later,
Pān Shūsì (潘叔嗣) first arrived in Tánzhōu (潭州).
Hearing that Wáng Kuí (王逵) had fled back to Lǎngzhōu (朗州),
he also hastened by boat, doubling his journey,
and arriving in Lǎngzhōu (朗州),
killed him."
Now, according to the Shìzōng Shílù (世宗實錄):
"On the bǐngyín (丙寅) day of the second month of Xiǎndé (顯德) 3rd year (956),
Wáng Jìnkuí (王進逵) of Lǎngzhōu (朗州) reported [he]
led a large army into the Huáinán (淮南) border;
on the gēngyín (庚寅) day, he reported entering the Èzhōu (鄂州) border
and capturing Chángshān Zhài (長山寨).
On the guǐsì (癸巳) day,
Gāo Bǎoróng (高保融) of Jīngnán (荊南) reported that Jìnkuí (進逵) led his troops from Èzhōu (鄂州) back to his own territory."
It also says:
"Pān Shūsì (潘叔嗣) was the vanguard.
When he reached Èzhōu (鄂州),
Shūsì (叔嗣) turned his spear and attacked Wǔlíng (武陵).
Jìnkuí (進逵), hearing this,
doubled his pace and entered Wǔlíng (武陵 first.
Shūsì (叔嗣) attacked the city.
Jìnkuí (進逵) was defeated and fled,
and was killed by Shūsì (叔嗣)."
It also says:
"On the rényín (壬寅) day of the third month,
Jìnkuí (進逵) dispatched a tooth-general to escort Chén Zé (陳澤) and other generals from Huáinán (淮南)."
It is probable that Jìnkuí (進逵) submitted his report before his defeat,
and it reached the provisional court only in the third month.
This is generally consistent with Xuē Shǐ (薛史) and the records transmitted from Húnán (湖南).
Only the Húxiāng Gùshì (湖湘故事) and Dīng Shú (丁璹)'s Mǎshì Xíngshì (馬氏行事) record Kuí's (逵) attack on Yúan zhōu (袁州) and Shūsì's (叔嗣) rebellion.
Cáo Yǎn (曹衍) says:
"Kuí (逵) arrived in Tánzhōu (潭州) in the third month.
In the fourth month,
Shūsì (叔嗣) rebelled."
Dīng Shú (丁璹) says:
"On the fifth day of the fifth month,
Shūsì (叔嗣) killed Kuí (逵) in Lǎngzhōu (朗州)."
All are erroneous.
When Zhōu Xíngfèng (周行逢) held Húnán (湖南),
official advancement still depended on family connections.
Yǎn (衍) repeatedly offered his writings,
but could not obtain a position.
He retired to his hometown to teach.
When Zhāng Wénbiǎo (張文表) rebelled,
Yǎn (衍) was appointed to a staff position.
When the affair failed,
he fled.
He was granted amnesty,
and then dared to emerge.
Impoverished and unable to advance himself,
he collected old accounts
and compiled twenty volumes of Húxiāng Mǎshì Gùshì (湖湘馬氏故事),
presenting them to the capital.
Tàizōng (太宗) pitied him for being poor and old,
and appointed him as Jiāngzuò Jiāncéng (將作監丞).
Yǎn (衍) was originally a petty person;
his language was vulgar and crude.
He did not intend to write a book,
so his narrative is disordered,
with contradictions between earlier and later parts,
and numerous instances of fabricating what did not exist.
He harbored a long-standing grudge against Zhōu Xíngfèng (周行逢)
and particularly slandered and defamed him.
Not wishing Xíngfèng (行逢) to be uninvolved in Shūsì's (叔嗣) plot,
he fabricated this account.
All the most egregious crimes attributed to Xíngfèng (行逢)
originate from Yǎn (衍)'s words.
Shú (璹) was also an early Song dynasty person.
It is suspected that his account was derived from Yǎn (衍)'s book,
and thus none can be taken as reliable.
We now follow the Shíguó Jìnián (十國紀年).
Someone advised Shūsì (叔嗣) to seize Lǎngzhōu (朗州).
Shūsì (叔嗣) said:
"I merely sought to escape death;
how dare I exalt myself?
It is appropriate to return the ducal residence to the Grand Commandant (tàiwèi 太尉) of Tánzhōu (潭州)."
At that time, Húxiāng (湖湘) regarded Lǎngzhōu (朗州) as the ducal residence.
The Grand Commandant (tàiwèi 太尉) of Tánzhōu (潭州)
refers to Zhōu Xíngfèng (周行逢).
This means Xíngfèng (行逢) would surely assign Tánzhōu (潭州) to himself.
"Chù" (處),
pronounced as "chānglǚ fān" (昌呂翻).
(He) sent the Commander of the Training Corps Li Jiǎn (李簡)
Pān Shūsì (潘叔嗣) was the Commander of the Yuèzhōu (岳州) Training Corps, and the Commander (pànguān 判官) was his subordinate.
The multitude said to Xíngfèng (行逢):
"You will surely bestow Tánzhōu (潭州) upon Shūsì (叔嗣)."
"Wèi" (謂)
means to tell or
to speak.
"Shūsì (叔嗣) treacherously murdered his commander;
his crime deserves execution of his clan.
What can be forgiven
is that he obtained Wǔlíng (武陵) but did not keep it,
instead handing it over to us.
If you immediately appoint him as a Jìedùshǐ (節度使),
the world will say that we conspired with him.
How can we clear ourselves?
It is proper to provisionally make him an Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬),
and after a year,
then bestow upon him the insignia of authority."
Seeing this,
Zhōu Xíngfèng (周行逢) originally intended to follow orders and campaign against Pān Shūsì (潘叔嗣).
Because Shūsì (叔嗣) welcomed him,
he did not carry it out.
(Xíngfèng (行逢)) led his troops into Lǎngzhōu (朗州),
proclaimed himself acting military commissioner of Wǔpíng (武平) and Wǔ'ān (武安),
and reported it to the imperial court.
Xíngfèng (行逢) wanted to hold both Tán (潭) and Lǎng (朗) simultaneously.
Shūsì (叔嗣) was angered
and feigned illness, not attending.
Xíngfèng (行逢) said:
"Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬)
is a position I once held."
Zhōu Xíngfèng (周行逢) was Wǔ'ān (武安) Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬);
see volume 291, Tàizǔ Guǎngshùn (太祖廣順) 3rd year.
"Shūsì (叔嗣) is still not satisfied.
Does he intend to plot against me again?"
Someone advised Xíngfèng (行逢):
"Grant Shūsì (叔嗣) the military commission of Wǔ'ān (武安) to lure him.
Order him to come to the ducal residence to receive the appointment.
Then he will be meat on the chopping block!"
Xíngfèng (行逢) followed this advice.
When Shūsì (叔嗣) was about to leave,
his close associates tried to stop him.
Shūsì (叔嗣) relied on the fact that he had always treated Xíngfèng (行逢) as an elder brother,
and that they were close and friendly.
The matter of Xíngfèng (行逢) and Shūsì (叔嗣) being close and friendly
first appeared in volume 291, Tàizǔ Guǎngshùn (太祖廣順) 2nd year, 9th month.
Xíngfèng (行逢) sent envoys to welcome him,
with their paths visible to each other along the way.
When he arrived,
(Xíngfèng (行逢)) personally went out to the outskirts to greet him,
and they met with great joy.
Shūsì (叔嗣) entered to pay his respects.
Before he reached the administrative hall,
(Xíngfèng (行逢)) sent someone to seize him,
had him stand in the courtyard,
and reproached him, saying:
"You were a mere junior officer without great merit.
Wáng Kuí (王逵) appointed you as a Commander of the Training Corps.
One day you suddenly turned and killed your commander!
Out of consideration for our past relationship,
I could not bear to execute you,
and appointed you as an Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬).
How dare you defy my command and refuse to accept it!"
Shūsì (叔嗣) knew he could not escape,
and pleaded for his clan.
(Xíngfèng (行逢)) then executed him.
