Later Scholarship, Tiāntái
Xiǎndé 3rd year (bǐngchén, 956)
1 In the third month,
on the jiǎwǔ day, the first day of the month,
the Emperor went to inspect the water encampment.
Arriving at the Fěi Bridge,
he personally picked up a stone
and carried it on horseback to the encampment for the catapults.
All officials who crossed the bridge also carried one stone each.
Emperor Tàizǔ rode a leather boat into the moat of Shòuchūn.
From atop the city walls, continuous crossbows were fired at him.
A leather boat
is made by sewing ox hides.
Continuous crossbows
are what are now called "huáchēnǔ".
Shè [meaning "shoot"],
also pronounced "ér yì fān".
The牙將 Yájìang, Zhāng Qióng of Guǎntáo, immediately shielded him with his body.
An arrow struck Zhāng Qióng's thigh,
and he died but then revived.
The arrowhead was lodged in the bone and could not be removed.
Zhāng Qióng drank a large goblet of wine
and ordered someone to break the bone to extract it.
Several liters of blood flowed,
but his demeanor was completely self-possessed.
History speaks of Zhāng Qióng's bravery.
Later, when Emperor Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Zhāng Qióng to command all the palace guards.
The ruler of Táng again appointed the Right Grand Master of the Secretariat Sūn Shèng as Minister of Works
and sent him, along with Minister of Rites Wáng Chóngzhì, to present a memorial and have an audience.
It stated:
"Since the Tiānyòu reign period,
the realm has fragmented.
Some occupy one region,
or have experienced dynastic changes.
'Occupying one region'
refers to the states that seized territory in the four directions.
'Experienced dynastic changes'
refers to the Central Plains frequently changing rulers.
Although we possess the Jiangbiǎo region,
considering that the 'watching the crow' is not yet settled,
how can we attach ourselves to the phoenix?
The Shī says: 'Where does the crow watch and stop?
On whose house?'
Gěng Chún of Hàn said:
'Climb the dragon's scales,
attach to the phoenix's wings.'
This means that if the true lord has not yet appeared,
then there is no one to whom to pledge allegiance.
If your moral influence extends far,
we wish to be like the two Zhè and Húnán,
respectfully accepting your legitimate rule,
and diligently guarding our borders.
The two Zhè, since Qián Liú,
and Húnán, since Mǎ Yīn,
have both for generations served the Central Plains.
Bó
means 'to press'.
Having bells and drums is called 'fá'.
The Shī says: 'Bó fá Xīróng.'
It also says: 'Bó fá Xiǎnyǔn.'
Beginning with a subordinate state,
and becoming your outer vassals,
then who will not submit
to your virtue of pacifying the distant? "
They also offered a thousand liǎng of gold,
one hundred thousand liǎng of silver,
and two thousand bolts of patterned silk.
Sūn Shèng said to Féng Yánjǐ:
"This mission should be undertaken by the Left Chancellor,
as Táng made Féng Yánjǐ the Left Grand Master of the Secretariat,
whose position was above Sūn Shèng,
which is why Sūn Shèng said this.
Otherwise, I would fail the late Emperor."
After he set out,
knowing that he would not escape,
in the middle of the night,
he sighed and said to Wáng Chóngzhì:
"Your family has a hundred mouths;
you should plan for yourself.
I have thought it through,
and I will never betray the 'yī péi tǔ' of Yǒnglíng;
I know nothing else!"
Yǒnglíng
was the tomb of the Táng ruler's father, Biàn.
Péi,
pronounced "pú méi fān".
Lù Guīméng of Táng, in his poem on building a city, said:
"On the city wall, yī péi tǔ;
in hand, ten million pestles."
Thus, péi tǔ means to add earth.
Yī péi tǔ
is like saying 'add one basketful of earth';
also pronounced "bó kǒu fān".
The Shuōwén says: Péilǒu
is a small mound.
Yī péi tǔ
is like saying 'a mound of earth'.
Ōu's History writes
"yī pōu tǔ".
【Zhāng: The Yǐ shíyī Háng Běn correctly writes
"pōu";
the Kǒng Běn is the same.
2 The Gānquán Palace Administrator of Southern Hàn, Lín Yányù,
was insidious and resourceful.
The ruler of Southern Hàn relied on and trusted him.
The extermination of his younger brothers
was all Lín Yányù's doing.
The matter of the Southern Hàn ruler executing his younger brothers has been mentioned before.
On the yǐwèi day,
the people of the state congratulated each other.
Lín Yányù fell seriously ill
and recommended the Palace Service Official, Gōng Chéngshū, to succeed him.
The ruler of Southern Hàn immediately promoted Gōng Chéngshū to oversee the Chéngxūan Office and the Palace Service Department.
Gōng Chéngshū
was from Pānyú.
Gōng Chéngshū succeeded Lín Yányù in power,
and Southern Hàn subsequently perished.
Fān
is pronounced "pān".
Yú,
pronounced "yú róng fān",
also pronounced "yú".

3 Hé Chāo, the Pacification Inspector of Guāng, Shū, and Huáng prefectures, and acting Prefect of Guāng prefecture, attacked Guāng prefecture with several tens of thousands of troops from the four prefectures of Ān, Suí, Shēn, and Cài.
The Jiǔ Yù Zhì says: Guāng prefecture
is six hundred lǐ southwest of Ān prefecture.
Suí prefecture is two hundred forty lǐ east of Ān prefecture,
and two hundred fifty lǐ northeast of Shēn prefecture.
Shēn prefecture is two hundred fifty-five lǐ east of Guāng prefecture.
Guāng prefecture is two hundred fifty lǐ north of Cài prefecture.
It was an attack by surrounding neighboring prefectural troops.
On the bǐngshēn day,
Hé Chāo reported that Zhāng Shào, the Táng Prefect of Guāng prefecture, abandoned the city and fled.
The Supervisor, Zhāng Chénghàn, surrendered the city.
On the dīngyǒu day,
Guō Língtú, the acting Prefect of Shū prefecture, captured Shū prefecture.
Lǐ Fú, a Táng general from Qí prefecture, killed its prefect Wáng Chéngxì
and surrendered the entire prefecture.
Qí Cángzhēn, the Director of the Six Bureaus, was sent to attack Huáng prefecture.
The Jiǔ Yù Zhì says: Shū prefecture
is two hundred ninety-eight lǐ west of Qí prefecture.
Qí prefecture is two hundred ten lǐ west of Huáng prefecture.
All three prefectures border the river.
4 Lǐ Yàn'yūn, the Acting Military Governor of Zhāngwǔ,
was greedy and cruel.
His people, along with the Qiāng and Hú, rebelled
and attacked him.
The Emperor summoned Lǐ Yàn'yūn back to court.
He was summoned back from Yán prefecture.
Huán,
pronounced "cóng xuān fān",
also as written.
Cháo,
pronounced "zhí yáo fān".
5 The pacification of Qín and Fèng
is recounted in the previous volume from the previous year.
The Wǔ Dài Huì Yào says: In the twelfth month of the second year of Xiǎndé,
the Sīchuān troops captured in the newly recovered Qín and Fèng prefectures were assigned to the Huái'ēn Army,
meaning they were enlisted in the army register.
They later deserted and defected to Táng.
On the guǐmǎo day,
the ruler of Táng presented a memorial offering one hundred fifty men;
the Emperor ordered them all to be executed.
6 The people of Shū prefecture drove out Guō Língtú.
Wáng Shěnqí of Luòyáng, the Commander of the Iron Cavalry, selected light cavalry
and launched a night raid on Shū prefecture,
recapturing it.
Guō Língtú was then able to return.
He was able to return to Shū prefecture.
7 Mǎ Xīchóng and Wáng Yánzhèng's son Jìyí were both in Yángzhōu;
an imperial edict ordered them to be treated kindly and preserved.
Chǔ and Mǐn had for generations served the Central Plains.
Later, they were captured by Southern Táng
and imprisoned in Yángzhōu.
Since Zhōu obtained Yángzhōu,
they were thus treated kindly and preserved.
8 On the bǐngwǔ day,
Sūn Shèng and others arrived at the emperor's location.
They arrived at the emperor's temporary residence.
On the gēngxū day,
the emperor dispatched an imperial envoy with Sūn Shèng to the foot of Shòuchūn City,
and to appeal to them.
Rénshàn saw Shèng,
and, clad in military attire, bowed from atop the city wall.
He saluted Shèng with the courtesy due from a frontier marshal to a chancellor.
“You have received great favor from the state,
you must not open the gates to let in bandits.”
The emperor, upon hearing this,
was very angry.
Shèng said:
“As
a chancellor,
how could I instruct a Military Governor to rebel outwardly!”
The emperor then released him.
Sūn Shèng’s words were upright,
why would Zhōu Shìzōng punish him!
9 The Táng ruler sent Lǐ DéMíng and Sūn Shèng to speak with the emperor,
requesting to relinquish the imperial title,
and to cede the six prefectures of Shòu, Háo, Sì, Chǔ, Guāng, and Hǎi.
These six prefectures were all close to the Huái River.
Once Zhōu obtained them,
Táng would lose the strategic advantage of the long Huái River.
Even if Zhōu had acceded to Táng’s request and ceased hostilities,
the lands north of the Jiāng River would also not have been defensible later.
The emperor, considering that half of the land south of the Huái River was already in Zhōu’s possession,
and daily victorious reports from his generals,
desired to obtain all the lands north of the Jiāng River,
and did not consent.
DéMíng, seeing the Zhōu troops advancing daily,
reported, stating:
“The Táng ruler does not know the immense strength of Your Majesty’s forces.
I beg for five days’ reprieve from execution,
to return and inform the Táng ruler,
and offer all the lands north of the Jiāng River.”
The emperor then granted his request.
Shèng thereupon submitted a memorial requesting to send Wáng ChóngZhì to return with DéMíng.
Wáng ChóngZhì served as Sūn Shèng’s deputy envoy.
A letter was bestowed upon the Táng ruler,
the gist of which was:
“Just preserve the imperial title,
what does it matter in the cold of winter!
Shuǎng means
difference.
It speaks of knowing the pine and cypress wither last in winter.
This pact is not in error.
It permitted the Táng ruler to be emperor of Jiāngnán himself.
Ultimately, one does not force people into danger.”
It also said:
“Await the arrival of all the prefectures,”
referring to all the prefectures north of the Jiāng River.
“Words end here,
no need for further talk;
fán means
labor.
It means no more need to talk.
Please cease from this point.”
He also bestowed letters upon their generals and chancellors,
instructing them to deliberate thoroughly and come.
The Táng ruler again submitted a memorial of thanks.
Lǐ DéMíng highly praised the emperor’s might and virtue, and the strength of his armed forces,
and advised the Táng ruler to cede the lands north of the Jiāng River;
the Táng ruler was displeased.
Sòng Qíqiū deemed the ceding of land useless;
DéMíng was frivolous,
his words often exaggerated,
and the people of the state did not believe him either.
The Grand Councilor Chén Jué and Vice Grand Councilor Lǐ ZhēngGǔ had long disliked DéMíng and Sūn Shèng,
and made Wáng ChóngZhì contradict his statements,
then slandered DéMíng to the Táng ruler, saying:
“DéMíng is selling out the country for profit.”
The Táng ruler was greatly enraged,
and executed DéMíng in the marketplace.
This became the root of the enmity between Zhōng Mó and Lǐ DéMíng.
10 Wú Chéng attacked Chángzhōu,
breaching its outer wall,
and captured Zhào Rénzé, the Táng Military Commissioner of Chángzhōu,
sending him to Qiántáng.
Rénzé saw the Wúyuè King Hóngchù but did not bow,
reproaching him for breaking their pact;
Táng and Wúyuè had originally been on good terms,
but Wúyuè, by Zhōu’s command, attacked Táng,
hence the reproach for breaking the pact.
His mouth was slit to his ears.
Yuán Dézhāo pitied his loyalty,
and applied good medicine,
thus he did not die.
It was not that Táng lacked loyal officials,
but that they could not be utilized.
The character 為 (wéi),
is pronounced “yú wěi”.
The Táng ruler, with Wúyuè troops in Chángzhōu,
feared they might encroach upon Rùnzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Chángzhōu is
one hundred seventy-one lǐ northwest of Rùnzhōu.
Fearing that he was not accustomed to military matters,
he recalled him to Jīnlíng.
His subordinate general Zhào Duó spoke to Hóngjì, saying:
“Your Highness is the marshal,
the reliance of all hearts.
If you retreat by yourself,
your subordinates will certainly fall into disorder.”
Hóngjì agreed with him,
declined the recall,
and assigned his various generals,
making preparations for battle and defense.
Chái Kèhóng, Commander of the Imperial Guards of the Longwu Corps,
was the son of Zàiyòng,
Chái Zàiyòng served the Yáng family as a general,
repeatedly achieving military merits,
and also served Xú Wēn and his son.
He did not manage family property.
Although he supervised the imperial guard,
he spent his days gambling and drinking with guests,
never speaking of military affairs,
and people at the time considered him unsuitable for a general’s command.
At this time,
someone spoke of Kèhóng not having been promoted for a long time,
so the Táng ruler appointed him Prefect of Fǔzhōu.
Kèhóng requested to fight to the death on the battlefield,
and his mother also memorialized, stating that Kèhóng had his father’s style,
and could be a general;
if he were not competent,
they would willingly accept their own and their family’s execution.
Zhào Kuò’s mother refused to vouch for her son,
while Chái Kèhóng’s mother personally recommended her son,
both knowing their children well.
Nú means
son.
It means to willingly suffer execution together with his son.
Háng (行) is pronounced
“hù gāng”.
Chén (陳) is
the same as zhèn (陣).
Shèng (勝) is
pronounced “shēng”.
Fēn (分) is pronounced
“fú wèn”.
Nú (孥) is
pronounced “nú”.
He was made to lead troops to rendezvous with Lù Mèngjùn, Prefect of Yuánzhōu, to relieve Chángzhōu.
At this time, Táng’s elite troops were all north of the Jiāng River,
and the several thousand men Kèhóng led were all weak and old.
The Grand Councilor Lǐ ZhēngGǔ furthermore supplied them with rotten and worm-eaten armor and weapons.
Kèhóng complained to ZhēngGǔ,
but ZhēngGǔ cursed him disdainfully.
Everyone was indignant,
but Kèhóng remained composed.
When he reached Rùnzhōu,
ZhēngGǔ sent an envoy to recall him,
and replaced him with Zhū Kuāngyè,
Commander of the Divine Guards.
Yānwáng Hóngjì said to Kèhóng:
“Wèi zhě” means
“to tell.”
“You just go and fight,
I will report it.”
He then memorialized that Kèhóng’s talent and strategy could achieve success,
that Chángzhōu was in imminent danger,
and that it was not appropriate to change the commander midway.
Kèhóng led his troops directly to Chángzhōu.
ZhēngGǔ again sent an envoy to recall him,
but Kèhóng said:
“I expect to defeat the bandits within days.
If you come to recall me,
you must be a traitor!”
He ordered him beheaded.
The envoy said:
“I came by order of Grand Councilor Lǐ.”
Kèhóng said:
“If Grand Councilor Lǐ comes,
I will behead him too!”
Chái Kèhóng’s composure of the previous day
had cultivated his present courage and decisiveness.
Initially,
Bāo Xiūrang and Luó Shèng were in Fúzhōu,
and had a feud with Wú Chéng.
In the twelfth year of Tiānfú of the Hàn,
the Wúyuè sent Bāo Xiūrang to guard Fúzhōu.
In that same year, Wú Chéng was appointed to镇 Fúzhōu.
Chéng suppressed and frustrated them,
and both men harbored resentment.
Prior to this,
the Táng ruler had sent the Zhongshū Shèrén Qíáo Kuāngshùn as an envoy to Wúyuè.
On the rénzǐ day,
Chái Kèhóng arrived at Chángzhōu.
He covered his boats with screens,
hid armed soldiers within them,
and declared that he was going to welcome Kuāngshùn.
Wúyuè scouts reported this,
and Chéng said:
"When armies engage,
if an envoy is caught in the middle,
use the saying from the Zuǒzhuàn."
Táng troops landed,
directly advanced towards the Wúyuè camp,
and Luó Shèng did not fight vigorously,
letting them rush towards Chéng's tent.
Chéng barely escaped with his life.
Kèhóng utterly defeated the Wúyuè forces,
beheading ten thousand.
Zhū Kuāngyè arrived at the marching camp,
and Kèhóng served him with great deference.
When Wú Chéng reached Qiántáng,
King Hóngchù of Wúyuè stripped him of all his official positions.
11 On the jiǎyín day,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Lǐ Tíngguī, the Pèngshèng Kònghè Dūzhīhuīshǐ, as the Zuǒyòu Wèishèng Zhūjūn Mǎbù Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
He also divided the Wèishèng and Kuāngshèng infantry and cavalry into ten left and right armies,
appointing Lǚ Yànqí, the Wǔdìng Jiédùshǐ, and others as their commanders.
They served as army commanders.
This was similar to Zhào Tíngyǐn's appointment.
Since the execution of Lǐ Rénhǎn,
Zhào Tíngyǐn had solely commanded all the palace guard armies.
Later, he was dismissed due to being slandered by Ān Sīqiān;
these events are all mentioned previously.
12 Originally,
Chái Kèhóng was the Xuānzhōu Xúnjiǎnshǐ.
When he first arrived,
the city walls and moats were not repaired,
and all the weapons were lacking.
An official said:
"Since Tián Yūn, Wáng Màozhāng, and Lǐ Yù successively rebelled,
in the third year of Tiānfù of Táng,
Tián Yūn rebelled against Yáng Xíngmì with Xuānzhōu.
In the second year of Tiānyòu,
Wáng Màozhāng rebelled.
In the second year of Qiànhuà of Liáng,
Lǐ Yù rebelled.
These events are all recorded in previous chronicles.
Yūn,
read as yúnlún fān."
Kèhóng said:
"Times have changed, and circumstances are different;
how can this be so!"
He had everything repaired and made complete.
Because of this, Lù Yànzhū was unable to conquer it,
and history states that Xuānzhōu was preserved,
which was also due to Chái Kèhóng's efforts.
On the yǐmǎo day,
he was recalled.
The Táng ruler appointed Kèhóng as the Fènghuà Jiédùshǐ.
Kèhóng again requested to lead troops to rescue Shòuzhōu,
but died before arriving.
There are those whose bodies perish but whose names live on,
and Chái Kèhóng is one of them.
Kèhóng could defeat Wúyuè,
but if he had encountered Zhōu's army,
he might not have been able to do so.
Fù,
read as fúyòu fān.
13 Bái Zhòngzàn, the Héyáng Jiédùshǐ,
fearing that Northern Hàn might invade while the Emperor was campaigning in the south,
repaired and completed the defenses,
and also requested troops from Xījīng.
Wáng Yàn, the Xījīng Liúshǒu, initially did not grant them,
but also feared that something extraordinary might happen,
so he personally led troops to assist.
Zhòngzàn, believing Yàn had come without an imperial edict,
refused to admit him,
and sent someone to tell him:
"Your Grace formerly rendered great service
in Shǎnfú,
(referring to the twelfth year of Tiānfú when Yàn surrendered Shǎn City to Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn).
Yàn was then concurrently Zhongshūlìng,
hence he was called Línggōng.
Shǎn,
read as shīrǎn fān.)
There is no need for you to trouble yourself by coming!"
Yàn returned, feeling ashamed.
The people of Mèng and Luò
were alarmed and disturbed for several days,
fearing that if Wáng Yàn's troops engaged those of Bái Zhòngzàn,
they would suffer the calamity.
14 The Táng ruler ordered Qí Wáng Jǐngdá, the marshal of all armies,
to lead troops to resist Zhōu,
appointing Chén Jué as the Jiānjūnshǐ
and Biān Hào, the former Wǔ'ān Jiédùshǐ, as the Yìngyuán Dūjūnshǐ.
Biān Hào had lost Tánzhōu and was stripped of his authority,
but was now reinstated.
"No one is more trustworthy than a princely king,
and no one is more important than a marshal.
What is the use of a Jiānjūnshǐ!"
(Punctuation.)
He sent Hónglúqīng Pān Chéngyòu to Quán and Jiàn to recruit brave and capable men.
Chéngyòu recommended Xǔ Wénzhěn, the former Yǒng'ān Jiédùshǐ,
Chén Déchéng, the Jìngjiāng Zhīhuīshǐ, and Zhèng Yánhuá and Lín Rénzhào from Jiànzhōu.
The Táng ruler appointed Wénzhěn as the Xīmiàn Xíngyíng Yìngyuánshǐ,
and Yánhuá and Rénzhào were both made generals.
Rénzhào
was Rénxún's younger brother.
Lín Rénxún is mentioned in volume 284, in the first year of Kāiyùn of Emperor Chūdì of Jìn,
which was the second year of Bǎodà of the Táng ruler.
15 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the jiǎzǐ day,
Lǐ Chóngjìn, the Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ and Guīdé Jiédùshǐ, was appointed as the Lúshòu Děngzhōu Zhāotǎoshǐ.
Wǔ Xíngdé, the Wǔníng Jiédùshǐ, was appointed as the Háozhōu Chéngxià Dūbùshǔ.
16 Lù Mèngjùn, the Táng Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn, led more than ten thousand troops from Chángzhōu towards Tàizhōu.
(Jiǔyù Zhì: From Chángzhōu north to Tàizhōu is 197 lǐ.)
Mèngjùn recaptured it,
recapturing Tàizhōu.
Mèngjùn advanced to attack Yángzhōu,
encamping on Shǔgāng.
Hán Lìngkūn abandoned Yángzhōu and fled.
(Shǔgāng is west of Yángzhōu city.
Yángzhōu city is southeast of Shǔgāng.
To the east, south, and north of the city is all flat land,
crisscrossed by canals and ditches.
Only the Shǔgāng mountains connect to Lú and Chú to the west.
Whenever northern troops invaded Yángzhōu from the south,
they typically followed the mountains,
occupying high ground to build camps and overlook the city.)
Now, Lù Mèngjùn occupied Shǔgāng to cut off the path for Zhōu reinforcements,
which is why Hán Lìngkūn was afraid and fled.
Lìngkūn re-entered Yángzhōu.
(Reinforcements arrived,
so he re-entered Yángzhōu.)
(Lùhé Xiàn
belongs to Yángzhōu,
130 lǐ northwest of the prefecture.
Liú Xù said: Lùhé
was Tángyì Xiàn of Línhuái Prefecture in Hàn,
Qínjùn was established in Jìn,
Qínzhōu was established in Northern Qí,
Fāngzhōu was established in Suí,
later abolished,
and Lùhé Xiàn was established in the early Wǔdé period of Táng.)
"Any Yángzhōu soldier who passes Lùhé
will have his leg broken!"
(Those returning from Yángzhōu northwest
must pass Lùhé,
hence this statement.)
(Zhē,
read as èrshè fān.)
Since the Emperor arrived at Shòuchūn,
he ordered all armies to attack the city day and night,
but they could not conquer it for a long time.
Coincidentally, there was heavy rain,
and the water in the camp was several feet deep.
Many siege tools and soldiers were lost.
At that time, Zhōu's forces used square boats to carry trebuchets,
attacking Shòuchūn city from the middle of the Féihé River.
They also bound hundreds of thousands of giant bamboos,
placed plank houses on top,
called them
"Bamboo Dragons,"
and carried armed soldiers to attack with them.
Coincidentally, the Féishuǐ suddenly swelled,
and both the trebuchet boats and Bamboo Dragons were swept towards the south bank,
where they were burned by Táng troops.
Lǐ Démíng failed to arrive on time.
(Lǐ Démíng was executed upon returning to Jīnlíng.)
Someone advised the Emperor to move east to Háozhōu,
claiming that Shòuzhōu had already fallen;
he followed this advice.
On the jǐsì day,
the Emperor traveled east from Shòuchūn along the Huái River,
and on the yǐhài day,
arrived at Háozhōu.
(Jiǔyù Zhì: Shòuzhōu
is 380 lǐ east of Háozhōu.)
Hán Lìngkūn defeated the Táng troops east of the city.
This was east of Yángzhōu city.
敗 (bài, defeat),
pronounced "bǔ mài" (as in 補邁).
Previously,
Mèng Jùn had deposed Mǎ Xī'è and enthroned Xīchóng.
The event can be found in Volume 290, Tàizǔ Guǎngshùn First Year.
A woman of the Yáng clan was beautiful,
and offered to Xīchóng.
When Lìngkūn entered Yángzhōu,
Xīchóng gave the Yáng woman to Lìngkūn,
and Lìngkūn favored her.
After capturing Mèng Jùn,
Lìngkūn was about to shackle him and send him to the Emperor.
The Yáng woman, from behind a curtain,
suddenly clutched her chest and wailed in grief.
Lìngkūn, startled, asked her about it.
She replied:
"When Mèng Jùn was in Tánzhōu,
he killed two hundred people of my family.
Seeing him today,
I ask to avenge their wrong."
Lìngkūn then killed him.
The historian says that one should not arbitrarily kill,
for even a woman can seek revenge.
17 Táng Qí Wáng Jǐngdá led an army of twenty thousand across the Jiāng river from Guāpù.
They were more than twenty *lǐ* from Liùhé,
where they set up barricades and did not advance.
The generals wanted to attack them,
but Emperor Tàizǔ said:
"They set up barricades to secure themselves,
fearing us.
Now, our troops are less than two thousand.
If we go and attack them,
they will see that our forces are few;
it is better to wait for them to come and then attack them,
and defeat will be certain!"
After several days,
Táng troops marched towards Liùhé.
Emperor Tàizǔ attacked them with vigor,
greatly defeating them,
killing and capturing nearly five thousand men.
More than ten thousand remaining troops
fled across the river,
and many drowned while scrambling for boats.
Thus, Táng's elite soldiers were all gone.
In this battle,
some soldiers did not exert themselves.
Emperor Tàizǔ pretended to supervise the battle,
striking their leather helmets with his sword.
The next day,
he inspected all their leather helmets.
Several tens of men had sword marks on their helmets,
and he had them all executed.
From then on, none of his troops dared not fight to the death.
Before this,
the Táng ruler, hearing that Yángzhōu had fallen,
ordered troops from all directions to retake it.
On the *Jǐmǎo* day,
Hán Lìngkūn reported defeating over ten thousand Yáng
zhōu troops at Wāntóuyàn.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Jiāngdū County, Yángzhōu, has Wāntóuzhèn,
which is fifteen *lǐ* north of present-day Yángzhōu city.
敗 (bài, defeat),
pronounced "bǔ mài" (as in 補邁).
Táng probably established Liánzhōu in Liánshuǐ County.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Liánshuǐ
is sixty *lǐ* southwest of Chǔzhōu.
[Defeated] over ten thousand men at Qūxīyàn.
Qūxī
is ten *lǐ* southwest of Xūyí County.
According to the *Zhāoxìn Tújīng*: Qūxīyàn
is also called Xīnhéyàn.
18 On the *Bǐngxū* day,
Xiàng Xùn, Commissioner of the Southern Bureau of Military Affairs, was made Jìedùshǐ of Huáinán and concurrently Recruiter and Commander along the Jiāng River.
At Guōkǒu, a report came that a new pontoon bridge had been completed.
On the *Dīnghài* day,
the Emperor traveled from Háozhōu to Guōkǒu.
Guōkǒu is
the mouth where the Guō River flows into the Huái River.
The *Jùnxìan Zhì* states: Guōkǒuchéng
is ninety *lǐ* southeast of Háozhōu.
渦 (guō),
pronounced "gē" (as in 戈).
The Emperor was eager to advance and seize territory,
wishing to go to Yángzhōu himself.
Fàn Zhì and others, citing tired troops and scarce provisions,
tearfully remonstrated and stopped him.
The Emperor once grew angry with Hànlín Scholar Dòu Yí,
and wanted to kill him.
Fàn Zhì came in to save him.
When the Emperor saw him,
he knew his intention and immediately rose to avoid him.
Zhì rushed forward, prostrated himself on the ground,
and
kowtowed, remonstrating:
"Yí's crime does not warrant death.
As your Prime Minister,
if I allow Your Majesty to wrongly kill a close minister,
the fault is entirely mine."
He continued with tears.
The Emperor's anger subsided,
and he released him.
19 The Northern Hàn buried Emperor Shénwǔ on Beishān in Jiāochéng.
Suí divided Jìnyáng County to establish Jiāochéng County,
naming it after the ancient Jiāochéng northwest of the county.
It was initially governed from Jiāoshān.
In the first year of Tiānshòu of Táng,
it was moved to Quèbōcūn.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is one hundred *lǐ* southwest of Yángqǔ County.
Sòng Bái said: Dàtōngjiān
was originally the land of ancient Jiāochéng,
overseeing the iron smelting operations of the eastern and western foundries.
The eastern foundry was in Miánshàng County,
and the western foundry was on Beishān in Jiāochéng County.
20 In the fifth month,
on the *Bǐng*
*chén* day, the first day of the month,
Guōkǒu was designated Zhènhuáijūn.
21 On the *Bǐngshēn* day,
Chén Huì, Jìedùshǐ of Yǒng'ānjūn of Táng, defeated Fúzhōu troops at Nántáijiāng.
Nine *lǐ* south of present-day Fúzhōu is Diàolóngtáishān,
overlooking the river,
so Nántáijiāng must be this place.
The *Xuē Shǐ Dìlǐ Zhì* states: Fútáng County, Fúzhōu,
was renamed Nántái County in the early Tiānfú period of Jìn,
probably naming the county after the river;
later it reverted to its old name.
The Táng ruler renamed Yǒng'ānjūn to Zhōngyìjūn.
In the second year of Kāiyùn of Jìn,
Táng conquered Jiànzhōu
and established Yǒng'ānjūn.
更 (gēng, rename),
pronounced "gōng héng" (as in 工衡).
[Chén Huì] was Dèchéng's father.
22 On the *Wùxū* day,
the Emperor left Lǐ Chóngjìn, the Commander-in-chief of the Palace Cavalry and Infantry, and others to besiege Shòuzhōu,
and returned north from Guōkǒu.
On the *Yǐmǎo* day,
he arrived at Dàliáng.
From Guōkǒu to Dàliáng is seven hundred forty *lǐ*.
23 In the sixth month,
on the *Rénshēn* day,
a general amnesty was granted to prisoners in the various prefectures of Huáinán,
and the unreasonable taxes and levies of the Lǐ clan were abolished.
Matters inconvenient to the people
were to be reported by the chief officials.
24 Lǐ Jìxūn, Commander-in-chief of the Palace Infantry and Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngxìn, was encamped south of Shòuzhōu city.
Liú Rénshàn of Táng, seeing Jìxūn unprepared,
led out troops to attack him,
killing several hundred soldiers
and burning his siege equipment.
25 Zhū Yuán, Assistant Director of the Bureau of Military Provisions (*Jiàbù Yuánwàiláng*) of Táng, discussed military strategies in a memorial.
The Táng ruler, thinking him capable,
ordered him to lead troops to retake the various prefectures north of the Jiāng River.
26 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the *Xīnmǎo* day, the first day of the month,
Zhōu Xíngféng was made Jìedùshǐ of Wǔpíng,
overseeing the military affairs of Wǔ'ān, Jìngjiāng, and other armies.
Having assumed overall command of Hú and Xiāng,
Xíngféng rectified the abuses of his predecessors,
focused on civil affairs,
abolished all the oppressive taxes of the Mǎ clan,
removed corrupt officials and cunning commoners who harmed the people,
and selected honest and fair officials as regional governors (*cǐshǐ*) and county magistrates (*xiànlìng*).
The populace of Lángzhōu was a mix of Han and non-Han,
and many former generals of Liú Yán and Wáng Kuí were arrogant and unruly.
Xíngféng governed them all by law,
without leniency,
causing resentment and fear among the populace.
A great general and more than ten of his associates plotted rebellion.
Xíngféng, knowing of this,
assembled all the generals.
He seized them at the gathering
and denounced them, saying:
"I wear coarse clothes and eat simple food
to fill the state treasury,
precisely for you all.
How have I wronged you that you rebel!
This meeting today
is my farewell to you!"
He immediately had them beaten to death,
causing those present to tremble.
Xíngféng said:
"Gentlemen, you have committed no crime;
you should all feel at ease."
He then joyfully drank with them before dismissing the gathering.
Xíngfèng was resourceful and
good at uncovering hidden plots.
If any of his generals or soldiers plotted rebellion or defected,
Xíngfèng would always discover it first
and capture and kill them.
His subordinates were awestruck.
However, he was suspicious and cruel by nature,
often secretly dispatching people to spy on affairs in various prefectures.
One who went to Shàozhōu
had no incident to report,
but merely said that the Cìshǐ, Liú Guāngwěi, frequently held banquets.
Xíngfèng said,
"Guāngwěi often gathers for drinks;
is he plotting against me?!"
He immediately summoned him back
and killed him.
Zhāng Wénbiǎo, the Commander of the Imperial Guards and Cìshǐ of Héngzhōu, feared being punished
and requested to return to his administrative seat;
he wished to be relieved of military command and return to Héngzhōu.
Wénbiǎo's annual tribute was very generous,
and he was diligent in serving those around Xíngfèng,
which allowed him to escape harm.
Later, when Xíngfèng was nearing death,
he said to his son, Bǎoquán,
"I rose from the fields,
becoming a commander of local militia.
Ten people who started with me were all executed;
only Zhāng Wénbiǎo survived."
At that time, Wáng Kuí, Zhāng Fǎng, Hé Jìngzhēn, Zhū Quánxiù, and Pān Shūcì were all dead.
Only Pú Gōngyì, Yǔwén Qióng, Péng Wànhé, and Wénbiǎo remained.
The historical records do not mention any other details about them,
but these three must have subsequently been killed by Xíngfèng,
while Wénbiǎo alone was spared.
After Xíngfèng died,
Wénbiǎo rebelled.
Xíngfèng's wife, Madame Dèng, the Countess of Yún,
was plain-looking but resolute,
and skilled at managing household affairs.
She once advised Xíngfèng that his application of the law was too strict,
and that no one would be close to him.
Xíngfèng angrily said,
"What do you women know?!"
Madame Dèng was displeased
and thereupon requested to go to a village estate to look after the fields and gardens,
and thereafter never returned to the prefectural mansion.
zhī,
wǎng yě.
shù,
chéng yǔ fān.
fù,
fú yòu fān.
fǔ shè,
Lángzhōu fǔ shè yě.
She did not come;
one day,
she personally led servants to deliver taxes.
Xíngfèng went to see her,
saying,
"I am a Jiédùshǐ;
why does my wife trouble herself like this?!"
Madame Dèng said,
"Taxes
are government property.
You are a Jiédùshǐ;
if you do not pay taxes first,
how can you lead your subordinates?!
Moreover, do you not recall the time when you were a lǐzhèng and paid taxes for others to avoid flogging?"
Xíngfèng wanted to return with her,
but she refused;
she would not return to the prefectural mansion.
"You have executed too many people,
and I often fear that one day there will be trouble.
A village estate is easier for fleeing and hiding."
Xíngfèng was ashamed and angry.
His subordinates said,
"Madame's words are direct;
you should heed them."
Xíngfèng's son-in-law, Táng Dé, sought to be appointed an official.
Xíngfèng said,
"Your talent is not fit for an official.
If I were to give you private favors now, that would be acceptable;
but if you act inappropriately in office,
I would not dare to pardon you by law,
and thus the affection between relatives would be severed."
He gave him an ox and farming tools and sent him away.
When Xíngfèng was young, he was once branded for a crime
and assigned to Tóngkēng in Chénzhōu.
Someone suggested to Xíngfèng,
"Your face has markings;
you might be ridiculed by envoys from the imperial court.
Please use medicine to remove them."
Xíngfèng said,
"I heard that Hàn had Qíng Bù,
who was not hindered from being a hero.
Why should I be ashamed of it?!"
The story of Qíng Bù is found in volume 8, Qín Èrshì, second year.
Since Liú Yán and Wáng Kuí,
troops were repeatedly raised,
and generals and officials who accumulated merit, as well as the pacified barbarians,
numbered in the thousands who were appointed as Jiǎnjiào Sāngōng.
jī mí mán yí,
refers to the various barbarians in the mountain valleys.
After Mǎ Xīguǎng was deposed,
he stayed home and did not go out.
The matter of Mǎ Xīguǎng's deposition is found in volume 289, Hàn Gānyòu, second year.
He was appointed Jiédù Pànguān.
Zhòngyǎ said,
"Xíngfèng once served me;
how can I be his staff officer?!"
He declined on grounds of illness and did not come.
Xíngfèng coerced and forcibly summoned him,
personally handing him official documents,
but he ultimately refused to take them.
Xíngfèng was angry
and banished him to Shàozhōu,
but later recalled him.
It happened to be Xíngfèng's birthday,
and various circuits sent envoys to offer congratulations.
Xíngfèng had a proud look
and said to Zhòngyǎ,
"Since I concurrently govern three prefectures—"
sān fǔ,
refers to the Wǔpíng, Wǔ'ān, and Jìngjiāng military prefectures.
Zhòngyǎ said,
"Within your territory, Shìzhōng,
Zhōu Xíngfèng was given the title Shìzhōng,
hence Xú Zhòngyǎ addressed him as such.
Sīkōng are everywhere;
how can our neighbors not fear?!"
Xíngfèng again banished him to Shàozhōu,
but ultimately could not make him yield.
There was a monk named Rénjí,
who was trusted by Xíngfèng,
and involved in all military and prefectural affairs.
He was also appointed Jiǎnjiào Sīkōng,
married several wives,
and traveled with an escort like a prince or duke.
On the 27th, Xīnhài,
Empress Xuānyì, Madame Fú, passed away.
On the 28th, Zhū Yuán, a general of Táng, captured Shūzhōu,
and the Cìshǐ Guō Língtú abandoned the city and fled.
Lǐ Píng captured Qízhōu.
The Táng ruler appointed Yuán as Shūzhōu Tuánliànshǐ
and Píng as Qízhōu Cìshǐ.
Yuán also captured Hézhōu.
Zhū Yuán and Lǐ Píng
were both sent by Lǐ Shǒuzhēn to seek aid from Táng;
this matter is found in volume 288, Hàn Gānyòu, first year.
Originally,
the Táng people used tea and salt to control the populace and levy grain and silk from them,
calling it "bózhēng" (forced levy).
They also established garrison farms in Huáinán,
which greatly distressed the people.
When the Zhōu army arrived,
the people eagerly offered oxen and wine to welcome and reward them.
However, the generals and officers showed no concern for them,
focusing solely on looting and capturing,
treating the people like dirt and weeds.
All the people were disappointed
and gathered in the mountains and marshes,
building strongholds and fortifying themselves.
They wielded farm tools as weapons
and stacked paper for armor.
People at the time called them
the "White Armored Army."
The Zhōu army attacked them
but was repeatedly defeated.
Many of the Táng prefectures previously captured
reverted to Táng control.
The Táng relief forces encamped at Zǐjīnshān.
Zǐjīnshān is south of Shòuchūn;
some say it is Bāgōngshān.
Xiàng Xùn, the Jiédùshǐ of Huáinán, submitted a memorial requesting to combine the forces from Guǎnglíng to attack Shòuchūn,
and after capturing the city, to plan further advances.
The emperor approved his request.
Xùn sealed the armory and treasury and handed them over to the official in charge of Yángzhōu.
He ordered the Yángzhōu Yájiàng to patrol the city in sections,
not taking even a single blade of grass.
The people of Yángzhōu were grateful and pleased.
When the army returned,
some carried provisions to send them off.
The defending general of Chúzhōu also abandoned the city and left,
all leading their troops to Shòuchūn.
The generals of Táng requested to hold strategic passes to confront the Zhōu army.
Sòng Qíqiū said:
"If we do this,
resentment will only deepen."
Thereupon, he ordered the generals to each defend their positions,
and not to sally forth to attack the Zhōu troops.
Because of this, the siege of Shòuchūn became more urgent.
Qí Wáng Jǐngdá was encamped in Háozhōu,
providing distant support for Shòuzhōu.
All military and administrative matters were handled by Chén Jué;
Jǐngdá merely signed the bottom of the papers.
He commanded fifty thousand troops,
but had no intention of a decisive battle.
Alas!
The fall of Xiāngyáng in previous years,
was it not the fault of the relief army failing to advance?
None dared to speak.
The 29th. In the eighth month,
on the day wùchén,
Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì Wáng Pò and Sītiān Shàojiān Wáng Chùnà
compiled the Xiǎndé Qīntiān Lì (Xiǎndé Imperial Calendar),
and presented it to the emperor.
Initially,
Wáng Chùnà privately created the Míngxuán Lì (Bright Mystery Calendar) at home,
which was an elucidation of the Chóngxuán Lì (Profound Mystery Calendar) that was in use during the Táng dynasty.
As the emperor knew Wáng Pò was skilled in calendrical calculations,
he ordered Pò to finalize it.
He organized it into four chapters: "Bu Rì" (Steps of the Sun), "Bu Yuè" (Steps of the Moon), "Bu Xīng" (Steps of the Stars), and "Bu Fāliǎn" (Steps of Expansion and Contraction),
combining them into a calendrical classic.
Additionally, he authored one scroll of the "Xiǎndé Sānnián Qīzhèng Xìxíng Lì" (Calendar of the Detailed Movements of the Seven Luminaries in the Third Year of Xiǎndé),
which constituted the Qīntiān Lì.
The 30th. Diànqián Dūzhīhuīshǐ and Yìchéng Jiédùshǐ Zhāng Yǒngdé was stationed at Xiàcài.
Táng general Lín Rénzhào led land and water forces to relieve Shòuchūn.
Yǒngdé fought against him.
Rénzhào loaded ships with firewood and straw,
and, using the wind, set them on fire,
intending to burn the pontoon bridge at Xiàcài.
Shortly after, the wind shifted,
and the Táng forces were defeated and retreated.
Yǒngdé made iron cables over a thousand *chǐ* long.
At a distance of more than ten *bù* from the pontoon bridge,
he stretched them across the Huái River,
and secured them with large logs.
Because of this, the Táng forces could not approach.
The 31st. In the ninth month,
on the day bǐngwǔ,
Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì, Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì, Quán Zhī Kāifēng Fǔshì Wáng Pò was appointed Hùbù Shìláng,
and concurrently served as Shūmì Fùshǐ.
The 32nd. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day guǐyǒu,
Lǐ Chóngjìn reported that the Táng people had raided ShèngTáng.
Tiěqí Dūzhīhuīshǐ Wáng Yànshēng and others defeated them,
beheading over three thousand.
Yànshēng was
a man from Shǔ.
The 33rd. On the day bǐngzǐ,
the emperor said to his attendant ministers:
"In recent dynasties, the collection of grain and silk
often does not await the completion of harvest and spinning."
Below "shìchén" (attendant ministers)
there is
the character "yuē" (said),
which completes the meaning of the sentence.
"Jìn cháo" (recent dynasties)
is synonymous with "jìndài" (modern times).
The character "cháo"
is pronounced zhíyáo (zhí yáo) according to the fanqie method;
the same applies below.
From now on, the summer tax will begin collection in the sixth month,
and the autumn tax in the tenth month.
The "Wǔdài Huìyào" (Essentials of the Five Dynasties) states: The collection of both taxes
begins on the first day of the month.
The 34th. Shānnán Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ, Shǒu Tàuwèi concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng Ān Shěnqí had been garrisoned in Xiāngzhōu for over ten years.
In the twelfth year of Tiānfú of the Hàn dynasty,
Ān Shěnqí was garrisoned in Xiāngyáng;
it had been ten years until now.
He was appointed Shǒu Tàishī,
and sent back to his commandery.
After he had departed,
the emperor asked the chancellors:
"Did you all see him off?"
They replied:
"We saw him off to the south of the city.
Shěnqí was deeply grateful for Your Majesty's grace."
Since the Five Dynasties,
when regional commanders came to court,
some were detained and not allowed to leave,
or were replaced.
Now, he was promoted and sent back to his commandery,
hence his gratitude.
"In recent dynasties, many have not treated the feudal lords with sincerity and trust.
Even if the feudal lords wished to demonstrate loyalty and integrity,
there was no way for them to do so.
If a ruler can merely uphold his trust,
why should he worry that the feudal lords will not pledge their allegiance?"
The 35th. On the day rénwǔ,
Zhāng Yǒngdé reported defeating Táng forces at Xiàcài.
At this time, Táng again attacked Yǒngdé with a naval force.
Yǒngdé, at night, ordered skilled swimmers to dive under their boats,
tie them with iron chains,
and then unleashed his troops to attack.
The boats could not advance or retreat,
and many drowned.
Yǒngdé awarded his golden belt to the skilled swimmers.
The 36th. On the day jiǎshēn,
Emperor Tàizǔ was appointed Dìngguó Jiédùshǐ concurrently Diànqián Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
Dìngguó Jūn
was the same as Tóngzhōu Kuāngguó Jūn.
When Emperor Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
to avoid his taboo personal name,
it was changed to Dìngguó Jūn.
Historians also recorded it with the later revised military designation.
The 37th. Zhāng Yǒngdé and Lǐ Chóngjìn were not on good terms.
Yǒngdé secretly memorialized that Chóngjìn harbored disloyal intentions,
but the emperor did not believe it.
At that time, both generals commanded large armies,
causing public anxiety and fear.
One day, Chóngjìn rode alone to Yǒngdé's camp.
Lǐ Chóngjìn was then beneath the walls of Shòuzhōu,
while Zhāng Yǒngdé's camp was at Xiàcài.
He said to Yǒngdé:
"You and I are fortunate to be generals, closely related as lungs and heart.
Why should we suspect each other so deeply?"
Yǒngdé's misgivings then dissolved,
and the hearts of the multitude were also settled.
The Táng ruler heard of this,
and sent a wax pellet message to Chóngjìn,
enticing him with great benefits.
The letter contained slanderous remarks and words of alienation;
Chóngjìn reported it.
Initially,
Táng envoys Sūn Shèng and Zhōng Mó followed the emperor to Dàliáng.
The emperor treated them very generously.
At every court assembly,
they were ranked after officials of the Zhōngshū Shěng.
From time to time, he summoned them,
offered them fine wine,
and questioned them about Táng affairs.
Shèng merely said,
"The Táng ruler fears Your Majesty's divine might,
and serves Your Majesty with no disloyal intentions."
When the Táng wax letter was received,
the emperor was greatly enraged.
He summoned Shèng,
and reprimanded him for his untrue statements.
Shèng, with a stern face and firm words,
requested death and nothing more.
When asked about Táng's true situation,
he remained silent.
In the eleventh month,
on the day yǐsì,
the emperor ordered Dū Chéngzhǐ Cáo Hàn to send Shèng to the Yòujūn Xúnyuàn.
The Shìwèi Qīnjūn (Imperial Guard) was divided into left and right armies,
each with a patrol bureau
for interrogating prisoners.
Hàn drank several rounds of wine with him,
and casually questioned him,
but Shèng still refused to speak.
Hàn then said:
"There is an imperial edict
granting death to Xiànggōng (Prime Minister)."
He addressed him by his Táng official title.
Shèng requested his robes and tablet,
straightened his attire,
and facing south, bowed, saying:
"Your servant dutifully repays the country with his death."
Then he proceeded to execution.
Over a hundred of his attendants were also killed,
and Zhōng Mó was demoted to Yàozhōu Sīmǎ.
Afterward, the emperor, pitying Shèng's loyalty and integrity,
regretted killing him.
He summoned Mó,
and appointed him Wèiwèi Shàogīng.
The 38th. The emperor summoned the reclusive immortal from Huàshān, Zhēnyuán Chén Tuán.
Zhēnyuán was
Hán Kǔxiàn.
During the Suí dynasty, it was Gǔyáng Xiàn.
In the first year of Gānfēng of Emperor Gāozōng of Táng, it was renamed Zhēnyuán Xiàn because it was the birthplace of Lǎozi.
In the first year of Zàichū, it was changed to Xiānyuán Xiàn.
In the first year of Shénlóng, it reverted to Zhēnyuán,
under Bózhōu.
In the seventh year of Dàzhōng Xiángfú of the Sòng dynasty, it was renamed Wèizhēn Xiàn.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: It is sixty *lǐ* west of Bózhōu.
"Tuán" is pronounced "túwán" (tú wán) according to the fanqie method.
"Fēishēng"
refers to ascending to immortality.
"Huángbái"
refers to refining white metal into yellow gold.
"Your Majesty is the Son of Heaven.
You should focus on governing the realm.
What use is this [alchemy]!"
On the day wùshēn,
he was sent back to the mountains,
and an imperial edict instructed the chief officials of the prefectures and counties to regularly visit and inquire after him.
In the 39th year, 12th month,
on the day Rénshēn,
Zhāng Yǒngdé was appointed Grand Inspector of the Palace Front Army.
Since the Later Táng dynasty,
when the imperial carriage went on an inspection tour or embarked on a military expedition,
the official position of Grand Inspector of the Imperial Household was established.
The Later Zhōu dynasty selected valiant and brave individuals to fill the various battalions of the Palace Front Army,
and first established the Grand Inspector of the Palace Front Army above the Commissioner-in-chief.
From the time Emperor Tàizǔ of Sòng ascended the throne as Grand Inspector of the Palace Front Army,
this position was no longer conferred thereafter.
The 40th year, an imperial order was issued to dispatch conscripted laborers from Chén, Cài, Sòng, Bó, Yǐng, Yǎn, Cáo, and Shàn prefectures
to construct fortifications around Cài.
In the 41st year,
the ruler of Táng issued an edict to abolish the agricultural colonies in Huáinán that were particularly detrimental to the people.
He sent Chén Chǔyáo, a director in the Ministry of War, with heavy gifts across the sea to Qìdān to request troops;
Qìdān was unable to dispatch troops for him,
and detained Chǔyáo, refusing to let him return.
Chǔyáo was upright and outspoken,
and after a long time,
he became indignant and resentful,
frequently reproaching the Qìdān ruler to his face,
but the Qìdān ruler did not punish him for it.
In the 42nd year, the Láo people of Shǔ's Líng and Róng prefectures rebelled.
Sòng Bái said: During the Tàiyuán era of Jìn,
Máo Qú, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, established the Western City Garrison in the eastern border of the Hàn county of Wǔyáng.
In the first year of Emperor Mǐn of Zhōu, Língzhōu was established here,
named after the Líng Well.
Róngzhōu
was the ancient Yèláng Kingdom,
opened by Hàn as the territory of Nán'ān county.
Xiāo Qí established Nán'ān Commandery here,
Suí abolished the commandery,
and its territory belonged to Zīyáng Commandery;
in the early Wǔdé era of Táng,
Dàláo and Wēiyuǎn counties were carved out of Zīzhōu to establish Róngzhōu,
named after Mount Róngdé in its territory.
Láo is pronounced Lǔ Hào.
The Zhígānpēnjì states: Táng had the Commissioner of the Imperial Bow and Arrow Arsenal,
while the Five Dynasties removed
the character
"內" (nèi, imperial).
In the 43rd year, Wúyuè King Hóngchǔ conscripted militia from within his territory,
causing much toil and disturbance.
Qián Hóngyì, the Prefect of Míngzhōu, submitted a strongly worded memorial,
and it was abolished.
first month,
on the day Jǐchǒu, the first day of the month,
Northern Hàn granted a general amnesty,
and changed its era name to Tiānhuì.
Wèi Róng, a Hanlin academician, was appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery and concurrently Grand Chancellor,
and Duàn Héng, the Commissioner of the Imperial Guest House, was appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs.
The 2nd year,
the chief ministers repeatedly requested the establishment of the imperial sons as princes.
The Emperor said:
"All my sons are young;
among my sons, Zōngxùn is Emperor Gōng,
followed by Xīràng, Xījǐn, and Xīhuì.
If I were to favor my own son first,
would he be able to feel secure! "
The 3rd year, the Zhōu army besieged Shòuchūn,
which had not fallen for years.
In the eleventh month of the previous year,
the Zhōu army began to attack Shòuzhōu.

Qí King Jǐngdá dispatched several tens of thousands of troops from Háozhōu, led by Xǔ Wénzhěn, the Commissioner for Reinforcements and Military Governor of Yǒng'ān, Biān Hào, the Commander of the Army, and Zhū Yuán, the Northern Pacification Commissioner,
to sail up the Huái River to relieve it.
They encamped at Zǐjīnshān,
forming over ten camps like a string of pearls,
corresponding with the city's beacon fires morning and evening.
They also built a covered pathway stretching tens of li
to Shòuchūn, intending to transport grain to supply it.
As they approached Shòuchūn,
Lǐ Chóngjìn intercepted and attacked them,
greatly defeating them,
with five thousand dead,
and captured two of their camps.
On the day Dīngwèi,
Chóngjìn reported this.
On the day Wùshēn,
an imperial edict proclaimed that the emperor would personally visit the Huái River next month.
Liú Rénshàn requested to have Biān Hào defend the city,
while he himself would lead the troops in a decisive battle;
Qí King Jǐngdá did not permit it,
and Rénshàn fell ill from indignation.
His youngest son, Chóngjiàn, secretly crossed the Huái River north by boat at night,
but was captured by a junior officer.
Rénshàn ordered him to be cut in half at the waist.
Those around him dared not intervene.
Zhōu Tínggòu, the Supervising Commissioner, wept at the central gate to intercede for him;
Rénshàn refused.
Tínggòu again sought help from his wife,
who said:
"It is not that I do not love Chóngjiàn,
but military law cannot be bent for private reasons,
and integrity cannot be compromised;
if we spare him,
then the Liú clan will be known as a disloyal family.
What face would I and you have to meet the generals and soldiers! "
She quickly ordered his execution,
and then held the funeral.
All the generals and soldiers were moved to tears.
Debaters thought that the Táng reinforcements were still strong,
and many requested to withdraw the troops.
The Emperor was uncertain.
Lǐ Gǔ was confined to his residence due to illness.
In the second month,
on the day Bǐngyín,
the Emperor sent Fàn Zhì and Wáng Pǔ to consult with him.
Gǔ submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Shòuchūn is in dire straits,
on the verge of falling at any moment.
If Your Majesty personally leads the expedition,
then the generals and soldiers will fight with enthusiasm,
the enemy reinforcements will be terrified,
and those in the city, knowing their doom,
will surely be conquered! "
The Emperor was pleased.
The 4th year, on the day Gēngwǔ,
an imperial edict ordered the relevant authorities to re-manufacture sacrificial vessels, sacrificial jades, and other items.
Niè Chóngyì, an Academician of the Directorate of Education, was commanded to discuss the regulations
and create diagrams for them.
Sacrificial vessels included zūn, yí, fǔ, guǐ, biān, and dòu.

Sacrificial jades included the azure bì for worshipping Heaven, the yellow cóng for worshipping Earth, the green guī for worshipping the East, the red zhāng for worshipping the South, the white hú for worshipping the West, and the black huáng for worshipping the North.
At that time, the ritual officials and academicians, in accordance with the edict, discussed the regulations for sacrificial vessels and jades.
Yǐn Zhuō, the Libationer of the Directorate of Education, quoted Cuī Líng'ēn's Sānlǐ Yìzōng, saying: The azure bì,
used for worshipping Heaven,
is twelve cùn long,
based on the twelve hours of the day.
He also quoted what was said in the Jiāngdū Jí, Báihǔ Tōng, and other books,
stating that all bì are round on the outside and square on the inside.
He also said that
the yellow cóng, used for worshipping Earth,
is ten cùn long,
based on the numbers of the Earth.
The cóng is square on the outside and round on the inside,
with eight corners and a hole.
Niè Chóngyì, an Academician of the Directorate of Education, believed that the bì was round both inside and out,
with a diameter of nine cùn.
According to Ruǎn's and Zhèng Xuán's diagrams, all stated nine cùn.
The Zhōulǐ Yùrén Zhí also mentioned a nine-cùn bì.
He also quoted the Erya, saying: When the flesh (outer part) is twice the good (hole), it is called bì;
when the good is twice the flesh, it is called yuàn;
when the flesh and good are equal, it is called huán.
Guō Pú's commentary stated: Hǎo (好)
means hole;
Ròu (肉)
means edge.
But it did not record the dimensions.
Chóngyì also quoted the Dōngguān Yùrén, saying: The bì's hole is three cùn.
The Erya says: When the flesh is twice the hole, it is called bì.
Thus, the flesh on both sides is three cùn each,
totaling nine cùn with the hole,
which clearly indicates the bì is nine cùn.
Chóngyì also said: The yellow cóng has eight sides to symbolize the Earth,
with each corner carved out one cùn and six fēn,
totaling eight cùn in length,
and one cùn in thickness.
According to the Zhōulǐ diagram and Ruǎn's diagram, none had a hole.
He also quoted the Dōngguān Yùrén, saying: The cóng has eight corners but no hole.
Chóngyì also said: Cóng, huáng, guī, and bì
are all vessels for worshipping Heaven and Earth,
but the Erya only mentions that bì, huán, and yuàn have holes;
it does not mention the other vessels like cóng and huáng,
so it is clear that the yellow cóng has eight corners but no hole.
At that time, Tán Mǐn, the Minister of the Grand Court, and others agreed that Chóngyì's citations from the official text of the Zhōulǐ were correct,
and thus followed his proposal.
更 (gēng)
is pronounced gōnghéng.
聶 (Niè)
is pronounced nízhé.
The 5th year, on the day Jiǎxū,
Wáng Pú was appointed Acting Commissioner of the Eastern Capital and concurrently Prefect of Kāifēng,
Zhāng Měi, the Commissioner of the Three Bureaus, was appointed Grand Inspector of the Imperial Household,
and Hán Tōng, the Commander of the Imperial Guard, was appointed Grand Inspector of the Capital's Inner and Outer Districts.
On the *yǐhài* day,
the Emperor set out from Dàliáng.
Earlier, when the Zhōu fought with the Táng,
the Táng navy was swift and agile,
and the Zhōu people had no way to match them.
The Emperor always resented this.
Returning from Shòuchūn,
he ordered the construction of several hundred warships on the Biànshuǐ River west of Dàliáng city,
and commanded Táng surrendered soldiers to teach the northern people naval warfare.
After several months,
they moved with great versatility,
almost surpassing the Táng troops.
At this point, he ordered Wáng Huán, the Grand General of the Right Valiant Guard, to lead several thousand naval troops from the Mǐnhé River along the Yǐng River into the Huái River.
Dīng Dù said: The Mǐnhé River
was originally called Pípágōu,
and is now named the Càihé River.
Yǐng
refers to the Yǐnghé River,
details of which will be found later under the Càihé River.
According to current accounts, the Càihé River enters the capital city from the Dàilóumén Gate of Dōngjīng,
exits through the Xuānhuà Shuǐmén Gate,
flows southeastward,
passes through Chénzhōu,
reaches Càikǒu,
and enters the Yǐnghé River.
The Yǐnghé River originates from Sōngshān,
flows from Yǐngchāng to the border of Lùyì,
passes the Càihékǒu,
merges with the Càihé River,
passes through Yǐngshàng County of Shùnchāng Fǔ,
reaches Xīzhèngyáng,
and enters the Huáihé River.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
the Emperor arrived at Xiàcài.
In the third month,
on the night of the *jǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor crossed the Huái River
and reached the foot of Shòuchūn city.
At dawn on the *gēngyín* day,
he personally donned armor,
and arrayed his army south of Zǐjīnshān Mountain.
He ordered Grand Progenitor Emperor to attack the Táng vanguard camp and a camp north of the mountain,
both of which were broken,
with over three thousand heads captured and slain.
Their supply road was cut,
thus the Táng troops could not assist each other from front to rear.
By dusk,
the Emperor divided his troops to guard the various camps
and returned to Xiàcài.
6 Zhū Yuán of Táng, relying on his achievements,
somewhat disobeyed the Marshal's orders;
Zhū Yuán relied on his achievement of retaking Shū and Hé.
Repeatedly, memorials were submitted stating that Yuán was fickle and
unfit to command troops.
The Táng ruler replaced him with Yáng Shǒuzhōng, the Military Commissioner of Wǔchāng.
When Shǒuzhōng arrived at Háozhōu,
he used the order of Qí Wáng Jǐngdá
to summon Yuán to Háozhōu to discuss matters,
intending to seize his troops.
When Yuán heard of this,
he was furious
and wanted to commit suicide.
His retainer Sòng Jì advised Yuán, saying:
"A true man can find wealth and honor anywhere;
why must you die for your wife and children?"
On the night of the *xīnmǎo* day,
Yuán, along with Zhū Rényù and others, the commander of the vanguard moat camp, led over ten thousand men of the camp to surrender.
His subordinate general Shí Hòuqīng did not comply,
and Yuán killed him.
The Emperor, fearing that the remaining troops would flee eastward along the river,
immediately ordered Zhào Cháo, the Commissioner of the Tiger Swift Left Wing.
*Wǔdài Huìyào*: In the first year of Guǎngshùn,
the Imperial Guard Cavalry was renamed the Dragon Swift Left and Right Armies,
and the Infantry was renamed the Tiger Swift Left and Right Armies.
Cháo
is pronounced as *zhí yáo fān*.
At dawn on the *rénchén* day,
the Emperor's army was at Zhàobù.
Zhàobù is a place on the north bank of the Huáihé River where boats are moored.
People dug into the bank to create paths for ascent and descent,
which were called *bù*.
Zhàobù was named
because the Zhào clan lived there.
Now, from Huāyàn Zhèn in Shòuchūn, going eastward along the Huái River for over a hundred *lǐ*,
one reaches Zhàobù Tān,
and further east past the north of Liángchéng Tān,
which was a strategic point controlled by Qí and Liáng.
In the Huái River, there is Liángchéng Tān,
and twenty-five *lǐ* further east is Luòhékǒu.
They were thoroughly defeated,
with over ten thousand killed and captured.
Xǔ Wénzhěn, Biān Hào, and Yáng Shǒuzhōng were captured.
The remaining troops indeed fled eastward along the Huái River.
The Emperor, from Zhàobù, led several hundred cavalry along the north bank in pursuit,
while the various generals led infantry and cavalry along the south bank in pursuit.
The naval forces went downstream in the middle of the river.
The Táng troops who died in battle, drowned, or surrendered totaled nearly forty thousand.
The captured ships, provisions, and weapons numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
In the late afternoon,
the Emperor galloped to Jīngshānhóng.
Jīngshān
is eighty-three *lǐ* west of Zhōnglí County in Háozhōu,
and is the place where Liáng Wǔdì built a dam.
Now, Huáiyuǎn Jūn is administered from Jīngshān.
That night,
he stayed at Zhènhuái Jūn.
Zhènhuái Jūn
was established at Wōkǒu at that time.
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
his entourage finally arrived.
Liú Rénshàn, hearing that the relief forces had been defeated,
sighed in despair.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
he mobilized laborers from nearby counties
to build Zhènhuái Jūn,
constructing two cities
straddling the Huái River,
and moving the floating bridge from Xiàcài between them,
thus blocking the reinforcement route between Háo and Shòu.
At that time, the Huái River swelled,
and Guō Tíngwèi of Péngchéng, the Superintendent of Háozhōu under Táng, led naval forces upstream on the Huái
intending to take them by surprise and burn the floating bridge.
Zhào Kuāngzàn, the Commander of the Right Dragon Martial Guard, observed this,
ambushed and attacked them,
and defeated them.
Qí Wáng Jǐngdá of Táng and Chén Jué both fled from Háozhōu back to Jīnlíng.
Only Chén Déchéng, the Commissioner of Jìngjiāng, returned with his entire army.
Chén Déchéng
was the son of Huì.
The character "還" (huán)
is pronounced *cóng xuān fān*,
or as written.
On the *wùxū* day,
Xiàng Xùn, the Military Commissioner of Huáinán, was appointed Military Commissioner of Wǔníng and Supervisor of the Huáinán Marching Army,
and commanded troops to garrison Zhènhuái Jūn.
On the *jǐhài* day,
the Emperor returned from Zhènhuái Jūn to Xiàcài.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
an imperial edict was bestowed upon Liú Rénshàn,
instructing him to choose his own fate, whether misfortune or fortune.
The Táng ruler discussed personally overseeing the generals to resist Zhōu.
Jiáo Kuāngshùn, a Scholar of the Central Secretariat, submitted a memorial sternly remonstrating,
but the Táng ruler considered it disheartening to the troops
and exiled him to Fúzhōu.
The Táng ruler asked Zhū Kuāngyè and Liú Cúnzhōng, Commanders of the Divine Guard, about defense strategies.
Kuāngyè recited a poem by Luó Yǐn, saying:
"When the time comes, heaven and earth lend their strength;
when fortune declines, even heroes lose their freedom."
Cúnzhōng considered Kuāngyè's words to be true.
The Táng ruler was enraged,
demoted Kuāngyè to Vice Administrator of Fúzhōu,
and exiled Cúnzhōng to Ráozhōu.
Afterwards, he indeed dared not go himself.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
the Emperor displayed his troops north of Shòuchūn city.
Liú Rénshàn, the Military Commissioner of Qīnghuái and concurrently Grand Councilor, was gravely ill
and unconscious.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Zhōu Tínggòu, the Supervising Commissioner, Sūn Yǔ, the Deputy Commissioner of Agrarian Affairs, and others composed a memorial on Rénshàn's behalf,
and sent an envoy to present it in surrender.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
the Emperor bestowed an edict upon Rénshàn,
and dispatched Wànnián Zhāng Bǎoxù, the Commissioner of the Palace Gate, to enter the city and proclaim the imperial will.
Rénshàn's son, Chóngràng, again came out to offer an apology.
On the *wùshēn* day,
the Emperor arrayed a grand display of arms
and received the surrender north of Shòuchūn city.
Tínggòu and others carried Rénshàn out of the city.
Rénshàn was lying down and unable to rise.
The Emperor comforted him, bestowed gifts,
and ordered him to return to the city to recuperate.
On the day of Gēngxū,
Shòuzhōu's administration was moved to Xiàcài.
Shòuzhōu
was elevated to Shòuchūn Fǔ by the Sòng dynasty.
To this day, its administration is in Xiàcài Xiàn,
while the old county of Shòuchūn itself became a county,
located south of the Huáishuǐ,
twenty-five lǐ northwest of Xiàcài.
After Gāozōng crossed to the south,
Anfēng Jūn was re-established in Shòuchūn Xiàn, the former seat of Shòuzhōu,
to serve as a strategic control point.
This is because of its inherent strategic importance,
which has remained unchanged throughout history.
Sòng Bái said: Xiàcài
was anciently the state of Cài,
and Zhōulái of Wú.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"Duke Chéng of Cài moved to Zhōulái,
which was called Xiàcài."
This is correct.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was Xiàcài Xiàn.
During the Liáng dynasty, a city was built on Jiáshí Shān to resist Wèi,
which is the current county seat.
The people of the prefecture who had received Tang documents and gathered in the mountains and forests
were all summoned and ordered to resume their livelihoods;
their past crimes were not to be investigated.
Those who had previously caused harm or death
were not to be subject to retribution or litigation.
Any government orders from previous days that were inconvenient for the people
were to be reported by the local prefecture for amendment.
On the day of Xīnhài,
Liú Rénshàn was appointed Tiānpíng Jiédùshǐ concurrently Zhongshūlìng.
The imperial edict roughly stated:
"Utterly loyal to your service,
maintaining integrity without flaw,
how many famous ministers of previous generations
can compare!
In Our campaign against rebels,
we owe much to you."
On this day,
he died,
and was posthumously granted the title of Péngchéng Jùnwáng.
The Lord of Táng, hearing of this,
also posthumously granted him the title of Tàishī.
The Emperor further changed Qīnghuái Jūn to Zhōngzhèng Jūn.
The Yáng family established Zhōngzhèng Jūn in Shòuzhōu,
later renamed Qīnghuái Jūn,
and now it is restored to Zhōngzhèng Jūn to commemorate Liú Rénshàn's integrity.
According to Xuē Shǐ: In the second year of Tiānchéng of Táng Míngzōng,

On the day of Jǐchǒu in the intercalary fifth month of the second year of Chángxīng,

On the day of Guǐyǒu in the eighth month,

in the first year of Tiānchéng of Hòu Táng, was elevated to Shùnhuà Jūn Jiédù.
These are all preserved for now,
awaiting further research.
Yáng Xìn, Right Yǔlín Tǒngjūn, was appointed Zhōngzhèng Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.

Chénzhōu

The people of Luòyáng feared him

Since the Emperor succeeded Tàizǔ,

He never went to Dàliáng.

fourth month,

shǐ Zhī Zášì Zhāng Shí and others

Sī [sī],

Tún [tún],
the same as dùn [dùn].

seventh month,

Huán [huán],

On the 24th day of the 9th month,
Dòu Yǎn (竇儼), Secretariat Drafter (中書舍人), submitted a memorial requesting that the competent authorities discuss ancient and modern rites and ceremonies,
compose the Dàzhōu Tōnglǐ (大周通禮),

He also stated:
"The foundation of governance
lies preeminently in selecting capable individuals;
and among the critical aspects of selecting individuals,
none is more important than the prime minister.
Since the end of the Dà Táng (大唐) dynasty,
official titles have been bestowed lightly,
and those who first became chief ministers (fǔbì 輔弼)
immediately concurrently held the offices of the Three Dukes (sāngōng 三公) and Grand Minister (púyè 僕射).
Therefore, when they had not yet obtained these positions,
they pursued them with fierce competition;
once they obtained them,
they made silence and acquiescence their business.
They merely sought to be relieved of urgent duties,
to retain their highly esteemed offices,
to enjoy leisure in their gardens,
and to ensure the safety of their clans.

I beg that effective immediately, the prime ministers, from among those holding the third rank in the Nángōng (南宮) and officials of the two departments (liǎngshěng 兩省) serving as remonstrance officials (gěi 給) and drafters (shě 舍) or above,
each recommend those they know to be capable.
'Effective immediately the prime ministers'
refers to those currently in prime ministerial positions.
'Nángōng'
refers to the Shàngshūshěng (尚書省).
'Third rank'
refers to the Six Ministers (liùbù shàngshū 六部尚書).
'Two departments'
refers to the Zhōngshūshěng (中書省) and Ménxiàshěng (門下省).
'Remonstrance officials and drafters'
refers to the Gěishìzhōng (給事中) and Zhōngshūshèrén (中書舍人).
They may then be appointed;
Yōng (庸)
means 'to employ'.
And let them provisionally oversee governmental affairs in their current capacities.
Within a year,
their performance of duties shall be observed.
If they are indeed found to be competent,
'competent'
means 'equal to their responsibilities'
and 'suitable for their duties'.
Chēng (稱)
is pronounced chìzhèng;
the same applies to 'not competent' below.
Then they shall be appointed as Grand Counselor (píngzhāngshì 平章事);
if they are not yet senior enough,
they shall be slightly transferred to other offices,
continuing to provisionally oversee affairs as before.
If any are found to be incompetent,
their governmental affairs shall be suspended,
and their recommenders shall be held accountable.
Furthermore,
among the ranks of officials,
more than half hold titles without actual duties,
such as the generals of various guards (zhūwèi jiāngjūn 諸衞將軍), officials of the Eastern Palace (dōnggōng guānshǔ 東宮官屬), and various palace envoys (nèi zhūshǐ 內諸使).
They should be assigned to external posts
and tested in practical matters.
They should
then be ranked according to their former positions.
Their administrative performance should be assessed;
those who are capable should be promoted,
and those who are not should be dismissed."
He also requested:
"Let bandits be encouraged to inform on each other,
and award them half of the reported assets;
or if a relative is the ringleader,
then their accomplices shall be prosecuted, and the one who reported them shall be pardoned.
If this is done,
bandits will be unable to gather.
This means that if relatives conspire to commit banditry,
and one among them is able to turn themselves in, they shall be pardoned,
while their accomplices shall be punished for their crimes.
Shǒu (首)
is pronounced shìyòu.
The villagers of Xīnzhèng (新鄭) formed voluntary defense corps (yìyíng 義營),
each establishing commanders and assistants.
If one household committed banditry,
the entire village was implicated;
if one household was robbed,
one commander was punished.
Whenever a robbery occurred,
drums were beaten and fires lit,
and able-bodied men gathered like clouds.
With few bandits and many commoners,
none could escape.
As a result, neighboring counties were overrun, but this one region remained uniquely peaceful.
'Overrun' and 'uniquely peaceful'
both refer to banditry.
This is also a method for stopping banditry.
Furthermore,
for successive reigns,
imperial edicts have repeatedly been issued,
allowing people to cultivate more land and expand their farming,
paying only the old taxes.
However, once they had planted,
the authorities would survey the fields and increase the taxes,
causing the people to be suspicious and fearful, and cultivated land did not increase.
The foremost principle of governance
is trustworthiness.
If trust is established,
then there will be no land not expanded,
and if land is expanded, grain will be abundant.
If grain is abundant, storing it among the people is like storing it in official granaries."
He also said:
"Your Majesty campaigned south against Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮),
and in one swift action gained eight prefectures.
'Eight prefectures'
refers to Guāng (光), Huáng (黃), Shū (舒), Qí (蘄), Hé (和), Yáng (揚), Chú (滁), and Tài (泰),
all of which were taken.
The events are described in the third month above.
There were no strong enemies before.
Now, with many troops attacking few,
and with order attacking chaos,
there is no doubt of victory.
However, speed is essential in action,
so that those people may be spared the disaster of capture and slaughter,
and these people may be relieved of the hardship of transportation and supply."
The Emperor read it and approved.
Yǎn (儼)
was Yí's (儀) younger brother.
On the 25th day of winter,
10th month,
on the day wǔwǔ (戊午),

examination categories were established for 'Worthy and Upright, Frank in Speech and Resolute in Admonition' (xiánliáng fāngzhèng zhíyán jíjiàn 賢良方正直言極諫), 'Profound in Classical Learning and Fit to Be a Teacher or Model' (jīngxué yōushēn kě wéi shīfǎ 經學優深可為師法), and 'Familiar with Official Administration and Proficient in Education' (xiángxián lìlǐ dá yú jiàohuà 詳閑吏理達於教化), etc.
These were called the 'Imperial Examinations' (zhìjǔ 制舉).
At that time, an imperial edict proclaimed that all types of people in the empire,
regardless of their former qualifications or current official positions,
