but Lúzhōu alone had not fallen,
probably because it had many garrisoned soldiers,
and the Zhōu army dared not lightly offend it.
趣,
read as qīyù.
The Táng Zhǔ, hearing that the emperor was on the river,
feared that he would cross south,
and also felt ashamed to lower his title and declare himself a vassal.
So he sent Bīngbù Shìláng Chén Jué to present a memorial.
Kǎoyì says: The Shíguó Jìnián:
"Sent Shūmìshǐ Chén Jué to present a memorial."
The Shílù records his memorial as saying:
"Now I send Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū, Bīngbù Shìláng, your servant Chén Jué, to personally await your imperial decree."
This was probably a temporary official title granted at the time.
We follow this.
(He) was sent to await orders from Zhōngguó.
At that time, of Huáinán, only Lú, Shū, Qí, and Huáng had not fallen.
On the day of Bǐngshēn,
Jué arrived at Yíngluán,
saw the might of the Zhōu army,
and reported to the emperor,
requesting that someone be sent to cross the river to receive a memorial,
offering the four prefectures,
and drawing the river as the border,
to seek a cessation of hostilities.
His words were full of grief.
The emperor said:
"We originally raised an army only to take the north of the river.
If your lord can lead his entire state to submit,
what more do We seek!"
Jué bowed in gratitude and withdrew.
On the day of Dīngyǒu,
Jué requested to send his subordinate Gémén Chéngzhǐ Liú Chéngyù to Jīnlíng.
The emperor bestowed a letter upon the Táng Zhǔ,
referring to him as
"The Emperor respectfully enquires of the Jiāngnán Guózhǔ,"
comforting and accepting him.
On the day of Wùxū,
Wúyuè reported sending Shàngzhí
Zhǐhuīshǐ, Chǔzhōu Cìshǐ Shào Kěqiān and Xiùzhōu Cìshǐ Lù Yànzhū with four hundred warships and seventeen thousand soldiers to garrison the south bank of Tōngzhōu.
After Zhōu captured Jìnghǎi Jūn,
Tōngzhōu was established.
The south bank of Tōngzhōu is the land of Fúshān Zhèn in Chángshú Xiàn, Sūzhōu,
which was Nánshā in the Eastern Jìn.
The Táng Zhǔ again sent Liú Chéngyù to present a memorial, styling himself as the Táng Guózhǔ,
requesting to offer the four prefectures north of the river,
and annually submitting tribute of ten
myriad (units).
At this, all north of the river was pacified,
gaining fourteen prefectures
and sixty counties.
The fourteen prefectures were Guāng, Shòu, Lú, Shū, Qí, Huáng, Chú, Hé, Háo, Sì, Chǔ, Yáng, Tài, and Tōng.
On the day of Gēngzǐ,
the emperor bestowed a letter upon the Táng Zhǔ,
instructing him that:
"All armies along the river, as well as those from Liǎngzhè, Húnán, and Jīngnán, should be dismissed and return.
As for the three routes of Lú, Qí, and Huáng,
their troops are also ordered to be withdrawn to the outskirts."
This refers to the Zhōu armies sent to attack Lú, Qí, and Huáng.
"Outskirts"
refers to outside the near suburbs.
"You may send people to summon the generals and officers to hand over the cities and towns to them.
If there are boats and ships in the river that need to travel back and forth,
they are all to be guided to the north bank."
All Táng boats and ships on the north bank
were allowed to be guided to the south bank.
On the day of Xīnchǒu,
Chén Jué took his leave,
and another letter was bestowed upon the Táng Zhǔ,
instructing him that there was no need to transmit the throne to his son.
On the day of Rén'yín,
the emperor returned from Yíngluán to Yángzhōu.
On the day of Guǐmǎo,
an edict ordered the Wúyuè and Jīngnán armies to each return to their respective regions;
Qián Hóngshù was bestowed with thirty thousand bolts of silk for his troops,
and Gāo Bǎoróng with ten thousand bolts.
The Wúyuè army was at Nánshā,
the Jīngnán army reached Èzhōu,
and both were rewarded and ordered to return.
犒,
read as kǔdào.
On the day of Jiǎchén,
Bǎoxìn Jūn was established at Lúzhōu,
with Yòu Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn Zhào Kuāngzàn as Jiedùshǐ.
On the day of Bǐngwǔ,
the Táng Zhǔ sent Féng Yánjǐ to offer one million in total of silver, silk, money, tea, and grain to reward the army.
Silver in taels, silk in bolts, money in strings, tea in catties,
and grain in shi,
each counted in myriads, their total number being one million.
On the day of Jǐyǒu,
Sòng Yánwò was ordered to lead three thousand naval troops up the river to patrol.
On the day of Gēngxū,
an imperial decree ordered that guardians be provided for the tombs of the former Huáinán Jiedùshǐ Yáng Xíngmì and the former Shēngfǔ Jiedùshǐ Xú Wēn;
their usurped posthumous titles were removed,
but their former towns retained.
Shēngfǔ is Jīnlíng.
Jīnlíng,
Shēngzhōu of Táng,
hence called Shēngfǔ.
The senior officials were also entrusted to inspect them regularly.
On the day of Xīnhài,
the Táng Zhǔ sent his Línrǔ Gōng Xú Liáo to come on his behalf to present birthday wishes.
It means presenting wine to wish longevity,
not on a imperial birthday.
The emperor was born on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month.
上,
read as shízhǎng.
19 In this month,
the mouth of the Biàn River was dredged,
guiding the Yellow River to reach the Huái River,
thereby establishing boat traffic between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
This was the transport route from the Táng era.
Since the separation of Jiāng and Huái,
transport was cut off,
and waterways were blocked.
Now it was dredged again.
20 In summer,
fourth month,
on the day of Yǐmǎo,
the emperor returned north from Yángzhōu.
The new Imperial Ancestral Temple was completed.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
the spirit tablets were moved into the temple.
In the third year of Tàizǔ's Guǎngshùn reign,
the Imperial Ancestral Temple was built in Dàliáng,
and it was now completed.
*Wǔdài Huìyào*: In the seventh month of the first year of Tàizǔ's Guǎngshùn reign,
Gāozǔ Jǐng was posthumously honored as Ruìhé Huángdì,
with the temple name Xìnzǔ;
Zengzǔ Chén as Míngxiàn Huángdì,
with the temple name Xīzǔ;
Zǔ Yùn as Yìshùn Huángdì,
with the temple name Yìzǔ;
Kǎo Jiǎn as Zhāngsù Huángdì,
with the temple name Qìngzǔ.
On the night of the 22nd, *xīnyǒu*,
fire broke out south of Qiántáng city,
spreading to the inner city,
destroying almost all official buildings and residences.
At dawn on the *rénxū* day,
the fire was about to reach the Zhènguó Granary.
Wúyuè Wáng Hóngchù, who had been ill for a long time,
forced himself to go out to fight the fire;
when the fire stopped,
he said to his attendants:
"My illness has healed because of this disaster."
The people's hearts were somewhat relieved.
When the Emperor campaigned in the south,
Qìdān took advantage of the emptiness to invade.
On the *rénshēn* day,
the Emperor arrived in Dàliáng,
and ordered
Zhāng Yǒngdé to lead troops to defend the northern border.
In the fifth month,
on the first day, *xīnsì*,
there was a solar eclipse.
An edict was issued to reward the soldiers who campaigned in the south and the recently surrendered people from Huáinán.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Tàizǔ Huángdì was appointed Commander of the Zhōngwǔ Military Governor,
and Ān Shěnqí was transferred to be Commander of the Pínglú Military Governor.
Guō Chóng, the Commander of the Chéngdé Military Governor, attacked and
captured Shùchéng from the Qìdān.
Shùchéng was
the Shùzhōu county of Hàn's Bóhǎi Commandery.
Suí renamed it Shùchéng.
In Táng, it belonged to Yíngzhōu.
In the sixth year of Sòng's Xīníng reign, Shùchéng was reduced to a town
and belonged to Héjiān.
The Lord of Táng, to avoid using the taboo name of Zhōu,
changed his name to Jǐng.
This was to avoid the taboo name of Zhōu Xìnzǔ.
*Gēng*,
pronounced as *gōnghéng fān*.
When called a "state lord,"
all imperial rituals and regulations were degraded.
The reign title was removed,
the Zhōu calendar was adopted,
and this was reported to the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
Fēng Yánjǐ, Left Grand Minister and Co-ordinator of State Affairs, was dismissed as Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
Yán Xù, Menxià Attendant and Co-ordinator of State Affairs, was dismissed as Junior Tutor.
Chén Jué, Privy Council Commissioner and Minister of War, was dismissed from his original post.
Initially,
Fēng Yánjǐ used his strategy for seizing the Central Plains to persuade the Lord of Táng,
thus gaining favor.
Yánjǐ once mocked Lièzǔ for "hoarding" troops, calling it petty,
saying:
"Only a few thousand soldiers were lost at Ānlù,
yet he stopped eating and sighed for ten days.
This refers to the defeat of Lǐ Chéngyù at Ānzhōu in the fifth year of Tiānfú of Jìn Gāozǔ,
details found in volume 282.
*Sàng*,
pronounced as *xīlàng fān*.
*Wéi*,
pronounced as *yúwěi fān*.
How can he achieve great things?
It is not like the present emperor, who keeps tens of thousands of troops campaigning outside,
while he plays polo and enjoys banquets as usual.
Truly an enlightened ruler!"
Yánjǐ and his clique, when discussing,
often took the affairs of the world as their personal responsibility,
echoing each other.
Hànlín Scholar Cháng Mèngxī repeatedly said that Yánjǐ and others were frivolous
and untrustworthy;
the Lord of Táng did not listen.
Mèngxī said:
"Slanderous words resemble loyalty.
If Your Majesty does not realize this,
the country will surely perish!"
When they submitted to Zhōu,
Yánjǐ's clique talked among themselves,
some calling Zhōu the "Great Dynasty."
Mèngxī laughed loudly and said:
"You gentlemen always wished to make your ruler like Yáo or Shùn,
why today do you consider yourselves a 'Small Dynasty'?"
The others fell silent.
Since the Lord of Táng submitted,
the Emperor only sent letters through his envoys,
never dispatching his own envoys to their country.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
for the first time, Tàipú Qīng Fēng Yánlǔ and Wèiwèi Shàopú Zhōng Mó were sent as envoys to Táng.
These two were originally Táng officials.
This also includes the Qīntiān Lì for this year.
When Liú Chéngyù returned from Jīnlíng,
he met the Emperor in the third month.
*Huán*,
pronounced as *cóngxuān fān*,
also as is.
He reported that Jiāngnán had no saline fields,
but the coastal areas were salty,
suitable for boiling salt.
Saline fields are
now called alkaline land.
*Lǔ*,
pronounced as *lánggǔ fān*.
*Jiǎn*,
pronounced as *gǔzhǎn fān*.
He proposed taking control of the salt administration in the south to support the army.
The Emperor said:
"Hǎilíng is north of the river,
making mixed residency difficult,"
meaning it was difficult to have Zhōu officials and Táng officials reside together.
Until this point,
an edict ordered 300,000 *hú* of salt to be supplied to Jiāngnán annually,
and the captured Jiāngnán soldiers
were gradually returned.
In the sixth month,
on the *rénzǐ* day,
Lǐ Jūn, the Commander of the Zhāoyì Military Governor, reported attacking the Shíhuì Pass of Běihàn,
capturing its six stockades.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Jìnzhōu reported that Dūjiān Lǐ Qiānpǔ attacked Běihàn,
defeating Xiàoyì.
Xiàoyì was
the territory of Hàn's Zhōngyáng county.
Later Wèi called it Yǒng'ān.
In the first year of Táng's Zhēnguān reign, it was renamed Xiàoyì,
belonging to Fénzhōu,
located southeast of the prefecture.
In the fifth year of Sòng's Xīníng reign, Xiàoyì was reduced to a town
and belonged to Jièxiū county.
Sòng Bái said: Xiàoyì county
was originally the land of Hàn's Císhì county.
Cáo Wèi moved Zhōngyáng county to its present seat.
After Yǒngjiā, it was incorporated into Xíchéng.
Later Wèi again divided Xíchéng to establish Yǒng'ān county
thirty *lǐ* east of present-day Língshí county.
In the first year of Zhēnguān, as the county name was the same as a Fúzhōu county,
it was changed to Xiàoyì,
named after Zhèng Xīng, a county resident known for his righteous conduct.
Gāo Bǎoróng sent an envoy to persuade the Lord of Shǔ to declare vassalage to Zhōu.
The Lord of Shǔ replied that Hú Lì had sent a letter to Zhōu the previous year but received no reply.
See last year in the previous volume.
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the *bǐngxū* day,
the Dà Zhōu Xíngtǒng (Penal Code of Great Zhōu) was first implemented.
The Emperor wanted to equalize land taxes.
On the *dīnghài* day,
Yuán Zhěn's "Chart for Equalizing Land" was distributed to all circuits.
The edict at the time stated:
"Recently, having reviewed Yuán Zhěn's *Chángqìng Jí*,
I saw the memorial on equalizing land that he submitted when he was in Tóngzhōu.
It meticulously details the advantages and disadvantages of the time,
so that all living beings in a region
received its benefits.
Transmitted in written records,
it can be consulted.
Therefore, I ordered it to be made into a plain chart,
directly recording its content."
*Zhěn*,
pronounced as *zhǐrěn fān*.
In the intercalary month,
Liú Cóngxiào, the Táng Qīngyuán Military Governor and concurrently Grand Councilor of the Secretariat,
(Táng established the Qīngyuán Army in Quánzhōu.)
placed a silk memorial in his leather belt
and came through secret routes to declare vassalage.
When Jìn Wáng Jǐngsuì, the Táng Military Marshal of Jiāngxī, went to Hóngzhōu,
(See third month above.)
he requested a high official to accompany him.
The Lord of Táng appointed Lǐ Zhēnggǔ, Vice Commissioner of the Privy Council and Vice Minister of War, as Vice Commander of the Zhènnán Military Governor.
Zhēnggǔ was arrogant and despotic.
Although Jǐngsuì was tolerant and benevolent,
after a long time he could not bear it,
and often wished to execute Zhēnggǔ
and submit himself to the authorities.
His attendants advised against it and he stopped,
but Jǐngsuì was constantly unhappy.
Crown Prince Hóngjì 弘冀 was often unlawful in the Eastern Palace.
The Táng 唐 ruler was angered,
and once struck him with a polo stick, saying:
"I should recall Jǐngsuì 景遂 again."
Yuán Cóngfàn 袁從範, the overseer of Zhāoqìng 昭慶 Palace, was Jǐngsuì's 景遂 chief military administrator in Hóngzhōu 洪州.
Someone slandered Cóngfàn's 從範 son to Jǐngsuì 景遂,
and Jǐngsuì 景遂 wanted to kill him.
Cóngfàn 從範 therefore harbored resentment.
Hóngjì 弘冀 heard of this,
and secretly sent Cóngfàn 從範 to poison him.
In the eighth month,
on the day Gēngchén 庚辰,
Jǐngsuì 景遂 was very thirsty after playing polo.
Cóngfàn 從範 offered him a drink,
Jǐngsuì 景遂 drank it and died.
Before the burial,
his body had already decomposed.
The Táng 唐 ruler did not know this,
and posthumously granted him the title of Imperial Younger Brother,
with the posthumous name Wénchéng 文成.
On the day Xīnsì 辛巳,
Nán Hàn 南漢 Zhōngzōng 中宗 died,
at the age of thirty-nine.
Jìxìng 繼興 ascended the throne,
changed his name to Chǎng 鋹,
and changed the reign title to Dàbǎo 大寶.
Chǎng 鋹 was sixteen years old,
and all state affairs were decided by the eunuch Gōng Chéngshū 龔澄樞, the overseer of Yùqīng 玉清 Palace.
Ōu Shǐ 歐史 says: The Liú 劉 family built detached palaces for hunting and recreation,
including Nángōng 南宮, Dàmíng 大明, Chānghuá 昌華, Gānquán 甘泉, Wánhuá 玩華, Xiùhuá 秀華, Yùqīng 玉清, Tàiwēi 太微, and other palaces,
all with palace overseers in charge.
Officials of the ministries and provinces merely held honorary positions.
On the day Jiǎshēn 甲申,
Táng 唐 first established a Memorial Presentation Office in Dàliáng 大梁.
As vassals, this was their custom.
On the day Rénchén 壬辰,
the emperor ordered Língshòu Cáo Bīn 靈壽曹彬, the commissioner of the Western Upper Palace Gate, to go on an envoy mission to Wúyuè 吳越,
and bestowed upon Wúyuè 吳越 King Hóngchù 弘俶 two hundred steel armors for cavalry,
five thousand armors for infantry, and other weapons.
Bīn 彬 returned quickly after completing his mission,
refusing all gifts.
The Wúyuè 吳越 people chased him with a light boat to give them to him,
four times.
Bīn 彬 said:
"If I accept them in the end,
it would be stealing a good name."
He listed the exact number of items,
and presented them to the emperor upon his return.
The emperor said:
"Previous envoys
begged insatiably,
causing the four quarters to slight imperial decrees.
It is excellent that you can be like this;
however, they gave them to you,
so you should take them yourself."
Bīn 彬 then bowed and accepted them,
distributing all of them among his relatives and acquaintances,
leaving nothing in his own household.
On the day Xīnchǒu 辛丑,
Féng Yánlǔ 馮延魯 and Zhōng Mó 鍾謨 returned from Táng 唐.
The Táng 唐 ruler sent a memorial to express gratitude.
"Shǒubiǎo 手表" means
"handwritten memorial."
"The grace of Heaven and Earth is profound,
the grace of parents is deep.
A child does not thank a parent,
how can a person repay Heaven?
Only with a loyal heart
can one respond to the great creator."
He also requested that he be treated as a vassal state
and be granted imperial edicts.
He also stated:
"There are matters of sentiment to be presented by Zhōng Mó 鍾謨,
I request that he be allowed to return soon."
The Táng 唐 ruler again ordered Mó 謨 to inform the emperor
of his desire to abdicate to the Crown Prince.
In the ninth month,
on the day Dīngsì 丁巳,
Yánlǔ 延魯 was appointed Minister of Punishments, and Mó 謨 was appointed Remonstrance Official.
The Táng 唐
ruler again sent Yīn Chóngyì 殷崇義, Minister of Personnel and Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, to congratulate on Tiānqīngjié 天清節.
The emperor was born on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month,
and this day was designated Tiānqīngjié 天清節.
The emperor planned to attack Shǔ 蜀.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Jǐmǎo 己卯,
Gāo Fáng 高防, Assistant Minister of Revenue, was appointed Commissioner for Water and Land Operations on the Southwest Front,
and Lǐ Yù 李玉, Right Palace Assistant, was appointed Judge.
On the day Jiǎwǔ 甲午,
the emperor sent Féng Yánlǔ 馮延魯, General of the Left Palace Gate Guard Xǔ Wénzhěn 許文稹, General of the Right Cavalry Guard Biān Hào 邊鎬, and Court of the Imperial Stud Zhōu Tínggòu 周廷構 back to Táng 唐.
Féng Yánlǔ 馮延魯 was captured, see Volume 292, Year 3.
Xǔ Wénzhěn 許文稹 and Biān Hào 邊鎬 were captured, see last volume, last year.
Zhōu Tínggòu 周廷構 surrendered, also see this year.
They were discarded and not reused.
Gāo Bǎoróng 高保融 again sent a letter to the Shǔ 蜀 ruler.
He had previously sent a letter,
see last sixth month.
The Shǔ 蜀 ruler convened his generals and ministers to discuss it.
Lǐ Hào 李昊 said:
"To comply would be a humiliation to the sovereign and father;
to refuse would surely bring the Zhōu 周 army.
Can the generals resist Zhōu 周?"
All the generals said:
"With Your Majesty's sagacity,
and the country's perilous and strong defenses,
how can we submit at the mere rumor of wind?
We have been preparing our horses and sharpening our weapons
precisely for this day.
We, your subjects, request to defend the altars of soil and grain with our lives!"
On the day Dīngyǒu 丁酉,
the Shǔ 蜀 ruler ordered Hào 昊 to draft a letter,
which expressed an absolute refusal.
An imperial edict ordered Lǐ Yǐng 李潁 of Xūchéng 須城, Right Palace Attendant, and thirty-four others
to go to various prefectures to equalize and set land rents.
Xūchéng 須城 County was part of Yùnzhōu 鄆州,
which was Táng's 唐 Xūchāng 須昌 County.
Later Táng 唐 changed its name to Xūchéng 須城
to avoid the taboo name of the ancestral temple of Xiànzǔ 獻祖.
Ài 艾
is a surname.
In Yànzi Chūnqiū 晏子春秋,
there was a minister Ài Kǒng 艾孔 in Qí 齊.
In Fēngsú Tōng 風俗通,
Páng Jiǎn's 龐儉 mother was from the Ài 艾 clan.
"Háng 行"
pronounced xià mèng fān (meaning xíng).
On the day Gēngzǐ 庚子,
an imperial edict ordered all prefectures to combine villages,
typically forming troups of one hundred households.
Each tuan 團 was to have three qícháng 耆長.
"Qí 耆"
means old.
Each tuan 團 had three elders as its leaders.
"Zhǎng 長"
pronounced zhī liǎng fān (meaning zhǎng).
Wooden figures of farmers and silkworm women were carved
and placed in the palace courtyard.
Sòng Yánwò 宋延渥, Military Governor of Wǔshèng 武勝, was ordered to patrol the river with a naval force.
Gāo Bǎoróng 高保融 reported
that he heard the imperial army was going to attack Shǔ 蜀,
and requested to lead a naval force to the Three Gorges.
An imperial edict praised him.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Gēngxū 庚戌,
an imperial decree ordered Dòu Yǎn 竇儼 to compile the *Dà Zhōu Tōng Lǐ* 大周通禮 and *Dà Zhōu Zhèng Yuè* 大周正樂.
Last year Dòu Yǎn 竇儼 requested to establish rites and music, see last volume.
On the day Xīnhài 辛亥,
Nán Hàn 南漢 buried Emperor Wénwǔ Guāngmíng Xiàohuáng 文武光明孝皇帝 in Zhāolíng 昭陵,
with the temple name Zhōngzōng 中宗.
On the day Yǐchǒu 乙丑,
the Táng 唐 ruler again sent Zhōng Mó 鍾謨, Assistant Minister of Rites, to have an audience.
Lǐ Yù 李玉 arrived in Cháng'ān 長安.
Someone said,
"Guī'ān Zhèn 歸安鎮 in Shǔ 蜀 is about three hundred *lǐ* to the south of Cháng'ān 長安,
and can be taken by surprise."
Guī'ān Zhèn 歸安鎮 should be in the territory of Jīnzhōu 金州 of Shǔ 蜀.
A dispatch was sent to Wáng Yànchāo 王彥超, Military Governor of Yǒngxīng 永興,
requesting two hundred soldiers.
Yànchāo 彥超 thought that the road to Guī'ān 歸安 was difficult and narrow, making it hard to take.
Yù 玉 said:
"I have received a secret imperial order myself."
Yànchāo 彥超 had no choice but to provide them.
Yù 玉 led them there.
In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Chéngxūn 李承勳, the defense commissioner of Guī'ān Zhèn 歸安鎮 in Shǔ 蜀,
ambushed him by holding a strategic choke point,
beheaded Yù 玉,
and all his troops were lost.
On the day Yǐyǒu 乙酉,
the Shǔ 蜀 ruler appointed Zhào Chóngtāo 趙崇韜, Commander of the Right Palace Guard Infantry, as Commissioner of Northern Expedition.
On the day Bǐngxū 丙戌,
Mèng Yíyè 孟貽業, Commander of the Imperial Guard, Military Governor of Wǔxìn 武信, and concurrently Chancellor, was appointed Commissioner of Zhāowǔ 昭武 and Wénzhōu 文州.
Zhāowǔ Zhāowǔ 軍 refers to Lìzhōu 利州.
From Lìzhōu 利州 to Wénzhōu 文州,
he was entrusted with controlling the strategic passes of Jiāngyóu 江油 and Jiàngé 劍閣.
Hán Bǎozhēn 韓保貞, Military Governor of Shānnán Xīdào 山南西道, was appointed Commissioner of Northern Expedition,
leading sixty thousand troops,
who were stationed in key locations to defend against Zhōu 周.
On the day Bǐngxū 丙戌,
an imperial edict ordered that all households subject to various levies and俸戶 (households whose taxes were used to pay officials' salaries)
be returned to the prefectures and counties.
In the early Táng 唐,
various ministries established capital funds for public offices,
using them for trade to earn interest,
and distributing monthly allowances based on the number of staff.
Later, these capital funds for public offices were abolished.
Instead, seven thousand prominent households across the realm were designated as *xūshì* 胥士 (tax-paying households that also performed miscellaneous duties),
and their taxes were collected
and distributed based on the number of officials. These were the so-called *kèhù* 課戶.
Táng 唐 also levied a small annual tax,
overseen by high-ranking households,
and the monthly interest collected was used to pay salaries. These were the so-called *fènghù* 俸戶.
In the beginning,
Sòng Qíqiū (宋齊丘), Grand Tutor and concurrently Grand Chancellor of the Secretariat, Duke of Chǔ (楚公), of Táng (唐), had many partisans,
wishing to exclusively consolidate his power in court.
Ambitious and impetuous men competed to attach themselves to him,
promoting him as an elder statesman of the country.
Chén Jué (陳覺), the Privy Council Commissioner, and Lǐ Zhēnggǔ (李徵古), the Vice Commissioner, relied on Qíqiū's (齊丘) influence
and were particularly arrogant and insolent.
When Xǔ Wénzhěn (許文稹) and others were defeated at Zǐjīn Shān (紫金山),
Jué (覺), Qíqiū (齊丘), and Jǐng Dá (景達) fled from Háozhōu (濠州) back to the capital.
The event is seen in the previous scroll, last year.
The Táng (唐) ruler once sighed, saying:
"My state has come to this in a single day!"
He then shed tears.
Zhēnggǔ (徵古) said:
"Your Majesty should marshal troops to resist the enemy.
What is the use of weeping?
Could it be that you drank too much,
or that your wet nurse has not arrived?"
The Táng (唐) ruler's expression changed,
but Zhēnggǔ (徵古) remained composed.
Coincidentally, the Bureau of Astronomy reported:
"There are changes in the astronomical phenomena;
the ruler should abdicate to avert disaster."
The Táng (唐) ruler then said:
"Calamities are rampant.
I wish to relinquish all state affairs
and find peace of mind.
Who can I entrust the country to?"
Zhēnggǔ (徵古) replied:
"Duke Sòng (宋公)
is the founder of the state.
If Your Majesty is weary of state affairs,
why not hand over the entire country to him?"
Jué (覺) said:
"Your Majesty resides deep within the palace.
All state affairs are entrusted to Duke Sòng (宋公),
who acts first and reports later.
We ministers occasionally attend upon Your Majesty
to discuss Buddhism and Daoism."
The Táng (唐) ruler was displeased in his heart
and immediately ordered Chén Qiáo (陳喬) of Yùzhāng (豫章), a Secretariat Drafter, to draft an edict for this purpose.
Hóngzhōu (洪州) was Yùzhāng Jùn (豫章郡).
He said:
"Once Your Majesty signs this edict,
I will no longer be able to see you!"
Then he strongly argued against its feasibility.
The Táng (唐) ruler smiled and said:
"You also know it's wrong?"
And then stopped.
Consequently, when the King of Jìn (晉王) was sent out to govern a region,
Zhēnggǔ (徵古) was made his deputy.
This event is seen above.
He was also dismissed from his close court positions.
Zhōng Mó (鍾謨) had always been on good terms with Lǐ Démíng (李德明).
Because of Démíng’s (德明) death, he resented Qíqiū (齊丘);
Lǐ Démíng’s (李德明) death is seen in the previous scroll, third year.
He spoke to the Táng (唐) ruler, saying:
"Qíqiū (齊丘), taking advantage of the country's danger,
hastily planned usurpation.
Chén Jué (陳覺) and Lǐ Zhēnggǔ (李徵古) served as his wings.
This is intolerable by reason."
Chén Jué’s (陳覺) return from Zhōu (周) is seen above, in the third month.
"I hear that Jiāngnán (江南) has repeatedly defied orders for several years,
all due to the schemes of Chancellor Yán Xù (嚴續).
He should be executed for me."
The Táng (唐) ruler knew that Jué (覺) had a long-standing feud with Xù (續),
and therefore did not believe him.
Zhōng Mó (鍾謨) requested to verify this in Zhōu (周),
to verify the truthfulness of his words in Zhōu (周).
He stated:
"My long resistance to the royal army
was due to my own foolish confusion,
not Xù’s (續) fault."
The Emperor, hearing this,
was greatly astonished and said:
"If this is truly the case,
then Xù (續) is a loyal minister.
He means that if Yán Xù (嚴續) could indeed devise strategies for his lord to resist Zhōu (周),
he is a loyal minister.
How could I instruct someone to kill a loyal minister?!"
Mó (謨) returned
and reported this to the Táng (唐) ruler.
The Táng (唐) ruler wished to execute Qíqiū (齊丘) and others,
and again sent Mó (謨) to inform the Emperor.
The Emperor, regarding them as ministers of another state,
offered no judgment.
On the day Jǐhài (己亥),
the Táng (唐) ruler ordered Yīn Chóngyì (殷崇義), Administrator of the Privy Council, to draft an edict exposing the crimes of Qíqiū (齊丘), Jué (覺), and Zhēnggǔ (徵古).
Qíqiū (齊丘) was permitted to return to his old hermitage on Jiǔhuá Shān (九華山),
with all his official titles and ranks remaining as before;
Sòng Qíqiū (宋齊丘) resided in seclusion on Jiǔhuá Shān (九华山),
seen in scroll 277, second year of Táng Míngzōng (唐明宗) Chángxīng (長興),
which was the third year of Wú Ruìhuáng (吳睿皇) Tàihé (太和).
Jué (覺) was exiled to Xuānzhōu (宣州);
Zhēnggǔ (徵古) had his official titles and ranks stripped and was granted self-execution;
his partisans were all pardoned.
An envoy was sent to report this to Zhōu (周).
On the day Bǐngwǔ (丙午),
Shǔ (蜀) appointed Gāo Yànchóu (高彥儔), Inspector-General and Director of the Canyon Roads, as General-in-Chief of the Expeditionary Forces.

Ān Yǒujìn (安友進), a servant of Ān Shěnqí (安審琦), the Military Governor of Pínglú (平盧), Grand Preceptor, Grand Chancellor of the Secretariat, and King of Chén (陳王), had an affair with his favorite concubine.
Fearing exposure, the concubine plotted with Yǒujìn (友進) to murder Shěnqí (審琦).
Yǒujìn (友進) refused,
but the concubine said:
"If not,
I will accuse you instead."
Yǒujìn (友進) was afraid and complied.
In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Guǐchǒu (癸丑),
Shěnqí (審琦), deeply intoxicated, was asleep.
The concubine took the sword from under Shěnqí’s (審琦) pillow
and gave it to Yǒujìn (友進), who killed him.
She then killed all the maidservants under the canopy to silence them.
Several days later,
his son Shǒuzhōng (守忠) finally learned of it
and arrested Yǒujìn (友進) and others.
Previously,
officials were about to set up the main court ceremony,
and installed musical instruments the night before in the palace courtyard.
Setting them up the night before is called 'setting in advance' (宿設).
Xuán (縣)
is pronounced xuán;
same below.
Seeing that some bells and chimes were set but not struck,
they asked the musicians,
but none could answer.
So Dòu Yǎn (竇儼) was ordered to study ancient and modern practices
and correct the court music.
Wáng Pú (王朴) was well-versed in music.
The Emperor consulted him about musical matters,
and Pú (朴) submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Ritual restrains external form,
music cultivates the heart;
when external form is orderly,
and the heart is harmonious within,
there has never been a case where the world was not well-governed.
Therefore, when ritual and music are cultivated by the ruler,
the myriad states are transformed below.
The teaching of the sages succeeds without coercion,
and their governance is effective without strictness.
This is recorded as the words of Kǒngzǐ (孔子) in the Xiàojīng (孝經).
Zhì (治),
pronounced as zhílì.
Music originates in the human heart and sounds are formed by objects.
Once object sounds are formed,
they can again move the human heart.
"In ancient times, Huángdì (黃帝) blew a nine-inch pipe
to obtain the true sound of huángzhōng (黃鍾).
Halving it produced the clear sound,
doubling it produced the slow sound.
By a process of 'three-part increment and decrement' (三分損益), he generated the twelve lǜ (律).
Subtracting or adding one-third, generating ascending and descending notes, the twelve lǜ (律) were complete.
This formed one jūn (均).
There are twelve jūn (均) and eighty-four diào (調) in total, making it comprehensive.
After Qín (秦) destroyed scholarship,
few who managed music in successive dynasties were able to use them.
During the reign of Táng Tàizōng (唐太宗),
Zǔ Xiàosūn (祖孝孫) and Zhāng Wénshōu (張文收) corrected the grand music
and completed the eighty-four diào (調);
seen in scroll 192, first year of Zhēngguān (貞觀).
Diào (調),
pronounced as túdiào;
same below.
Eight or nine tenths of the instruments and artisans were lost,
and by the time of Huáng Cháo (黃巢),
they were completely destroyed.
At that time, there was Tàicháng Bóshì (太常博士) Yīn Yíngsūn (殷盈孫),
who, following the Kǎogōng Jì (考工記),
cast twelve bóchóng (鎛鍾)
and two hundred and forty biānzhōng (編鍾).
Large bells are called bóchóng (鎛).
Sixteen small bells arranged on one stand are called biānzhōng (編鍾).
Bó (鎛),
pronounced as bǔgè.
What is currently suspended [in the court] are these.
Although they have the form of bells and chimes,
they utterly lack corresponding harmony.
The bóchóng (鎛鍾) are struck without regard for musical theory,
merely in sequence.
The biānzhōng (編鍾) and biānqìng (編磬) are merely suspended.
The string, wind, gourd, and earthenware instruments only have seven notes,
called the gōng (宮) of huángzhōng (黃鍾).
Of those that remain, there are nine melodies.
Upon examination, three melodies conform to the lǜ (律),
while six melodies involve various other diào (調).
Indeed, the decay and incompleteness of music
have never been worse than today.
Your Majesty's martial achievements are already manifest,
and your intention is directed towards rites and music.
As your servant once studied lǜlǚ,
you displayed ancient and modern music records,
commanding your servant to discuss them.
Your servant, strictly following ancient methods,
used *jùshǔ* to determine the *chǐ*.
A tube nine *cùn* long and three *fēn* in diameter was made for *Huángzhōng*,
which corresponds to the sound of *Huángzhōng* today.
By extending this,
the twelve *lǜ* were derived.
Considering that mutually blowing many tubes
is inconvenient for producing sound,
I made a *lǜzhǔn*
with thirteen strings,
nine *chǐ* long.
The *lǜzhǔn*
is presumably a method left by Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
and Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, in turn, based it on Jīng Fáng.
Pillars were set in sequence,
creating eleven *lǜ*,
and the clear sound of *Huángzhōng*.
Seven *lǜ* were then used to form one *jūn*.
The principal tone of the *jūn*
is *gōng*;
*zhǐ*, *shāng*, *yǔ*, *jiǎo*, *biàngōng*, and *biànzhǐ* follow.
By producing the sound of its principal tone
and returning to the *lǜ* of the original sound,
they respond alternately without disorder,
thereby forming the melodies,
totaling eighty-one melodies.
Pǔ's words say: "By imperial decree, I followed the Zhōu method,
using *jùshǔ* to calibrate and set the standard measurements.
Nine *cùn* in length,
and three *fēn* in inner diameter,
formed the tube for *Huángzhōng*,
corresponding to the sound of *Huángzhōng* currently existing.
By extending this with the method of mutual generation from above and below,
the twelve *lǜ* tubes were obtained.
Considering that mutually blowing many tubes
is inconvenient for producing sound,
I made a *lǜzhǔn*
with thirteen strings for producing sounds.
It is nine *chǐ* long with strings stretched.
Each string is like the sound of *Huángzhōng*.
A pillar is set at six *chǐ* on the eighth string
for *Línzhōng*.
A pillar is set at eight *chǐ* on the third string
for *Tàicù*.
A pillar is set at five *chǐ*, three *cùn*, four *fēn* on the tenth string
for *Nánlǚ*.
A pillar is set at seven *chǐ*, one *cùn*, three *fēn* on the fifth string
for *Gūxǐ*.
A pillar is set at four *chǐ*, seven *cùn*, five *fēn* on the twelfth string
for *Yìngzhōng*.
A pillar is set at six *chǐ*, three *cùn*, three *fēn* on the seventh string
for *Ruíbīn*.
A pillar is set at eight *chǐ*, four *cùn*, four *fēn* on the second string
for *Dàlǚ*.
A pillar is set at five *chǐ*, six *cùn*, three *fēn* on the ninth string
for *Yízé*.
A pillar is set at seven *chǐ*, five *cùn*, one *fēn* on the fourth string
for *Jiázhōng*.
A pillar is set at five *chǐ*, one *cùn* on the eleventh string
for *Wúshè*.
A pillar is set at six *chǐ*, six *cùn*, eight *fēn* on the sixth string
for *Zhōnglǚ*.
A pillar is set at four *chǐ*, five *cùn* on the thirteenth string
for the clear sound of *Huángzhōng*.
Among the twelve sounds,
seven sounds are then used to form a *jūn*.
The principal tone of the *jūn* is solely *gōng*;
*zhǐ*, *shāng*, *yǔ*, *jiǎo*, *biàngōng*, and *biànzhǐ* follow.
By producing the sound of its principal tone
and returning to the *lǜ* of the original sound,
the seven sounds respond alternately without disorder,
thereby forming the melodies.
Each *jūn* has seven melodies,
and there are twelve *jūn* for the sounds,
totaling eighty-four melodies,
from which songs and instrumental pieces emerge.
The sound of *xuángōng* had long been lost,
but was restored in a single day,
derived from my unique insight.
The *Tōngjiàn* briefly recorded its essence,
and now it is fully documented here.
'Derived from my unique insight,
I request that all officials be gathered to review its merits and demerits.' "
The imperial edict followed it.
All the officials agreed,
so they implemented it.
At that time, Zhāng Zhāo (張昭), Minister of War, and others deliberated, saying:
"When Dì Hóng Shì (帝鴻氏) created music in the past,
he observed the wind sounds of the eight seasons
and measured the upright qi (氣) of the four seasons.
The clarity or turbidity of qi cannot be imparted by writing,
and the quality of sound cannot be transmitted by word of mouth.
Therefore, Fú Shì (鳧氏) cast bells,
Líng Lún (伶倫) cut bamboo,
to calculate the mutually generative lǜlǚ (律呂)
and the perfectly harmonious sounds of gōngshāng (宮商).
These were then broadcast through wind and string instruments
and proclaimed through bells and lithophones.
Only then did the sentiments of Heaven and Earth harmonize,
and the qi of yin and yang become one.
The eight qì (氣) followed the lǜ (律) without deviation,
and the five sounds formed patterns without disorder.
The melodies of Kōngsāng (空桑) and Gūzhú (孤竹) were sufficient to ritualize the spirits,
and the forms of Yúnmén (雲門) and Dàxià (大夏) perfectly embodied virtue.
However, the lunar lǜ (律) had the method of xuán'gōng (旋宮),
which was fully understood by the office of Tàishī (太師).
After Qín (秦) destroyed scholarship,
the refined way declined.
What the Zhì Shì (制氏) in early Hàn (漢) regulated
only preserved drumming and dancing,
and the method of xuán'gōng (旋宮)'s twelve jùn (均) being used interchangeably
was unknown to the world.
During the reign of Hàn Yuán Dì (漢元帝),
Jīng Fáng (京房), who was skilled in the Yì (易) and discerning sounds,
explored ancient meanings.
Using the jùn (均) method of the Zhōu Guān (周官),
each month he used the five sounds interchangeably,
eventually achieving accurate tuning.
By rotating the palace notes (gōng 宮),
he formed sixty tunes.
He also analyzed the day method into three hundred and sixty parts,
which was transmitted to the Yuèfǔ (樂府).
The arranged suspensions were restored,
and the lǜlǚ (律呂) had no discrepancies.
Upon the decline of Hàn (漢) in the middle period,
the refined music was lost and incomplete.
Though there were repeated mentions of Jīng Fáng's (京房) lǜzhǔn (律準),
the matter was never completed.
Qián Lè (錢樂) merely recorded its name,
and Shěn Chóng (沈重) only listed its theories.
The sixty lǜ (律) methods
became desolate and were not continued.
Liáng Wǔ Dì (梁武帝) was deeply skilled in music theory.
He personally created four-hole and twelve-hole flutes to describe the eight sounds.
He also introduced the ancient five primary and two changing sounds,
rotating them as the palace note (gōng 宮),
obtaining eighty-four tunes.
These were identical in sound but different in number from the tunes regulated by the lǜzhǔn (律準).
During Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) rebellion,
his music was again lost.
When the Suí (隋) dynasty first established refined music,
factions obstructed the discussions,
and it was not completed for years.
However, Pèi Gōng (沛公) Zhèng Yì (鄭譯), using the seven sounds of the Kūchē (龜茲) pipa, matched the lunar lǜ (律).
The five primary and two changing sounds,
making seven perfectly harmonious tunes,
by rotating them as the palace note (gōng 宮),
again formed eighty-four tunes.
The artisan Wàn Bǎocháng (萬寶常) further reduced the number of strings,
making the sound somewhat ancient and pure.
Suí Gāo Zǔ (隋高祖) did not value refined music.
He ordered his officials to gather and discuss,
and the scholar Hé Tuǒ (何妥) submitted a refuting memorial,
causing all eighty-four tunes proposed by Zhèng (鄭) and Wàn (萬) to be abolished.
The music played in the Suí (隋) dynasty's suburban temples
consisted only of the huángzhōng (黃鍾) jùn (均),
and when welcoming the qi (氣) at the five suburban altars,
ruíbīn (蕤賓) was mixed in,
but only seven tunes were used.
The other five bells
were suspended but not played.
For court banquets over three reigns,
nine sets of informal music were used.
Until the revolution,
this could not be changed.

Táng Tài Zōng (唐太宗) then ordered old artisans Zǔ Xiàosūn (祖孝孫) and Zhāng Wénshōu (張文收) to organize and compare the seventy-seven tunes and eighty-four melodies regulated by Zhèng Yì (鄭譯) and Bǎocháng (寶常).
Only then were string and wind instruments used together,
and bells and lithophones played in unison.
The sounds of the seven origins were revived,
and the melodies of the four sides were all in harmony.
Since the An-Shi Rebellion and the overthrow of Xián Qín (咸秦),
instruments with carved teeth and feathered banners
were completely swept away.
Artisans who struck and beat instruments
did not continue for years.
The music played in suburban temples
was no different from the Southern Dipper,
lost and unrecoverable,
and those who understood music were almost extinct.
We, your ministers, humbly believe that the origin of sound
comes from the human heart.
Kuí (夔) and Kuàng (曠) cannot live forever,
and human affairs cannot always be peaceful.
When people die, sounds cease;
when the world is in chaos, music collapses.
If one does not understand the essence of ritual and music,
how can one comprehend the fundamentals of their creation!
We, your ministers, based on the memorial submitted by Pú Shì (樞密使) Wáng Pú (王朴),
adopted Jīng Fáng's (京房) tuning method,
refined Liáng Wǔ Dì's (梁武帝) comprehensive sounds,
examined the seventy-seven tunes of Zhèng Yì (鄭譯) and Bǎocháng (寶常),
and checked the nine changes of Xiàosūn (孝孫) and Wénshōu (文收).
We measured by accumulating millet grains to determine their pitch,
and listened to musical poems to ascertain their sentiment.
Following the previous texts on weights and measures,
we grasped the main idea of comprehensively numerous and harmonious sounds,
applied it to bell stands,
and it was sufficient to harmonize with xiāosháo (簫韶) music.

On the nineteenth day of this month, we, your ministers, assembled at the Tàicháng Sì (太常寺) and ordered Tàiyuè Lìng (太樂令) Jiǎ Jùn (賈峻) to play Wáng Pú's (王朴) new method of huángzhōng (黃鍾) tune and seventy-seven melodies.
The pitch and rhythm were harmonious,
not clashing with each other.
As for the remaining eleven pipes and various tunes,
we request that they be taught and practiced according to the new method,
to be used by the ritual department.
The great ceremonies for the Five Suburban Altars, Heaven and Earth, Ancestral Temples, Altars of Soil and Grain, and the Three Courts,
which require the use of twelve pipes and various tunes,
are recorded in the Táng Shǐ (唐史) and Kāiyuán Lǐ (開元禮)
and have been regularly performed in recent times.
In the Guǎngshùn (廣順) era,
Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿) Biān Wèi (邊蔚) was commanded to set the names of dances, musical pieces, and lyrics for the aforementioned sacrifices, festivals, and court assemblies.
The temple administration should have records.
We are concerned that what was set may not harmonize in tune and rhythm with the new method.
We request that the Tàicháng Sì (太常寺) be ordered to inspect and test them.
If there are discrepancies,
we request that the temple, according to the tunes and rhythms of the new method,
compose new musical scores and dance pieces,
and have the singers practice them."
This was followed.
Sòng Qíqiū (宋齊丘) arrived at Jiǔhuá Shān (九華山).
The Lord of Táng (唐) ordered his residence to be locked,
and food and drink to be supplied through a hole in the wall.
Qíqiū (齊丘) sighed, saying:
"In the past, I offered a scheme to secretly yield the emperor's clan to Tàizhōu (泰州).
This event is recorded in volume 281, Jìn (晉) Tiānfú (天福) second year."
Then he hanged himself and died.
A differing account states: The Jiāngbiǎo Zhì (江表志) says:
"Qíqiū (齊丘) arrived at Qīngyáng (青陽),
abstained from food for several days,
and his family also looked sickly.
An imperial envoy said: 'When the Duke has passed away,
then food will be supplied.'
His family plugged his mouth with cotton floss, and he died."
Today, we follow the Jiāngnán Lù (江南錄) and Jìnián (紀年).
Initially, Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士) Cháng Mèngxī (常夢錫), who was in charge of the Xuānzhèng Yuàn (宣政院),
participated in state affairs.
He deeply resented Qíqiū's (齊丘) faction,
and repeatedly told the Lord of Táng (唐):
"If this group is not removed,
the state will surely be in peril and perish."
He frequently argued with Fēng Yánjǐ (馮延己), Wèi Cén (魏岑), and their ilk.
After a long time,
the Xuānzhèng Yuàn (宣政院) was abolished.
Mèngxī (夢錫) was dejected and discontent,
no longer involved in affairs.
He succumbed to illness due to excessive drinking and died.
The Tōngjiàn (通鑑) volume 285, Jìn (晉) Qí Wáng (齊王) Kāiyùn (開運) third year,
already recorded Cháng Mèngxī's (常夢錫) excessive drinking.
Last year, it also recorded Mèngxī (夢錫) mocking Fēng Yánjǐ's (馮延己) faction.
Indeed, he had been drinking excessively for more than a day;
after a long time, he developed an illness and died.
The Lord of Táng (唐) said:
"Cháng Mèngxī (常夢錫) wanted to kill Qíqiū (齊丘) his whole life.
It's a pity he didn't live to see it!"

The Emperor said:

The great principle between Our nation and yours is established,

repair your armor and weapons,

"I heard that the Mǎ clan's enterprise

The Emperor wished to appoint Privy Councilor Wèi Rénpǔ as chancellor.
Objectors argued that Rénpǔ had not entered officialdom through the imperial examinations
and thus could not be chancellor.
(Wèi Rénpǔ rose through the ranks from a clerk in the Privy Council to Privy Councilor.)
"Since ancient times, those with literary and military talents have been appointed as輔佐 (fǔzuǒ) (assistants),
why must they all come through the imperial examinations?"
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Wáng Pǔ was promoted to Menxià Shìláng (Palace Attendant)
and, along with Fàn Zhì, became a participant in Privy Council affairs.
Rénpǔ was made Zhōngshū Shìláng (Grand Imperial Secretary) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (Chancellor with Equal Authority),
his position as Privy Councilor remaining unchanged.
Although Rénpǔ held a powerful position, he was modest and prudent.
The Emperor's temperament was severe and impatient,
and when close officials offended him,
Rénpǔ often took the blame upon himself to save them.
He saved seven or eight out of ten lives,
so although he started as a scribe
and rose to the position of chancellor,
people at the time did not consider it an impropriety.
Furthermore, Wú Yánzuò, the Commissioner of the Southern Bureau of the Department of Imperial Insignia, was appointed Left Galloping Guard Grand General,
and also served as Privy Councilor;
Hán Tōng, Military Commissioner of Guīdé and Imperial Army Commander, and Zhāng Yǒngdé, Military Commissioner of Zhènníng and Palace Army Inspector-General, were both promoted to Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and Tōng was also appointed Deputy Commander of the Imperial Army;
Emperor Tàizǔ was appointed concurrent Palace Army Inspector-General.
The Emperor once asked Zhāng Zhāo, Minister of War, about ministers suitable for chancellorship.
Zhāo recommended Lǐ Tāo.
The Emperor was astonished and said:
"Tāo is frivolous and lacks the demeanor of a great minister.
I asked about chancellors, and you immediately recommended him, why?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty blames him for minor conduct,
but what your servant commends is his great integrity.
In the time of Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn,
Zhāng Yànzé cruelly killed innocent people.
Tāo repeatedly memorialized to have him executed,
believing that if he were not killed, he would become a national calamity.
(See Volume 283, Jìn Gāozǔ, Tiānfú Period, Year 1.)
Tāo also submitted a memorial requesting to relieve the late emperor's military authority.
(See Volume 288, Hàn Yǐndì, Qiányòu Period, Year 1.)
This is truly the caliber of a chancellor,
which is why your servant recommended him."
The Emperor said:
"Your words are very good and utterly impartial.
However, a person like Tāo
can ultimately not be placed in the Central Secretariat."
Tāo was fond of humor,
and disregarded conventions.
He and his brother, Huàn, were both famous for their literary talent.
Although they were very affectionate,
they were often playful and disrespectful,
lacking the proper decorum for age differences.
The Emperor thus slighted him.

On the day Guǐsì,
the Emperor's illness worsened.
He summoned Fàn Zhì and others to receive his dying wishes.

Zhì and the others left
and said to each other:

Be careful not to reveal these words."
On that day,
the Emperor died.
He was thirty-nine years old.
When the Emperor Shìzōng was still in the imperial household,
he often concealed his abilities and intentions.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
he crushed the rebels of Gāopíng,
as recorded in Volume 291, Year 1.
In commanding his army,
his orders and prohibitions were strict and clear;
no one dared to violate them.
When attacking cities or facing enemies,
arrows and stones would fall to his left and right,
and although others lost color, the Emperor barely changed his expression.
He made decisions and responded to situations
in ways that surprised everyone.
He was also diligent in governing,
remembering every detail of
the registers and records of the various offices upon seeing them,
exposing evil and uncovering hidden schemes,
with divine insight and perceptiveness.
In his leisure, he would summon Confucian scholars to read historical records,
discussing the great principles.
He was not fond of music, silks, or precious objects.
He often said that Taìzǔ had allowed Wáng Jùn and Wáng Yīn to become corrupt,
leading to the failure of the relationship between sovereign and minister.
He demoted Wáng Jùn and
executed Wáng Yīn,
as recorded in Volume 291, Taìzǔ, Guǎngshùn 3rd year.
(Fēn,
pronounced Fú Wèn.)
If they submitted, he pardoned them;
if they had merits, he richly rewarded them.
He employed both civil and military officials,
each to their full ability,
and everyone feared his perceptiveness while cherishing his kindness.
Therefore, he was able to defeat enemies and expand territory,
invincible in all directions.
However, his application of law was too strict.
If an official was slightly remiss in their duties,
they were often given the extreme penalty.
Even those with established talent and reputation
were not pardoned.
Soon after, he regretted this,
and in his later years, he gradually became more lenient.

Your servant Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光) states: Formerly, I received an imperial edict to compile the deeds of monarchs and ministers throughout history.
I also received a sacred decree bestowing the name Zīzhì Tōngjiàn (資治通鑑).
It is now completed.
I, your humble servant, am of foolish and dull disposition,
my scholarship is neglected and deficient.
In all my undertakings,
I fall short of others.
Only in previous histories
have I roughly exerted myself,
from youth to old age,
I have delighted in them without satiety.
I have always been troubled that since [Sīmǎ] Qiān and [Bān] Gù,
writings have become excessively numerous,
so much so that even common scholars
cannot read them all,
let alone a sovereign
who has myriad affairs to attend to daily;
how can they have leisure to peruse them thoroughly?
I often, not knowing my own limitations,
wished to abridge and condense
and extract the crucial points,
focusing solely on matters concerning the rise and fall of states,
and the well-being and suffering of the people,
those good deeds that can serve as models,
and evil deeds that can serve as warnings.
I wished to compile a chronicle,
so that events would follow in proper sequence,
and the essential and the trivial would not be mixed.
However, my private resources were meager,
and there was no way I could accomplish it.
Then, I had the honor of meeting Emperor Yīngzōng,
who possessed an intelligent and sagacious nature,
and displayed a civilized and enlightened reign.
Desiring to survey ancient affairs
to expand great policies,
he issued an edict to me,
commanding me to compile it.
My long-cherished wish
was thus fulfilled in a single day.
I accepted with joyful trepidation,
fearing only that I might not be worthy.
The late emperor also ordered me to select my own officials,
established a bureau in the Chóngwén Yuàn,
allowed me to borrow books from the Lóngtú, Tiānzhāng Gé, Sān Guǎn, and Mì Gé,
bestowed upon me imperial brushes, ink, silk, and imperial money for fruits and sweets,
and appointed an internal eunuch as supervisor.
The honor of such favor
was unsurpassed among close ministers.
Unfortunately, before the book could be presented to the emperor,
the late emperor passed away, abandoning his humble servant.
Your Majesty, succeeding to the great imperial lineage,
respectfully continued the former emperor's wishes,
honored [the book] with a preface,
and bestowed upon it an auspicious name.
Whenever the Jīngyán lectures were held,
you always commanded it to be presented and read.
Although I am dull and foolish,
having received such profound trust and favor from both emperors,
even if I were to perish and lose my head,
it would not be enough to repay it.
If my intellect and strength allow,
how dare I neglect anything!
Later, I was dispatched as the Administrator of Yǒngxīng Jūn,
but due to old age and illness, I was unfit for demanding administrative duties,
and I requested to remain in the capital.
Your Majesty graciously acceded to my wish,
and generously allowed me to recuperate,
appointing me concurrently as the Administrator of the Xījīng Liúsī Yùshǐ Tái and the Director of the Xījīng Sōngshān Chóngfú Gōng.
Through six successive appointments,
I was still permitted to keep the historical bureau with me,
and was granted a stipend and rank,
without being held accountable for official duties.
Since I had no other obligations,
I was able to devote my full concentration and exhaust my thoughts,
pouring out all my resources.
Daytime hours were insufficient,
so I continued into the night.
I thoroughly reviewed old histories,
and extensively collected from minor accounts.
The pile of documents was enormous,
vast as a smoky sea.
I delved into the obscure and hidden,
and meticulously verified every detail.
Starting from the Warring States period
and ending with the Five Dynasties,
a total of 1362 years,
I completed 294 volumes.
Furthermore, I briefly listed the events,
arranged by year and interwoven with national affairs,
to facilitate searching,
compiling 30 volumes of a table of contents.
I also referenced various other books,
critiquing their similarities and differences,
to reconcile them into a unified account,
compiling 30 volumes of "Examination of Differences" (Kǎoyì), totaling 354 volumes.
From the establishment of the bureau in the Zhìpíng era
until its completion today,
many years have passed.
Any discrepancies within it,
I dare not vouch for.
The gravity of my shortcomings and offenses
is indeed inescapable.
I, Sīmǎ Guāng, am truly filled with awe and trepidation,
and kowtow repeatedly.
I reflect again that I have been away from the imperial court
for fifteen years.
Although my body is in the outer regions,
my humble heart,
day and night, waking and sleeping,
has never been absent from Your Majesty's side!
Considering my limited talent and lack of ability,
I am suitable for nothing.
Therefore, I have dedicated myself solely to writing,
to repay Your great kindness.
I hope to contribute a drop of dust,
to slightly aid the great mountains and seas.
Now my bones are emaciated and frail,
my eyesight is dim and near-sighted,
my teeth are few,
and my mind and consciousness are decaying.
What I do immediately
is forgotten in an instant.
My vital energy
has been entirely expended on this book.
I humbly implore Your Majesty to pardon the offense of my presumptuous work,
and to discern my intention of loyalty.
In your moments of leisure,
please deign to peruse it,
to observe the rise and fall of past generations,
to examine the successes and failures of the present,
to commend the good and pity the evil,
to adopt the right and reject the wrong.
This will be sufficient to advance your splendid virtue of investigating antiquity,
and to attain an unparalleled reign of ultimate peace.
May all living beings within the four seas
uniformly partake in its blessings.
Then, even if I lay my bones in the netherworld,
my lifelong aspiration will be eternally fulfilled.
Respectfully I present this memorial to report the completion.
I, Sīmǎ Guāng, am truly filled with awe and trepidation,
and kowtow repeatedly.
I humbly speak.

Imperial Edict of Commendation
Edict to Sīmǎ Guāng: On the completion of the compilation of the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.
Historical scholarship has long been in decline;
its arrangement is disorderly,
its discussions unclear,
how can it serve to admonish and encourage,
or clarify for future generations!
You are broadly learned and widely read,
comprehending both ancient and modern times.
From the late Zhōu [Dynasty]
down to the Five Dynasties,
you have elucidated and organized,
completing a unique historical work.
Your praises and criticisms, choices and rejections,
are all well-substantiated.
Since reviewing it,
I am deeply filled with admiration!
Now I bestow upon you silver and silk, a set of clothing, a belt, a saddle and bridle, and a horse,
as itemized in the separate record.
You may receive them.
This commendation is hereby given,
you should be fully aware.
As winter is cold,
I hope you are well.
This letter
does not convey much else.
